Course Notes — SESSION 1
THE GENERAL PROBLEM OF INTELLIGENCE: CREDIT ASSIGNMENT
In the Course Introduction, we laid out a view of AI and organizations as direct analogs.
Intelligence in either was seen as the ability to learn to solve complex problems to pursue
goals. Before we start to explore this analogy, however, we need to agree on some ways of
talking about what we actually mean by “learning” and “complex problems”. To do so, this
week’s course notes provide a precise yet general way to talk about learning in AI and
organizations called credit assignment that we can use throughout the semester. The notes also
provide intuition on what we mean by a “complex” problem. We will unpack complexity more
precisely in subsequent sessions.
Before we begin, you should note that current AI discourse you may be familiar with mostly
talks about learning too narrowly for the purposes of our course — as a specific set of
technologies called “machine learning”. Machine learning technologies typically learn statistical
patterns from large volumes of data, for the purposes of making statistical predictions. Large
language models (LLMs), for example, learn statistical patterns in text data to solve problems of
predicting new text to generate. In organizations, these machine learning technologies are often
viewed in narrow economic terms as “prediction machines” that lower managers’ costs of
prediction (Aggrawal, Gans & Goldfarb 2018; 2024).
Most foundational AI ideas are about learning patterns other than statistical patterns. And their
analogs in organizations are interpretive processes that go beyond statistical prediction. To
explore the full range of foundational AI ideas and their relationship to organizations, we will
have to step outside of the gravitational pull of the currently-popular “prediction machine” view
of AI. We need a general way of talking about learning any patterns that might be helpful to
solving complex problems intelligently.
Founders of AI referred to this general problem of intelligence as that of learning to assign
credit (Samuel 1959; Minsky 1961; Holland 1975). Credit assignment refers to any process for
evaluating (“assigning credit” to) effects of individual actions on solving a problem. In LLMs,
individual actions are generating text fragments. Credit is assigned using statistical predictions to
evaluate whether fragments are good.
During the course, we will look at many other actions and evaluation mechanisms beyond those
considered in LLMs or machine learning. For this week, our purpose is to develop a nuanced
understanding of the idea of credit assignment so that we have a shared, general way of talking
about learning across diverse AI ideas and analogous phenomena in organizations. We will do so
by looking at two paradigmatically-different learning strategies in AI and organizations, one
called reinforcement learning and the other called learning in a “society”. Exploring and

debating tensions among these paradigms (or alternatives to either) as they relate to the general
problem of credit assignment will be a focus of our journey throughout this course.

1. Introducing the credit assignment problem
To introduce the credit assignment problem, let us first consider a few common examples of
learning to solve problems in organizations.
(1)​A new shipbuilding company is formed1. It takes them a much longer time to build their
first ship than their competitors, and the ship has many defects. They build their second
ship, which takes them slightly less time and has fewer defects. Many years later, having
built hundreds of ships, management claims to have “learned” to make them faster and
with fewer defects than its competitors. Yet how did management know which changes to
the vast number of interdependent actions in the shipbuilding factory actually caused
faster production speed and fewer defects, versus which were merely correlated?
(2)​An app development team wants to improve the usability of a social media app2. The
team brainstorms a set of possible features that users might like. They evaluate each one
using “A/B testing”, in which users are randomly given the app with a feature (version A)
or without it (version B). By launch time, the team claims to have “learned” the optimal
app features that its users want. Yet how could they tell whether they learned the features
of a social media app that users actually want, or just which features users relatively want
among the ones that they tested?
(3)​A budgeting committee3 for a pharmaceutical company meets at the beginning of every
quarter to decide how to allocate the marketing budget across business units responsible
for different drug categories. The committee allocates their budget based on information
about each business unit’s sales for the previous quarter, as well as by talking to business
unit heads and reading reports about market trends in the industry. After several years and
many quarterly meetings, sales consistently increase. The committee claims to have
“learned” how to allocate the budget effectively. Yet many business unit heads believe
sales would have grown even more if more budget had been allocated to their units.
1.1 Individual actions as “generate-and-test” processes
What should you take away from these examples? For one, they embed some shared building
blocks of individual actions that we can use for talking about credit assignment across any AI
idea or organizational theory. As depicted in Figure 1 below, all three examples involved (1)
goal-directed agents who (2) generated actions (3) tested the effects of actions on goals using
(4) trial-and-error feedback, and used this feedback to (5) modify actions.

The agents were shipbuilding workers of managers, app team developers, or budget committee
members; their goals were reducing costs and defects when building a ship, improving the
features of a social media app, or increasing sales across business units. Actions generated
included building ships, experimenting with app features, and allocating quarterly budgets.
Testing meant using feedback to assign credit to the generated actions according to their effects
on goals. Feedback included data on ship defects, on how users engaged with app features, or on
business unit sales figures. Modifications of actions were refinements to shipbuilding techniques,
adding or removing app features, or changes to business unit budgets.

text_units.section: 1.2 Credit assignment as the problem of generating intermediate feedback
text_units.text:
1.2 Credit assignment as the problem of generating intermediate feedback
The three examples also embed the concept of assigning credit — that of learning to evaluate the
effects of individual actions on solving a problem — as one of effectively using feedback to
modify subsequent actions. Testing the effects of any particular action (e.g., choices of
shipbuilding techniques, app features, or business unit budgets) on a goal required understanding
how it depended on other actions. We will refer to this requirement as the challenge of assigning
credit arising from the interdependence of actions. Further, the examples all show how “tests”
of actions do not necessarily provide adequate feedback for evaluating them. Feedback about
goals (e.g., ship defects, user issues with the app, or changes in pharmaceutical sales) was either
delayed until well after actions were generated, or ambiguous. While the organizations
“learned” something through the process depicted in Figure 1, there was no easy way to know
whether they learned the right things due to these challenges of assigning credit of delayed and
ambiguous feedback regarding interdependent actions.
The shape of the general solution to challenges of credit assignment was initially described by
the IBM scientist Arthur Samuel in 1959 regarding his pioneering AI program for learning to
play the game of checkers. Good checkers players, Samuel noted, do not wait until the end of a
game to assign credit to sequences of interdependent actions (moves). During a game, they count
the number of pieces left, and monitor how the pieces are distributed across the board to evaluate
how they are doing. The number and distribution of pieces are proxies indicating progress
towards a goal. Samuel called the evaluation of such proxies the use of “intermediate
feedback” to assign credit.
3

text_units.section: 1.2 Credit assignment as the problem of generating intermediate feedback
text_units.text:
Solutions to the credit assignment problem, Samuel argued, are generally of this form: they are
ways of generating-and-testing various types of intermediate feedback. As examples, the
shipbuilding company may have counted the number of defects in particular parts; the app
development team may have defined key performance indicators (KPIs) for each step of a
customer “journey”; the budgeting team may have set milestones for business units and required
periodic reports from them.
Samuel’s checkers program generated-and-tested various sources of intermediate feedback under
one paradigm that has become known in the AI field as reinforcement learning. In a famous 1961
agenda-setting paper for the AI field, Marvin Minsky, co-founder of the MIT AI lab, disagreed
that reinforcement or similar strategies offers a general solution to assigning credit. He proposed
a distinct paradigm he called learning in a “society of mind”. Next, we explore these two
paradigms, both to better understand the idea of credit assignment and to encourage you to start
to think critically about the diverse types of solutions to the problem that may be possible.

text_units.section: 2. Paradigm 1: assigning credit by reinforcement learning
text_units.text:
2. Paradigm 1: assigning credit by reinforcement learning
In reinforcement learning, an agent assigns credit simply by “reinforcing” actions that seem to
have the effect of getting it closer to its goal. Any such effects of actions on goals are called
rewards. The overall goal in reinforcement learning is to “maximize rewards”. This view of an
AI agent is similar to a utility-maximizing individual in microeconomics4. By seeing how the
process of reinforcing and maximizing rewards operates, you will get a basic feel for the
dynamics of credit assignment, and of how economic (as distinct from organizational) ideas may
more generally run into limits as ways of generating intermediate feedback.
Let us first put the above description a bit more formally. Reinforcement means that, when an
action leads to a reward, credit is assigned to this action by increasing the probability that it
will be generated the next time. We will call these probabilities for generating actions “beliefs”,
in that they capture not facts about reality per se, so much as an estimate by some agent of how
much credit individual actions should get based on whatever intermediate feedback the agent has
received so far. The amount of credit that the agent assigns to an action — the amount that the
probabilities of generating an action are modified when a reward is received — is based on what
is called the agent’s policy. Put another way, a policy5 in reinforcement learning is a set of rules
defining how to update probabilities of beliefs about actions.
4

text_units.section: 2. Paradigm 1: assigning credit by reinforcement learning
text_units.text:
The similarity of rewards to microeconomic utility functions arises from later integration (from the late 1970s) into
reinforcement learning models of econometric techniques from operations management (Sutton & Barto 2015, Ch.
1; Mirowski 2003). I will use the terms “reinforcement” and “rewards” here with some reluctance, in deference to
their current familiarity. Samuel’s (1959) and earlier foundational studies in this area (e.g., Shannon 1950) make no
mention of either term, and were based on electrical and software engineering models rather than econometrics.
5
A policy in reinforcement learning in AI is the same concept of a policy used in formal models of decision-making
in fields such as political science, economics, and management theory.

text_units.text:
Hence, learning to assign credit here refers to updating (i.e., modifying) the probabilities for
generating actions as trial-and-error feedback accumulates. The policy refers to the amount of
updating after each action, called a learning rate, that ranges from 0 to 1, and which is
multiplied by the prior belief (probability) to get the new belief. This learning rate can be
different for “successful” actions that increase rewards versus “unsuccessful” actions that
decrease rewards6. Hence, in reinforcement learning, learning can be expressed as follows:

2.1 Navigating a T-maze
To concretize the above discussion, let us first look at the use of reinforcement to assign credit in
a simple problem. In fact, let us look at perhaps the simplest type of reinforcement learning
problem, in which the policy concerns how to assign credit among just two possible actions.
Imagine a mouse who generates actions in a T-shaped “maze”7 (i.e., the simplest kind of maze
we can think of) to find cheese as a reward, as depicted in Figure 2. The mouse is placed at the
bottom of the maze, and looks for cheese once a day for 1,000 days, with a goal of maximizing
the amount of cheese it eats. It can take only one of two possible actions, turn left or right. The
left hand “goal-box” and the right hand “goal-box” of the T-maze are hermetically sealed, so that
the mouse cannot get “feedback” from smelling the cheese until after generating a “left” or
“right” action. Imagine that each day, a human manager of the maze decides where to place the
cheese by flipping a coin, where Heads = Left, and Tails = Right. Further, imagine a coin that is
weighted on one side so that the average number of “heads” for 1000 tosses will be 700 (70%)
and the average number of “tails” will be 300 (30%).

A well-known finding in research on organizational learning is that failed trials are more likely to induce a change
in actions, with successes more likely to encourage maintaining the status quo.
7

FIGURE 2: A T-maze (Lave & March 1975: p. 250).

The mouse’s “policy” should be to go left every time, as going left will always be more likely
(70% versus 30%) to have cheese. Yet on Day 1, the mouse has no feedback to believe that left is
different from right — that is, it has no basis to assign credit either to the action of going left or
to the action of going right. Its best policy is to act randomly — to go left 50% of the time and
right 50% of the time. Now, imagine the mouse randomly goes left and finds the cheese. What
does it do on Day 2? The key idea is that, rather than suddenly go left 100% of the time, it
realizes that the feedback from Day 1 is really only intermediate. That is, it has a credit
assignment problem. It knows that the human maze manager may not make things so simple.
Instead, our mouse designs a policy of using a learning rate that updates (increases or
decreases) probabilities of generating a left or right action in the next trial.
To avoid updating probabilities beyond 100%, we need to assume that the mouse’s learning rate
is only proportionate to whatever is left to learn (Lave & March 1975: 254). For example, if the
initial beliefs (probabilities) are 50% left and 50% right, then we will say that the mouse has 50%
more to learn. Under a 10% learning rate of going left, and assuming left is rewarded, then the
probability for trial 2 will be updated by 0.5 + (0.1(1-0.5)), or 5%, and the new belief will be
55%. As shown in Table 1 below, for both 10% or 30% learning rates, updates get progressively
smaller as the amount left to learn is reduced. Note in both columns of Table 1 that, while the
mouse’s policy still is not optimal after eight trials, it has at least “reinforced” actions that are
closer. After 1,000 days of updating its beliefs through trial-and-error for either learning rate, the
mouse will likely have enough feedback to have not just updated its beliefs, but to have
“learned” a policy simply to go left 100% of the time, maximizing its reward of cheese.

Since the mouse seems to have the ability to learn to eventually solve the T-maze problem under
either learning rate, should we call it “intelligent”? Let us leave aside whether a T-maze is too
simple to be a true test of intelligence. Instead, the general way in reinforcement learning of
thinking about this question is to start by assuming that feedback is costly (again, note the close
ties here to economics — here, the scarce resource to be “economized” is that of doing a trial to
get more feedback). Hence, intelligence requires policies that balance the need to assign credit to
beliefs efficiently, not just effectively.
Compare, for example, how the learning rates in Table 1 change the efficiency and effectiveness
of updating the mouse’s probability of going left. Under the 10% learning rate, even if credit is
assigned ineffectively for any particular trial (i.e., the mouse gets a reward for going right), it
will result in only small updates to the probabilities. This conservatism requires an inefficiently
large number of trials to assign credit effectively (i.e., to identify the policy of going left 100% of
the time that will maximize rewards). Conversely, under the 30% learning rate, if credit is
assigned accurately initially, the mouse efficiently updates its beliefs rapidly in the right
direction. This boldness, however, carries the risk that, if the wrong actions happen to be
rewarded early on, then the mouse may assign credit ineffectively, and its beliefs may rapidly
converge in the wrong direction. Alternatively, a high learning rate may lead its beliefs to
fluctuate wildly and never converge on the policy that maximizes rewards.
AI and organizational researchers call a policy of using a low learning rate exploitation, in that it
“exploits” learning based on prior trial-and-error actions (rather than rapidly “forgetting” this
learning by making sudden large updates to beliefs). Conversely, they call a policy of using a
high learning rate as exploration, in that making large updates amounts to taking a risk on a new
belief without much basis in prior feedback, and then seeing if it works. The need to balance the
efficiency and effectiveness of these policies is famously called the exploration-exploitation
tradeoff. This tradeoff frames the solution to the fundamental problem of credit assignment in
our first AI idea. In reinforcement learning, the solution is simply to design a policy (learning
rate) that balances the trial-and-error exploration and exploitation of beliefs.
2.2 Navigating two, interdependent T-mazes
Next, imagine that our mouse instead has to navigate two T-mazes, as depicted in Figure 2 below,
and where the cheese is only placed in the second one. The mouse now has to assign credit to
two sets of interdependent beliefs instead of one. That is, it has to update probabilities for going
left or right in the first T-maze and in the second T-maze. The key idea here is that the credit

assignment problem is not just twice as hard! The second T-maze in fact is itself really two
different ones, depending on the sequence of actions taken in the first T-maze. By adding just a
single action to our T-maze, we ended up with four paths of actions to which to assign credit.
You should see that continuing to add a third and fourth T-maze would make things far more
challenging still.
FIGURE 2: Two t-mazes increases complexity combinatorially

More precisely, a linear increase in interdependent actions leads to a combinatorial increase in
the cost of trial-and-error learning. In fact, it can be formally shown that even small increases in
the number of interdependent actions, measured as the combinatorial complexity of a problem,
overwhelm the effectiveness of trial-and-error learning policies such as those in Table 1. This is
called combinatorial explosion. Combinatorial explosion helps explain why our three
organizations struggled to assign credit to what they had learned. Lacking enough intermediate
feedback about interdependent actions, they could not tell if the beliefs they reinforced about
these actions were true or just “superstitious”. This phenomenon — reinforcing beliefs without
enough feedback to assign credit — is called superstitious learning (Levitt & March 1988).
2.3 Navigating arbitrarily complex mazes: Sutton’s “reward hypothesis”
In the late 1970s at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, Richard Sutton and his colleague
Andrew Barto developed a reinforcement learning approach to address combinatorial explosion
that they called temporal differencing, or TD. Their key insight was that learning may not in
fact require beliefs about interdependent actions. Instead, an agent may learn to act effectively
by assigning credit to a much simpler “value function” that only estimates actions’ aggregate
rewards (also called their “cumulative expected value”).
The insight is that, rather than rely on intermediate feedback in a given domain (such as counting
checkers pieces in the domain of checkers), you start by just generating tentative beliefs about
8

the rewards of actions during intermediate steps. Then, after the actual feedback on the
intermediate trials is received, you can just update the beliefs based on the evidence. The key
idea is that, similar to the “time value of money” used in economic models for valuing the cash
flows of investments, how much you update beliefs depends on the time difference (hence the
name) between successive predictions.
The intuition is much like that of economic valuation techniques such as net present value
(NPV) that managers commonly use when deciding to invest in a project. NPV estimates the
“reward” of an investment simply as the sum of cash flows generated by all the complex actions
taken during a project. Intermediate feedback is simply any cash flows observed during a project.
The manager uses this feedback to modify the cumulative expected value of the project, without
needing to know which actions to assign credit to or “blame”. Put another way, rather than
reinforcing specific actions, the agent reinforces only the cumulative outcomes that
interdependent actions generate. Sutton and Barto claim that this approach offers a general
solution to the credit assignment problem, corresponding to what they call the “reward
hypothesis”.
REWARD HYPOTHESIS: “all of what we mean by goals and purposes can be well thought of as the
maximization of the expected value of the cumulative sum of a received scalar signal (called reward)”.
(Sutton & Barto, p. 57).

The “reward hypothesis” suggests credit can be assigned just by evaluating how things are going
and modifying actions in ways that seem more valuable. TD is their trick to do so. It refers to
how any intermediate feedback during one time period can be used to modify one’s running
estimate of the cumulative rewards at any “temporally-different” period as a basis for assigning
credit to actions. To bring things back to our multiple T-maze example, TD allows the mouse to
use the eventual discovery (or not) of cheese to estimate rewards at any of the earlier sections in
the maze, without having to evaluate paths of interdependent actions. These reward estimates can
then be used as a basis for evaluating and reinforcing individual actions (i.e., for solving the
credit assignment problem).

text_units.section: 3. Minsky and the limits of the reinforcement paradigm
text_units.text:
3. Minsky and the limits of the reinforcement paradigm
Sutton’s reward hypothesis proposes reinforcement learning as a general solution to credit
assignment for any problem requiring intelligence. Is this really plausible? A counterargument in
the AI field is from Minsky. In his view, credit assignment is not about finding solutions to
maximize rewards, nearly as much as it is about understanding problems themselves. As he
emphasized, “you first must be able to do something before you can be rewarded for doing it”.
Minsky argued feedback is not just uncertain or ambiguous but sparse, meaning that only a
small subset of actions generate feedback useful for assigning credit. Consider, for example, if
our shipbuilding company experiences a massive and prolonged fall in sales, as competitors
begin to produce ships with low costs and defects. Its managers realize they can no longer
survive as a traditional shipbuilding company and must change their strategy. Yet they lack even
superstitious beliefs for what novel strategies may work, and have no clear way to think of
“rewards” — feedback is sparse regarding most of the possible actions they could take to
reformulate their strategy.
How to learn to assign credit for such problems of sparse feedback? Minsky proposed that doing
so would require at least two key departures from the reinforcement paradigm that we just
looked at. First, feedback needs to be actively constructed to understand the nuanced structure of
the problem itself. Whereas Sutton sought to avoid such structure (i.e., how beliefs are
interdependent) by using a simple value function, Minsky went the opposite direction in seeking
to assign credit not only to beliefs about actions, but to understandings of how actions fit
together. Second, Minsky argued that, since problems of intelligence are complex, agents
construct feedback about only small parts of it. Rather than Sutton’s idea of reducing problems to
a single value function, learning to assign credit is done in what Minsky called a “society” (i.e.,
organization) of multiple agents that generate intermediate feedback based on coordinating and
cooperating actions. We next explore this idea of learning in a society as an alternative
paradigm for thinking about the general problem of credit assignment.

text_units.section: 4. Paradigm 2: assigning credit by learning in a “society”
text_units.text:
4. Paradigm 2: assigning credit by learning in a “society”
4.1 Revisiting the T-maze
To introduce this alternative paradigm of assigning credit by learning in a society, let us revisit
our earlier T-maze problem from a different point of view. Imagine the problem is not for a
mouse to find the cheese in the maze, but for a human — let us call this human Geoffrey — to
construct (i.e., design and build) the maze itself. Geoffrey is provided with certain blocks of
wood for building the walls of the maze, as well as some smaller blocks for building the starting
box, left-hand goal box, and right-hand goal box in Figure 2. Minsky suggests we think of the
fundamental actions here as managerial or administrative: they concern delegating actions to

text_units.section: 4. Paradigm 2: assigning credit by learning in a “society”
text_units.text:
other “agents”, rather than actual designing or building. Geoffrey is a sort of “CEO” agent,
whose actions manage lower-level agents in his mind or body needed to construct the maze.
Let us say, for example, that Geoffrey delegates the overall problem of constructing a maze to a
“Builder” agent in his mind, who is specialized in making stuff like mazes out of blocks.
“Builder” does not actually know how to build a maze, only that certain other agents, including
one called “Add” (who takes actions of adding blocks to the maze) is needed for the job. Yet
“Add” itself does not actually know how to construct the walls. It does know, however, that it
needs another agent “Grasp” to pick up the actual blocks, and “Move” to put them in the position
of the maze. These agents, the story continues, only know that they need to delegate their actions
to thousands of other agents who control the muscle fibers of Geoffrey’s fingers.
In this set up, how should we think about learning to assign credit? In some sense, each agent’s
action of delegating to other agents might be thought of as a “policy”, just as in reinforcement
learning. Geoffrey’s “policy” is to delegate to “Builder” when the problem is constructing a
maze, perhaps having “learned” to assign credit to this agent from past experience of using it to
build mazes successfully. Yet stop and think: what is the goal (i.e., “reward” to be maximized)?
Can such goals really be allocated to each individual agent?
Certainly, Minsky pointed out, one goal has to be that the T-maze should have the property of
containment, meaning that the mouse cannot escape the maze and only take left or right actions.
Yet who is rewarded for this goal? Consider that “containment” is a property of the entire maze,
not of any of the blocks. Hence, neither “Builder”, nor “Add”, “Remove”, or “Grasp” agents are
really rewarded for this goal. So who is rewarded? Minsky’s answer is that it is all of the agents
together, and what is “rewarded” is how they have structured into a society for constructing
mazes.8
Could Geoffrey’s intelligence be explained as a “society” where agents in his mind individually
learn to reinforce actions that maximize rewards for their own individual goals (as in a free
market), such that the maze and its containment property just emerge? Minsky says no. For one,
given a goal of “containment”, for Geoffrey and other higher-level agents (e.g., “Builder”) to
delegate actions effectively to lower-level agents (e.g., “Builder” and “Grasp”), they must have
already had some theories that decomposed the overall problem into simpler subproblems in
some meaningful way.
That is, our “CEO” Geoffrey is really always also partly a “designer” or “architect”, who has
some theory of how the agents’ actions will fit together to, e.g., achieve the “containment”
property in the maze. Hence, learning to assign credit cannot be abstracted from the problem of
8

text_units.text:
For Minsky, such a society of agents may exist within a single human mind (i.e., the different components or parts
of the brain or nervous system), an AI system, an organization, or in a conventionally-understood society itself (cf.
Wiener XX).

text_units.section: 4. Paradigm 2: assigning credit by learning in a “society”
text_units.text:
learning about the “society” itself — what its structure is and how it functions, and how this all
maps to the structure of the underlying problems. To be intelligent, Geoffrey learns to assign
credit not like in reinforcement learning to some beliefs about some interdependent set of
actions, nor to a value function, but rather to some (1) space of possible decompositions of a
problem and to (2) ways of organizing actions for solving this decomposed problem into a society
of agents.
Learning here is not about exploring or exploiting specific actions, so much as considering how
to use feedback to modify the overall decomposition of the problem and how actions for
understanding it or solving it are delegated to diverse agents in the society. These agents need not
“maximize” individual rewards (though this is one possibility); mostly, they fit into the society
by learning to coordinate and cooperate with many other agents using a variety of evaluative
criteria for assigning credit, always evaluated with respect to actions of many other agents.
4.2 Constructing two different mazes
You should start to see how, even for a seemingly simple problem of constructing a T-maze from
a few blocks, the credit assignment challenge is radically different from that in the reinforcement
learning example of the mouse in the T-maze. Next, consider how these differences also have
distinct implications for our earlier discussion of complexity. In the mouse example, the
challenge of assigning credit increased combinatorially as we added more actions, such as
making a mouse go through two T-mazes instead of just one. Yet when learning in a “society” to
construct two T-mazes, such an increase in actions adds little to the credit assignment challenge
if the actions are all the same. The reason is that constructing two T-mazes should involve pretty
much the same society of agents as constructing one, since there are no new actions. Once one
has understood how to construct one T-maze, constructing another one is a snap!
In contrast, what if Geoffrey encounters, or imagines, a new problem of constructing a T-maze,
out of rows of hedges, rather than blocks of wood? In this case, Geoffrey has to learn to assign
credit to a “new” society of agents, with agents specialized in, for example, trimming hedges. Yet
certainly, in this new hedge maze, the goal of “containment” is still maintained. It would be
inefficient to throw away all the credit assigned when constructing the first T-maze from blocks
of wood. Geoffrey’s credit assignment challenge is, thus, Minsky claims, largely a matter of
figuring out what to remember and what not to about how the previous problem was decomposed
and managed. Yet it is not only Geoffrey, but all the other agents (“Builder”, “Add”, etc.) who
also have to figure out what to remember when constructing a new hedge maze. Hence, Geoffrey
is really not just a CEO managing how to delegate actions for constructing a maze to lower-level
agents, but also how to manage their memories that enable efficiently constructing new mazes.

4.3 The management hypothesis
Geoffrey’s credit assignment challenge is vastly more complex (or, at the least, qualitatively
different) from the challenge in the reinforcement learning paradigm of modifying beliefs or
value functions. Actions to assign credit include not just going left or right in a maze, or even
delegating subproblems for constructing a maze, but also actions for how and whether to store
feedback as a memories for future use and when to use these memories. For a lower-level agent,
such as “Grasp”, such memory-related actions might concern just when to delegate grasping
actions to the muscle fiber “agents” in Geoffrey’s hands. At the higher-level of Geoffrey himself,
memory-related actions amount to learning to store and use feedback about his theories or
designs of the overall maze and how to organize its construction.
Finally, since there are likely far too many agents for Geoffrey to remember in detail, he also
needs to simplify all these memories, such as decomposing agents into hierarchical levels and
assigning credit to their actions at these aggregate levels, akin to managing an organization. All
of this leads to an overall view of how to address the general problem of credit assignment that
we will call in this course the “management hypothesis”.
MANAGEMENT HYPOTHESIS: All of what we mean by goals and purposes can be well thought of as managing processes of
decomposing problems, and memories about these problems, into societies of agents, and assigning credit within these societies
in ways that enable them to satisfy some higher-level evaluative functions.

Managing processes of learning to assign credit in a “society” means that, when the society
collectively generates actions that lead to “rewards” in a broader sense (i.e., either of some
economic reward, or just understanding things better), what is “reinforced” is really what Minsky
called a “society of memories” about some goals. Put another way, “reinforcement” here
increases the probability that a configuration of agents forms again in similar circumstances. Yet
this overstates the comparison between the “reinforcement” and “society” paradigms of learning
to assign credit in AI. Minsky’s societies are agents who operate at different levels of abstraction,
with different goals, and different knowledge, rather than on a single value function or belief
system. Further, when they collectively assign credit to their configuration of agents, the novel
configuration may form a new goal. Even if there is just a rearrangement of goals, the “reward”
is not maximization, so much as learning a new skill or satisfying the needs of the society.
5. Conclusion
What should you take away from our discussion so far? First, you should see that any AI ideas
(or analogous organizational theories) can be understood in terms of how they propose solving
the general problem of assigning credit. Second, you should see from our two discussions of the
credit assignment problem (reinforcement learning, and learning in a society) that different AI
ideas can offer paradigmatically different views of learning and intelligence. Hence,
understanding AI will require you to form your own perspective based on thinking critically
about diverse ideas about intelligence that are often in tension.

6. Appendix
6.1 Historical link between the AI ideas and organizations
Reinforcement learning has roots in 1940s-1950s research in the US, famously by Richard
Bellman, an applied mathematician at a US government think tank called the RAND
Corporation in Santa Monica, California. Called “operations research”, early computers were
combined with econometric techniques to optimize inventory, logistics, and supply chain
processes for US military and corporate bureaucracies that were rapidly growing and becoming
more complex in the post-World War II era. The logic was economic: given a measurable
“reward”, compute policies to maximize it. This logic carries forward today. Technology
platforms rely on reinforcement to control how large volumes of data inform actions. Social
media firms such as Facebook treat “engagement” (how much users interact with the platform)
as a reward to be maximized, without explicit beliefs or theories of social interaction. Today,
reinforcement is being applied to far broader domains, and for far more general rewards. Its
proponents argue credit assignment by maximizing rewards should generalize to any problem.
The AI idea of learning in a society begins with Minsky’s work at MIT from the late 1950s. It
indirectly relates to work during the 1940s-1950s of Herbert Simon (1947) at Carnegie-Mellon
on how organizations represent problems and goals, and of Norbert Wiener’s (also from MIT)
proposal that actual societies required a more complex mathematics to be managed effectively,
which he called cybernetics. Minsky was not interested in optimizing operations in military or
corporate hierarchies; he was asking how intelligence itself works. His answer, based in part on
observations of children playing with blocks (called the “blocks world”, and used in our earlier
example of building a T-maze), is fundamentally organizational. Though reinforcement and other
machine learning strategies have dominated popular discourse about AI in recent decades,
current uses of AI increasingly involve managing systems of AI “agents”. Hence, as AI becomes
increasingly embedded in organizations, the AI field may be circling back to Minsky’s paradigm.

Course Notes — SESSION 2
INFORMATION PROCESSING
1. Introduction
In our previous session, we characterized learning in AI systems and organizations as a process
of using feedback to assign credit to problem-solving actions. We saw how assigning credit
becomes challenging as a problem grows more complex. Finally, we viewed the complexity of
the credit assignment problem under two AI paradigms — as the combinatorial complexity of
actions to explore or exploit (reinforcement learning), or as the complexity of managing how
actions are organized (learning in a society).
This discussion of credit assignment and complexity was evocative but imprecise. We talked in
intuitive terms, such as a mouse going left or right in a maze, or managing various tasks for
building this maze. To establish credit assignment as a basis for studying foundational AI ideas
for the rest of the course, we need to be clearer about what we mean by a “complex” problem.
In this session, we will define complexity as feedback required to learn to solve a problem that
we can actually measure, or at least talk of, in formal (mathematical) terms. Our goal will be to
think of feedback as something like quantifiable units akin to atoms or molecules.
By convention, we will from now on usually refer to feedback as “information”. This term
“information” will flexibly stand in (for now) for any other term that we might think of for
feedback, such as data, sense perceptions, or knowledge. Defining what we mean by information,
however, will require precise assumptions. If information units are our building blocks, our
assumptions about them will shape how we think about the very nature of credit assignment. It
may be tempting just to try to define information using the most basic units we can imagine,
similar to atoms (or subatomic particles) in physics. Yet consider how biologists study entire
cells as the building blocks of living systems, and are less interested in sub-cellular units such as
atoms. Likewise, the question that we really need to ask is: what units of information will be
most helpful for us to study processes of intelligently learning to assign credit in AI systems and
organizations?
To explore this question robustly, we will, as in our last session, consider two paradigmaticallydifferent approaches to information in the study of AI systems and organizations. One approach,
called Shannon information, after its pioneer Claude Shannon (1916-2001, a co-founder of the
AI field from MIT), measures information as meaningless units called bits. The reinforcement
paradigm that we looked at in the previous session, along with other types of machine learning
that we will look at later, are consistent with Shannon’s approach. A different approach, which
we will call Simon information, after Herbert Simon (1916-2001, also a co-founder of the AI
field, from Carnegie-Mellon University) instead measures information as meaningful units

called lists. The paradigm of learning in a society from last session, along with many other AI
ideas outside of machine learning, are closer to Simon’s approach.

2. Establishing some shared terminology (and convenient fictions)
Before diving into the two approaches to information, let us establish some shared terminology.
This shared terminology will empower us to think about credit assignment in precise terms
across diverse AI ideas. As you will see, however, it will also require us to maintain convenient
fictions about information that we will need to keep carefully in mind.
First, by information, we will refer not just to numerical data, but to any types of symbols for
describing physical objects in, or concepts about, the world (i.e., problem-solving environments).
Symbols may include alphabetic characters, words, images, videos, sound waves or any other
observations that can be recorded. A pilot, for example, receives feedback as symbolic
information in the visual displays of cockpit instruments, audio updates from air traffic control,
or ear pressure from a sudden change in altitude. Symbols may be received either from another
agent (human or artificial), or just by interacting with the physical world (e.g., gravity).
Second, we will refer to any use of information to learn to assign credit to a problem as
“information processing” (indeed, an early proposal was to name the field “complex
information processing” rather than AI). By information processing, we will refer broadly to any
actions for “storing, manipulating, displaying, and otherwise trafficking in information”
(Cantwell-Smith 2021) by agents (any entities taking goal-directed actions) interacting with
problem-solving environments (anything external to agents that is also relevant to a problem).
For the pilot, such actions could be physical movements (e.g., pulling on the throttle in the
cockpit), choices or decisions (e.g., switching from autopilot to manual mode), or simply
observations (e.g., checking the altitude, air pressure, or remaining fuel).
Third, we will view information processing as acts of communication among agents, and AI
systems and organizations as communication systems. What agents do to be intelligent is
essentially “package” information into “messages” that they send, or receive and evaluate
messages from other agents. These actions are collectively referred to as “message passing”,
such that AI systems and organizations can also be called “message passing systems”. This view
of information processing as communication requires maintaining our first convenient fiction,
which is that an agent’s problem-solving environment is simply other agents who process
information, even if some or most of the environment is really not agentic (e.g., the atmosphere
that the pilot interacts with). This fiction will allow us to talk about agents and environments as a
single system in which messages are passed back and forth and, hence, allow us to formalize
ways of talking about the complexity of the system.

text_units.section: 2. Establishing some shared terminology (and convenient fictions)
text_units.text:
Shannon, whose approach to information we will describe momentarily, famously displayed this
convenient fiction in a robotic mouse he built in 1950 called Theseus, which “learns” to navigate
a maze whose walls can be flexibly configured (as depicted on the left). Theseus’s maze
“environment” is really a network of electrical circuit “agents” when you open it up (as depicted
on the right). When Theseus takes actions in a part of the maze, the relevant circuits “send
messages” to him about whether a particular path in the maze is open or blocked.
Conjuring an agent’s problem-solving environment in this way — as communicating agents akin
to a circuit network — has been a dominant perspective in the AI field since it emerged in the
1940s and 1950s (when designing circuits for telephone networks was a canonical example of a
complex problem), and on up to today (where the canonical example is designing the networks
of circuits in semiconductor chips), It equally has led to theories of organizations as essentially
communication systems designed to structure flows of information. Though this characterization
helps us define information about a problem, keep in mind that it also blurs the distinction
between an agent and its environment. For example, in Theseus, the mouse’s “information
processor” is really in the maze circuitry. This agent-environment distinction will not matter so
much for the purposes of this session, but we will need to think carefully about it later on.
Claude Shannon’s Theseus robot (1950)

text_units.text:
Fourth, we will (for now) refer to all basic actions underlying information processing or message
passing as “symbol manipulation” operations. Such operations refer to diverse actions, ranging
from applying arithmetic or algebraic rules, to using formal logic, to moving icons on a laptop
screen, to speaking in natural language, to writing a prompt in a GenAI tool. Common to all such
symbol manipulation operations, however, is that learning to assign credit arises from
evaluating information in patterns of the symbols. Such evaluation may involve either pattern
matching (matching exact symbols) or pattern recognition (matching similar symbols)).
Note that this symbol manipulation assumption will require us to maintain a second fiction,
called the “digital abstraction”, which is that we can talk about information as a symbolic thing,
independent of the physical world. Consider that Shannon’s Theseus depicted above has no overt
symbols — the maze is just some electromechanical circuits connected by physical wiring, such
3

text_units.text:
that “messages” passed from the maze to Theseus are really analog electrical pulses. The digital
abstraction, however, is convenient (if we are careful about using it) by enabling us to relate any
actions (analog or otherwise) to a single, coherent system for evaluating and transforming
patterns of symbols into other patterns and, hence, for talking about information as a
formalizable quantity that varies based on the complexity of a problem.
Fifth and finally, leveraging this convenient fiction, we will think of the complexity of a problem
as the amount of symbol manipulation actions for solving it — or, more precisely, the complexity
of the symbolic patterns that need to be matched or recognized to solve a problem. In AI, this
quantity is often analogized to how much “energy” or “work” is required for solving a problem
intelligently. Hence, we will say that processing more complex information requires greater
“processing power” or “processing capacity”. For example, solving the problem of
downloading the information in a video file of a lecture typically takes more “capacity” from
your computer than an audio file of the same lecture, since the video file has more information
(e.g., the file size is much larger).
With this terminology (and convenient fictions) established, we can now frame the general
intelligence problem of credit assignment (for now) a bit more formally — in information
processing terms or, equivalently, as a problem of message passing (of communicating patterns
in symbols) among agents:
Assigning credit is an information process of evaluating (i.e., matching or
recognizing) patterns in symbols about problems. Challenges of assigning credit
arise from the need to evaluate more complex symbolic patterns.
Further, now we can frame a bit more formally what is meant by paradigmatically-different
approaches to assigning credit in intelligent systems:
AI ideas differ in the symbolic patterns that they take to be the basic units of
information and, as a result, in how they conceive of the capacity (i.e.,
complexity) required to process these patterns.

3. Approach 1: Shannon information (syntactic information processing)
In a 1948 paper, Shannon introduced an approach to thinking about information that has been so
influential to the study of AI and organizations (and many other scientific and engineering fields)
that it is still often simply called “information theory”. He developed his approach in the 1930s
and 1940s, ostensibly to solve problems of routing calls over complex telephone networks while
working at Bell Labs, the research lab of American Telephone & Telegraph Company (AT&T),
which was the largest telephone operator in the US at the time. Yet Shannon had in mind a

general theory of communication in any system which, as he demonstrated with his 1950 robot
Theseus, could in fact be used to develop machines that could in some sense be said to “learn”.
We will understand the Shannon information approach in terms of three assumptions:
information processing as syntactic; units of information as meaningless bits; and processing
information to learn to assign credit intelligently as ultimately a matter of brute force.
3.1 Learning to assign credit based on syntactic information processing
Shannon’s approach is based on his insight that, in an electrical engineering sense at least, the
semantic content (the meaning) of messages sent over a telephone network (or any other
communications system) is irrelevant. AT&T’s real problem was simply to ensure that
information about the syntactic structure of symbolic patterns in messages is sent accurately.
For example, when a pilot sends a message to air traffic control about the plane’s altitude, the
altimeter reading needs to be accurate in the sense of the sequence of numerical symbols (e.g., if
the altitude is 30,000 feet, ensuring that the reading is a “3” followed by four zeros). This
syntactic information about the altitude is separate from whether the pilot or air traffic control
interprets the meaning of 30,000 feet as too low or too high.
In the context of AI, Shannon’s key insight was that, remarkably, intelligently learning to assign
credit might be thought of as similar to how AT&T needed to route calls in a telephone network
— an intelligent agent needed only to process syntactic information to learn to solve a complex
problem. His Theseus robot, for example, could “learn” to navigate any configuration of the
maze by using “messages” sent by the maze circuits to assign credit to certain paths as good or
bad, and then to modify its selection of sequences of actions over time. Such “learning” did not
require Theseus to interpret the sequence of actions he took, other than associating the actions
with good or bad paths, similar to the reinforcement paradigm that we studied last session.
3.2 Units of information: bits
Shannon proposed binary digits — 0’s or 1’s — that he called “bits” as the building block units
of syntactic information processing. Bits are linked together into “messages” as patterns of 0’s
and 1’s called bit strings. All symbols can be reduced to bit strings. Converting symbols into bit
strings is called encoding a message; reconstructing the symbols in the original message is called
decoding it. For example, a standard way of encoding the letter “A” in a computer is as the bit
string “01000001”. Since messages often have redundant sequences of symbols (e.g., repeating
the same words or grammatical patterns), the encoded bit strings in them are not a true measure
of the number of bits required to communicate the message. What counts is how efficiently the
message can be communicated after statistical redundancies are removed, a process that allows
the original message to be “compressed” into a smaller number of bit strings that, in turn,
reduces the processing capacity required.

The amount of information in a message, however, is not measured simply by counting the
number of compressed bits. For Shannon, this amount instead refers to the uncertainty reduced
about the probability distribution of outcomes from receiving a compressed message. This
uncertainty reduction depends on (1) the complexity of the problem, or how many possible
“messages” could be received (e.g., how many sequences of interdependent actions Theseus
could take in a maze), and (2) the perceived probability of a message by the agent, given what
the agent has already learned (e.g., if Theseus “exploits" similar sequences of actions to what he
already tried, the messages that he “receives” from the maze will give him less information than
if he explores new sequences).
A crowning achievement of Shannon is to formalize a measure of uncertainty about the statistical
distribution of the probabilities of messages as a quantity that he called “entropy”, named for its
similarity to entropy in thermodynamics. Shannon entropy can be thought of as the information
in each possible bit string message (e.g., each possible sequence in Theseus’s maze) weighted by
the probability that the message occurs (e.g., how likely Theseus believes that each sequence of
actions is to lead to a reward). Hence, the amount of information in a message is inversely
related to its probability, with rare messages having more information than common ones (hence,
exploring new actions generates more information than exploiting existing ones).
In the language of our course, you can think of Shannon entropy roughly as a more precise way
of measuring the combinatorial complexity of a problem by doing so in probabilistic terms
(i.e., in terms of a statistical distribution of the probabilities of actions (messages)). Whereas
combinatorial complexity captures simply the number of possible action sequences in a problem,
entropy also accounts for how likely some action sequences are. In this sense, Shannon entropy
measures not just the objective complexity of a problem, but how an agent’s uncertainty about
this complexity may be reduced as it “learns” by processing syntactic information about it.
3.3 Credit assignment as a challenge of limited “channel capacity”
What do Shannon’s assumptions about the units (bits) and complexity (entropy) of information
imply about the general problem of intelligence in AI systems and organizations — the problem
of learning to assign credit? Overall, the implication is, for solving any particular problem, an
agent’s ability to learn to assign credit is entirely a matter of their capacity for processing
syntactic information (i.e., of the capacity to evaluate patterns in bit strings that encode symbolic
patterns in messages). Hence, you can think of all AI ideas consistent with Shannon information
as various ways of dealing with limits to syntactic processing capacity.
Shannon described these limits as arising from how communication, while based on syntactic
symbols, still ultimately happens over physical channels, or restricted pathways to send and
receive messages, such as AT&T’s telephone network or fiber optic cables today. Beyond
electronic or digital equipment, channels can refer to any way of restricting the processing of

information. The structure of an organization, for example, is a channel in the sense that it
controls who can communicate with whom in the organization (Cyert & March 1955). A rigid
hierarchy is typically thought of as channeling information in a more restrictive fashion (up and
down) than a non-hierarchical organization (though with possible advantages of greater
efficiency and control).
Limits to channel capacity mean that only a certain amount of information, or “bandwidth”,
can be processed at a certain speed over any one period of time. A conventional TV channel, for
example, has access to only a limited amount of bandwidth, while fiber optic cables in a 5G
network have more capacity. Channel capacity limits mean that information in messages is what
Shannon called “noisy” — that the symbolic patterns encoded into bit strings are only
communicated with a certain probability. “Noise” (communication of wrong or irrelevant bit
strings) is contrasted with “signals”, or the accurate communication of bit strings in a message.
The signal-to-noise ratio is a measure of how reliable a message can be communicated.
A fundamental mathematical finding of Shannon’s is that, as signal-to-noise increases, the
amount of information that can be reliably transmitted increases combinatorially. Hence, in
theory at least, a linear increase in channel capacity may be enough to address the issue of
combinatorial explosion (or, in information processing terms, of expanding “entropy”) from our
last session. Hence, Shannon information implies solving the problem of credit assignment in AI
systems and organizations is ultimately a matter of increasing channel capacity.
3.4 “Brute force” solutions to credit assignment
In 2019, Richard Sutton, whose ideas about reinforcement learning we looked at last session,
wrote a short blog post titled “The Bitter Lesson”. His post went viral, and has come to
epitomize a dominant view of AI today beholden to the Shannon information approach. For
Sutton, the “bitter lesson” is the result of over seven decades of research and practice in the AI
field (roughly since Shannon demoed his Theseus robot in 1950). This result, in his view, is that
“progress” in the AI field has mostly been made not by AI researchers thinking of complex
strategies for assigning credit, but rather of embarrassingly simple strategies (e.g., Sutton’s idea
of a value function) paired with massive increases in channel capacity (exponential gains in
semiconductor speed and data storage and availability).
In AI, having a system learn to assign credit intelligently just by pairing a simple strategy with
essentially big computers is called a brute force strategy. You should see that a belief in brute
force rests on a specific assumption in Shannon’s approach: that any combinatorial explosion in
the complexity of problems will be more than made up for by the exponential increase in
signal-to-noise from just a linear increase in channel capacity.
If the brute force assumption about AI is correct, then you should see that, given expected
continued vast expansion in digital infrastructure, there are few obvious limits to how the AI field
7

will progress. Consider the estimate from some neuroscientists that the human brain has 100
trillion synapses. If all the brain is analogous to a Shannon information processor — if the
functioning of the brain can be fundamentally understood as the processing of bit strings to send
and receive messages among neuron “agents” — then it is straightforward to calculate how much
information processing capacity would be required to construct an artificial brain. Given that
such capacity is simply a matter of adding more digital infrastructure (i.e., more chips and data
storage), then constructing an artificial brain is just a matter of time. This way of thinking has led
some in the AI field to conclude that we will soon get a generally intelligent or superintelligent
AI system, including fears that such a system poses an existential threat to humankind.
Before we move on, it is worth noting that Shannon himself would likely not have believed any
of the above claims about brute force and intelligence. The ambitious term for his approach
(“information theory”) was insisted on by his co-author; the term “entropy” was chosen also for
rhetorical reasons, to make the theory itself sound complex and mysterious. Shannon viewed his
approach to syntactic information processing as a powerful, but targeted solution for certain
engineering problems, and as a way to start to think about how to design learning systems in the
nascent AI field. Infatuation with Shannon information as a “theory of everything” in AI and
science more broadly arose as early as the 1950s, shortly after his paper was published, in ways
that mirror some of the rhetoric in the AI field today. Shannon himself wrote a commentary
calling those who exaggerated the implications of his approach as on the “information
bandwagon”, and cautioned for the need for diverse ideas for understanding intelligence.

4. Approach 2: Simon information (semantic information processing)
In a famous 1962 paper titled “The Architecture of Complexity”, Herbert Simon described an
alternative to Shannon’s approach to understanding information and its relationship to intelligent
learning. Simon developed his approach out of his research on decision-making processes in
organizations from the 1930s to 1950s, including a field study of the budgeting bureau in a city
government, and by observing corporate managers make decisions under experimental settings.
Though ostensibly the research was to improve administrative decision-making, Simon had in
mind a general theory of problem-solving, which he demonstrated in the mid-1950 using
simulations of solving logic puzzles and playing chess (developed with his colleague, and fellow
AI co-founder Allen Newell).
We will contrast Simon information from Shannon’s approach in terms of three assumptions:
information processing as semantic and not just syntactic; the fundamental units of information
for intelligence as meaningful lists, rather than meaningless bits; and intelligent information
processing as ultimately a matter of abstracting a problem to modularize (i.e., decompose) it,
rather than just a matter of adding channel capacity (i.e., brute force).

text_units.section: 4.1 Learning based on semantic information processing
text_units.text:
4.1 Learning based on semantic information processing
Simon’s approach emerged from his insight that in organizational decision-making — or, it
seemed to him, any complex system — syntactic information processing on its own would be
far too slow and inefficient for intelligence to emerge, even if possible in theory. The real
problem was instead to identify semantic structure in symbolic patterns that would allow
information about complex problems to be decomposed into these structures. Consider our
example from the previous session of a budgeting committee of a pharmaceutical company that
needs to decide in which business units to invest. In theory, the managers on the committee could
make their budgeting decisions by processing bit strings extracted from dense reports consisting
of detailed numerical data on past performance and future sales forecasts. In practice, they rely
on semantic categories, such as the names of the business units and the types of innovations that
they propose, and summaries of numbers such as last year’s sales figures.
In the context of AI, Simon’s key insight was that such reliance on semantic categories was not
just due to human managers’ limited “channel capacity”. Rather, how managers make complex
decisions in such settings may be thought of as similar to how semantic information is
fundamental to learning to solve any combinatorially complex problem in any intelligent system.
Shannon’s Theseus, under this view, “learned” without such categories since the maze was still
relatively simple. Sutton’s “bitter lesson”, Simon might have said, can be explained by how AI
technologies based on syntactic information processing (e.g., reinforcement learning) only
“learned” when provided with a vast infrastructure of meaningful symbols (e.g., carefully
designed programming languages, databases, software architectures, etc.).
In his 1962 paper, Simon famously illustrated the need for semantic information through his
watchmaker parable. In Simon’s parable, the problem is to learn to assemble a mechanical
watch of 1,000 parts. There is a chance of the assembly task being interrupted, in which case any
incomplete assemblies fall apart and the task starts over. Simon describes two watchmakers. One
decomposes the watch into 100 named (i.e., meaningful) modules (i.e., components) of 10 parts
each. The other assembles the 1,000 parts one at a time. Even assuming a modest chance of
interruption of 1%, Simon calculates, the first watchmaker needs to repeat only a handful of
subtasks per interruption, while the second requires repeating 100 subtasks on average, and
around 4,000 times longer to complete the overall assembly task.
4.2 Units of information: lists
Simon proposed that, rather than reduce symbols to individual bits that are formed into
meaningless strings of 0’s and 1’s, the bits should be organized into meaningful patterns (e.g.,
names of the components of watches) that he called lists. Lists differ from bits in that they are
not just arbitrary strings of 0’s and 1’s — they have a name, followed by the “items” of the list.
The name of the list is a label that “designates” the meaning of the symbols (“items”) on the list
— that is, the name indicates what the symbols externally refer to in the physical or conceptual
