text_units.text:
world that are relevant to a problem. Whereas bits are packaged into bit strings, lists can be
“linked” together into arbitrarily abstract patterns, such as concepts, sentences, paragraphs,
blocks of code, or equations. For example, while Shannon information encodes the letter A as the
bit string “01000001”, Simon information might encode it as the list: (Letter A), where “letter” is
the name designating a letter of the alphabet, and “A” is the “item” of the alphabet that is
relevant here.
In their Turing Award speech (the equivalent to the Nobel Prize in computer science lecture),
Simon and his colleague Newell explained this idea for list processing through what they called
the “physical symbol system hypothesis” (1976). This is the hypothesis that “physical symbols”
— symbols that meaningfully refer to the outside world, rather than just being stored as
meaningless bit strings — are a “necessary and sufficient basis for intelligence” in an AI system
or organization. The implication is that efficient intelligent systems arise not by sheer scaling of
syntactic processing capacity, but by how meaningful abstractions of bit strings eliminate the
need to process information about every detail of the environment. The key argument underlying
the physical symbol system hypothesis is that, with a good enough set of ideas on how to
develop abstractions (e.g., a good enough set of languages), agents can reason about any
information in a meaningful way that, in turn, leads to efficient credit assignment.
To continue the comparison, whereas in Shannon information, the number of bits for learning to
solve a problem refers to the required bits after statistical redundancies have been removed, in
Simon information, such redundancies are among meaningful lists at various levels of
abstraction and complexity. What matters, then, is not the total number of non-redundant lists per
se (as in Shannon entropy), but rather the agent’s ability to describe the problem at a higher-level
of abstraction and, hence, with fewer lists (i.e., describing a mechanical watch in terms of 10
components, rather than 1000 parts). A bit more formally, the key efficiency mechanism shifts
from the compression of bit strings, to the abstraction of list structures.
4.3 Credit assignment as a challenge of limits to one’s abstractions
What do Simon’s different assumptions about the fundamental units of information (lists) imply
about the general problem of intelligence in AI systems and organizations — i.e., the problem of
learning to assign credit? In Simon information, the point is not really to have vast channel
capacity for processing information. There is little interest in “noise” of information, or the
“signal-to-noise” ratio. Processing information structured into lists that each designate meaning
in the world implies that any noise will eventually be identified and eliminated. Agents do not
have to just guess using probabilities to match patterns; they dynamically reason using their
understanding of how information about the problem maps to the world.

text_units.section: 4.1 Learning based on semantic information processing
text_units.text:
Hence, the fundamental assumption in Shannon assumption that a linear increase in channel
capacity can exponentially reduce signal-to-noise is not so relevant under Simon information.
One is better off just trying to find better and higher-level abstractions (i.e., decompositions of
problems) to avoid having to process so much information in the first place. Limits to an agent’s
ability to learn to assign credit in complex problems arise instead from limits of the agent’s
abstractions (i.e., the types of lists and list operations available to an agent) for describing the
problem as it relates to (designates) stuff in the world.
You can think of such limits as on the “languages” available to agents for designating and linking
lists and their abstractions, rather than one of channel capacity for sending and receiving
messages. An organization, Simon observed, does not just impose hierarchy or other structure to
channel syntactic messages; it develops a “shared language” among members to communicate
meanings that can be mutually understood. Similarly, advances in the intelligence of digital
computers depend not just on digital infrastructure (faster chips and more data processing
capacity), but also on languages that offer novel abstractions (i.e., coding libraries, and the ability
to generate code using natural language).
4.4 “Modularity” as a solution to credit assignment
In 2019, the same year as Sutton’s “The Bitter Lesson” blog post, an influential article appeared
by Saleema Amershi and her colleagues at Microsoft Research called “Software Engineering for
Machine Learning: A Case Study”. The article concerned their observations and experience of
how Microsoft organized teams to build machine learning models for using large volumes of
data to deploy applications such as recommender systems or computer vision tools at scale.
A main finding was that effective deployment required not just vast chip and data storage
capacity to improve individual machine learning models. As Amershi et al. explain, “one cannot
(yet) take [a] model of English and add a separate… model for ordering pizza and expect them to
work properly together. Similarly, one cannot take that same model for pizza and pair it with an
equivalent… model for French and have it work”. Instead, effective deployment depended on
organizational processes of interpreting the collective outputs of diverse models that were
“entangled” in their effects on application performance. Hence, even in machine learning —
technologies explicitly adhering to Shannon information — the general problem of learning to
assign credit is subsumed within a broader system for semantic information processing,
consistent with the Simon information approach.
In the study of AI systems and organizations, having a system learn to assign credit not through
brute force, so much as through how problem-solving is abstracted into meaningful modules akin
to Simon’s watchmaker is called a modularity strategy. You should see that a belief in
modularity rests on a specific assumption intimately linked to Simon’s approach that contrasts
with what is implied by Shannon information: that any combinatorial “explosion” in the
complexity of problems will not be made up for by an exponential increase in the signal-to-noise
11

text_units.section: 4.1 Learning based on semantic information processing
text_units.text:
ratio produced by a linear increase in channel capacity. More bluntly: adding bigger computers to
an AI system will not lead to a disproportionately large increase in the ability of the system to
learn to assign credit.

text_units.section: 5. Dynamics of information processing: IID versus OOD problems
text_units.text:
5. Dynamics of information processing: IID versus OOD problems
As we have discussed them, the credit assignment mechanisms (brute force in the Shannon
information approach; modularity in the Simon information approach) have been mostly static —
applying to a particular problem. The Amershi et al. article points to a neglected aspect of our
discussion, which is the dynamics of processing information across novel problems. Recall from
our previous session how in Minsky’s idea of learning in a society, a fundamental challenge of
assigning credit arose from the need to deal with novel problem-solving environments — even
for problems as seemingly simple as constructing a T-maze out of different materials. To round
off our discussion of information as an AI foundation, we need to extend our two approaches to
account for such dynamics. A common way to do so in the AI field is to distinguish what are
called “IID” and “OOD” problems.
5.1 Shannon information and the IID assumption
To see why the dynamics of information processing are important, let us first draw attention to a
subtle yet strong assumption of Shannon information. It assumes an agent has access to a
statistical distribution of probabilities regarding the possible bit strings of a message. This
really means that, even though the agent may face uncertainty about the exact content of the
message, it has perfect certainty that the bit strings will be something within some set of possible
messages. For example, when you prompt an LLM in English to predict the next word of a
sentence, we assume that the LLM has perfect certainty that it will be some word in English, and
not another language or another kind of symbol (i.e., a soundwave or a picture) altogether. In this
sense, Shannon information implies the world stays basically the same — or, more formally, the
set of possible outcomes (i.e., messages) have a consistent statistical distribution.
In statistics, this is called the assumption that the outcomes of a function are independently and
identically distributed, or “IID”. “Independent” means that outcomes are not interdependent.
“Identically distributed” means that the distribution of outcomes — the probabilities of getting
each of the possible outcomes — does not change over time. These two ideas capture the basic
idea in statistics of “random sampling”. A canonical example is a coin toss, assuming a fair coin.
The first coin flip does not depend on the second coin flip, and vice versa. Therefore, the coin
flips are independent. Further, the probability of heads or tails is both 50%, and these chances in
theory should never change, no matter how many times you flip the coin. Therefore, the
probabilities in the coin flips are identically distributed.

text_units.section: 5. Dynamics of information processing: IID versus OOD problems
text_units.text:
Now consider another example of a coin toss where other factors may come into play. The coin
may not be fair (it may be weighted more on one side); the coin may have a wide edge such that
there is a chance it will land on the edge; the coin toss may take place over deep water, where
there may be no way to actually read the result after the coin sinks to the bottom of the water.
These and many other possible violations of the basic IID coin toss set-up can be thought of as
out-of-distribution, or “OOD”. In coin tosses, such possible violations may be unlikely, but in
many or most real-world settings, they are the rule rather than the exception, and this was
precisely Minsky’s point. To go back to our maze example, Minsky might say it is ultimately
more apt to frame the credit assignment problem in AI as: how to navigate any maze of any size,
where the configuration and materials of the maze may change at any time, where even the goal
of navigating the maze may be initially unclear, and where you might even need to understand
the maze first and how to build it.
5.2 How to process information about OOD problems?
It may seem that, if credit assignment in AI is ultimately about OOD problems, then the Simon
information approach is the only valid one. It makes no assumption that an agent has access to a
stable statistical distribution of outcomes for a problem. Yet there are at least two complications;
we only touch on these here, but you should keep them in mind as we explore diverse ideas
related to both approaches to information throughout the semester.
First, Simon information assumes all problems can be described in terms of lists as the
fundamental informational units. Whether that is adequate for processing information across
OOD problems, however, is an empirical question. In Simon’s famous watchmaker parable, the
watch is given — just like under Shannon information. What if the watchmaker has to assemble
many different kinds of watches? Minsky (and many others in the AI field) argue that, to “learn
in a society”, or through some other similar way, agents need to process units of information that
are often more complex than lists, and of many types. Consider, for instance, how programming
languages today have many types of information (called “data types”), such as dictionaries,
tuples, functions, and objects. Perhaps in order to learn to solve OOD problems, some diverse set
of information types is a minimal requirement. We will consider such ideas later in the course.
Second, in the total opposite direction of Minsky, could we think about Shannon information
differently, such that reducing all information to bit strings is in fact a perfectly natural approach
to solving OOD problems — indeed, the only imaginable way? Consider if we think of the IID
versus OOD distinction as really only applying to the outcomes of problems that we describe
using complex symbols (lists or otherwise), but which we also ultimately describe these symbols
in a computer in terms of bit strings. In this case, we might assume a statistical distribution only
among the bit strings, and make predictions about these bit strings that will then generate more
complex symbols that we do not need to assume follow such distribution. Consider prompting an
LLM in English to solve an OOD problem. The prompt that you give it may be a problem that is

text_units.section: 5. Dynamics of information processing: IID versus OOD problems
text_units.text:
radically different from any one it has been given before; yet the English words in the text of
your prompt, describable in bit strings, may still be more or less consistent with the overall
distribution of English words that the LLM has processed before.
6. Conclusion
In current AI discourse, it is common to relate ideas closer to Shannon information as belonging
to “cutting edge” machine learning technologies, while those closer to Simon information are
related to supposedly “old-fashioned” AI research. The former is taken to mean an AI system
designed to learn with a minimum of “hand-coded” information. The latter is taken to be the
opposite, where information is carefully crafted by the designers of the system in advance. In this
course, we will look at this way of partitioning the AI field as historically inaccurate and grossly
misleading. We will view approaches to information in the study of AI and organizations as an
ongoing debate about ways of learning to assign credit, rather than a progression from
“old-fashioned” to “cutting edge”. As this week’s course notes have illustrated, a better way to
partition the AI field is really more like the distinction between physics and biology — it is about
what one considers to be the fundamental units of information (e.g., more atomic bits, or more
aggregate lists) for learning to assign credit intelligently. Through this week’s lecture notes, you
should see that such assumptions are at once subtle, consequential, and controversial.

Course Notes — SESSION 3
SEARCH
1. Introduction
The previous session introduced a view of credit assignment as processing syntactic (bits)
or semantic (physical symbols) information. This view implied the reinforcement
learning paradigm in AI is driven by brute force (big computers), while the
learning-in-a-society paradigm is driven more by having good abstractions (languages).
In this session, we turn to a further AI idea about information processing called search.
Studying search will illuminate fundamental ways to assign credit in either paradigm
more efficiently (i.e., to reduce the need for brute force, and to make better use of
abstractions), as well as to surface some distinct limits.
To see what is meant by search, imagine we have stacked a large number of T-mazes,
such that our mouse’s problem of finding the cheese is complex to the point of being
combinatorially explosive. Let us change, however, how we visualize the maze. First,
each T-maze will be a simple point that we will call a “node”. Second, we will now flip
the maze upside down, so the mouse starts from a single action on top, and can select
among various “paths” of nodes that correspond to possible action sequences.
Combinatorially-explosive T-mazes
The same picture, as nodes of a search tree

What do you see in this new picture? One neat thing is that the maze looks something
like a hierarchical division of labor (later, we will call this a search tree) — a rough
version of Minsky’s idea of a “society”. Think of the top node as our mouse “CEO”; the
levels beneath it as middle managers; and further down, staff. The mice navigate the
maze by sending and receiving messages up and down this hierarchy. They specialize in
simple problems, corresponding to some level of nodes in the maze, and controlled by
levels above it. This picture gives a first intuition of the AI idea of search:
If a problem is too complex, divide it into simpler ones.
Next, consider that we need not divide the labor for each mouse to just a single level. A
mouse with some processing capacity can do “planning” — looking ahead by evaluating
possible sequences of actions — across at least some subset of interdependent nodes. By
remembering good sequences of actions, the mouse can have beliefs about its plans and
1

not just individual actions. Hence, the mice can divide the labor of the problem in many
possible ways, according to the plans that they are able to make:
If a plan (sequence of actions) for solving a problem is too complex, divide
it into simpler plans.
Finally, assume that, as this organization of mice learns to plan its way through this maze,
it also learns beliefs about individual actions at certain nodes of the maze, and later uses
these beliefs to inform how they navigate other similar mazes. The beliefs may not not
perfect, but “good enough” for the mice to use them as a stable basis for making plans in
these other mazes. In search, such imperfect but stable beliefs about problems are called
heuristics, or rules-of-thumb for guiding individual actions. Using heuristics economizes
on information processing capacity, in that starting closer to a solution to a problem (not
just having 50-50 beliefs about whether to go left or right at each node of the maze)
reduces the need for costly learning and, hence, is more efficient:
Agents make plans (sequences of actions) to solve problems efficiently
(economizing on information processing) by learning and using heuristics.
The above discussion explains what will be meant by the AI idea of search in our course:
dividing the labor of solving a complex problem into plans, using heuristics to economize
on information processing. Our questions for this session, hence, will be: What is meant
by “plans” and “heuristics”? What does a “search process” look like? And what
implications does search have for the credit assignment problem?
To study these questions robustly, we will, once again, consider two paradigmaticallydifferent approaches. A first approach, which we will call von Neumann search, after
one of its pioneers, the mathematician John von Neumann (1903-1957), conjures search
as playing a well-defined game, such as a player searching for a sequence of moves in
chess. This approach extends our previously studied ideas of reinforcement learning,
Shannon information, and of credit assignment as a matter of brute force. A second
approach, which we will call Simon search, after Herbert Simon (1916-2001), instead
conjures search as an open-ended process of understanding and structuring an ill-defined
problem, such as an entrepreneur developing a new product for an uncertain market.

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
In AI textbooks, search is commonly introduced by the example of planning the shortest
route to travel from A to B, such as from home to the airport, where the nodes in between
are various intermediate locations such as a bus stop or train station. This course will take

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
a different approach, focusing instead on our fundamental analogy between AI and
organizations. As implied in the section above, search for us will be narrated as the
making of plans based on some division of labor and, hence, as about coordinating
interdependent tasks. To make this story stick, we will need a somewhat unfamiliar shift
in perspective — one that takes a detour into 19th century industrial factories and early
examples of computers. The payoff of this detour will be a basis for understanding the
foundational AI idea of search less in terms of optimizing a route from A to B, and more
as a fundamental approach to assigning credit for any complex real-world problem.
2.1 The division of labor as a general solution to credit assignment
The modern concept of dividing the labor of a problem dates back to the start of the
industrial revolution in 18th century Europe. The Scottish economist Adam Smith
explained the logic in his 1776 book The Wealth of Nations, giving the example of a
stylized pin factory that, as depicted below, divides the problem of making pins into tasks
involve making pin heads and pin bases, and tasks of assembling them.

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text: Tasks of (1) making pin bases; (2) making pinheads; and (3) assembling pins in a pin factory.

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
Smith considers two strategies for organizing the three tasks. In the first strategy, three
“generalists” are used, meaning each worker makes both the head and the base, and who
assembles the two parts. In the second strategy, the labor of each the three tasks is divided
across three “specialists”, meaning each focuses on just one of the tasks. Smith explained
how the latter is more economical thanks to gains to specialization. Why? In the
parlance of our course: simpler tasks have less interdependencies by definition, which
reduces the complexity of the credit assignment problem. Put another way, simple tasks
better enable learning how to do the tasks well. Hence, it is not just that a simple task
done by a specialist is easier to perform, but that it is easier to learn to perform.
Building on Smith’s insight on the gains to specialization, 19th century English
economist Charles Babbage made three bold proposals in a famous 1834 book titled On
the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures. First, Babbage proposed, any complex
task can be divided into simpler subtasks, such that gains to specialization can be
achieved for any problem of any complexity, In the parlance of our course, the division of
labor is a general solution to the problem of learning to assign credit. Second, once one

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
has learned to divide labor into simple enough tasks, any task can be mechanized (i.e.,
built into an AI system). Third, this logic applies not just to physical tasks like making
pins, but equally to any problems of thinking; further, if thinking problems can be divided
into simple enough mental tasks, it is possible to mechanize thought by building a general
purpose “thinking machine”.
2.2 Dividing labor into plans (programs)
Babbage’s analytic engine was inspired by a newly invented technology at the time called
the Jacquard loom, in which the pattern to be woven into a fabric could be mechanized
as a sequence of instructions for actions corresponding to holes punched into a card, as
depicted below. Babbage called this sequence of instructions as the algorithm, which you
can think of as some “precise and unambiguous specification for controlling a sequence
of steps that can be carried out mechanically” (XX).

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
A program being inserted in a Jacquard​
loom for making a fabric pattern.

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
A punched card produced by IBM to store programs,
and widely used in digital computers into the 1960s.

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
Babbage proposed further that physically implementing plans (i.e., mechanizing any
sequence of actions for any task) could be done in the same way, as the loom — as
“punched cards” that he called “programs”. In this definition, a program involves both
the software and hardware for “getting it done” — for executing a plan. Collections of
programs can be stored and accumulated and inserted into a machine as desired, hence
serving as a kind of “memory” (e.g., just as a weaver may accumulate “programs”
(punched cards) for many fabric patterns). Finally, given a complex problem, Babbage
noted that programs could mechanize only subsets of tasks. Hence, intelligent
problem-solving ultimately involved learning a collection of programs (i.e., plans) for
subtasks, and learning to select specific programs for specific tasks as needed.
2.3 Effective procedures as measures of program complexity
Babbage’s proposals imply a complementary view of the complexity of a problem (i.e., of
the challenge of credit assignment) from our previous session, not in terms of the amount
of information required but the number of actions to take — that is, the complexity of
executing plans or programs. We will refer to this measure as procedural complexity, in
that the sequence of actions for executing a plan is essentially a step-by-step procedure —
and of the minimum number of actions for a plan or program as the minimal effective

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
procedure. The standard way of measuring the effective procedure was introduced in
1936 by the mathematician and co-founder of the field Alan Turing, which he illustrated
through a mathematical model of a hypothetical computing machine (also called an
automaton), now called a Turing machine.
The Turing machine consists of a memory in the form of an infinite tape of symbols of
0’s and 1’s that can be inputted into each “cell” of the tape. You should note: the symbols
may look similar to the 0,1 bit strings in Shannon information, but this is just an example;
the values of the cells in a Turing machine can contain any symbol. The Turing machine
has a “head” (depicted as the bold square below, on the middle cell), which can do any of
three operations: (1) read the symbol, (2) modify the symbol, or (3) move left or right.
Programs consist of logical rules for executing sequences of such operations. A program
to change the five symbols in the cells above to their opposite (X,0,X,1,X,1,0,0,X,X,X →
X,1,X,0,X,0,1,1,X,X,X), for example, would consist of a procedure for the Turing
machine to move left or right and modify the five cells by flipping their values from 0 to
1 or 1 to 0. Each move or modification of a cell is said to transition the machine into a
new state of the machine. A state refers to the current values of each cell after a
particular move and the current location of the head.

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
A slice of the “infinite tape” of a Turing machine
The complexity of a program can be measured as the number of states in which the
program needs to make moves or modifications (i.e., the length of the “effective
procedure”). Hence, the complexity of a problem refers to the amount of states that a
program needs to transition through. The example above illustrates just a tiny program;
Turing and his successors in theories of computation have shown mathematically that as
the program size grows, the complexity of moves and modifications grows
combinatorially.
3. Search processes
Let us return to our earlier depiction of the process of search as structured into nodes
arranged from top to bottom like a hierarchical organization. You can think of the nodes
as the possible “states” of a problem, and now refer to this picture as a search tree (or,
equivalently, a state space or search space). In a search tree, a state refers to a description
of a problem adequate to guide an agent’s actions towards a goal akin to the states of a
Turing machine. A state should provide enough information (intermediate feedback) for

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
an agent to trigger some heuristic (rule-of-thumb) that guides its selection of the next
action. Agents start in an initial state. They then generate actions to “transition” the
agent to intermediate states until (hopefully) eventually reaching a goal state. The
credit assignment challenge is how to make such transitions efficient, which we look at
next as based on heuristics (3.1), including a special heuristic called satisficing (3.2).
3.1 Search as a heuristic process
We will call any process of transitioning from an initial state to a goal state in a search
tree as a search process. Agents search by generating, evaluating, and selecting among
plans — i.e., sequences of actions that transition them from an initial state toward a goal
state — using heuristics to guide which plans (or parts of plans) to generate-and-test and
which to ignore.
Why call this process “search”? The term is meant to evoke how, given limited
processing capacity of agents and the combinatorial complexity of a problem’s search
tree (e.g., complexity of the “effective procedure”), agents cannot evaluate every possible
action or path. Hence, we use this term by contrast to brute force: rather than describe
and test out every state, search involves economizing by using heuristics to make
educated guesses about which actions to try, evaluating only parts of the search tree.

(e.g., “path A” could be all possible
solutions beginning with “0”).

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
Consider, for example, searching for a sequence of six numbers needed to open the safe
depicted above. If an agent tries to identify the solution through brute force, this would
involve trying out as many as 1 million combinations (if the possible values are 0-9),
starting with (0,0,0,0,0,0) and going as far as (9,9,9,9,9,9). If the combination for the safe
is set randomly, then this complexity cannot be avoided. In most problems, however,
there are ways of learning or acquiring heuristics that dramatically reduce the size of the
tree that has to be searched. This effect of search is called “pruning” the search tree, in
that using heuristics — essentially, rules that guide or stipulate what actions to take or

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
consider at a particular node — often has the effect of eliminating large sequences of
actions or paths (also often called “branches”).

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text: “Pruning” a “branch” of a search tree.

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text:
Search processes may be informed by a variety of heuristics. As depicted below, they
may be generic strategies in an AI system, such as “breadth-first” (search many possible
paths, only generating-and-testing a few actions for each path), or “depth-first” (search
only one or a few paths, but generate-and-test many actions for each path). Heuristics
may also be rules learned by organizations based on specific experiences. For example, a
management team might learn rules of testing a product in at least two markets before
investing in scaling it.

text_units.section: 2. Plans: dividing the labor of problem-solving
text_units.text: Breadth- versus depth-first

3.2 Search as a satisficing process
Given that an agent cannot evaluate every state of a search tree and must use heuristics, it
cannot be guaranteed of finding the best plan for solving a problem. Based on this
observation, Simon famously proposed that intelligent agents “satisfice”, meaning that
they search only for satisfactory plans for solving problems, rather than for optimal
plans or by maximizing rewards. Satisficing is itself a heuristic, corresponding to a rule
of “generate plans until a satisfactory solution is identified, then stop generating plans”.
Simon proposed his theory of satisficing based, firstly, on economic assumptions about
information processing costs that hold under either Shannon or Simon information. Plans
for solving problems become “good enough” (satisfactory) for an agent when
economizing on the time and effort involved in searching for better plans outweigh the
benefits of doing so. For this to occur, plans must be close enough to a goal state to cross
a satisfactory threshold, or what Simon called an agent’s “aspiration level”. For
7

example, a management team might have a satisficing heuristic of withdrawing from
efforts to innovate a new product if profits fall under its aspiration level for six months.
Second, satisficing also follows from Simon’s physical symbol system hypothesis that
we looked at in the previous session. Given information about states of a search tree are
physical symbols, they only designate objects or concepts in the external world, they do
not constitute it. This physical world, he emphasized, will always have vastly more
information than any state descriptions. Problems are therefore always solved based on
limited information relative to the real world, even given seemingly unlimited “channel
capacity”. Agents simplify descriptions of states using what he called models of the
world. As mere simplifications, such models satisfice rather than optimize.
Finally, Simon emphasized that satisficing arises from how complex problems have goals
that are inherently organizational. By organizational, he meant that goals are multiple,
often contradictory, and often qualitative in nature and hence ambiguous in terms of the
supposed “optimality” of a particular solution. For example, fulfilling the mission of an
organization to “contribute to society” could have multiple interpretations, which may
vary by department and be mapped to hundreds or even thousands of metrics. Hence,
plans used in search are really better thought of as like organizational programs, where
the complexity is not just that implied by a Turing machine but extends to how processes
for learning and selecting these programs are bound up in complex organizational goals
that map to problems with no clearly “optimal” solution.
3.3 Paradigmatically-different approaches to search
This section has defined search in general terms as a heuristic process of generating and
evaluating satisfactory plans to solve problems. You can understand search as a general
strategy for learning to make and select plans (programs) for solving problems in an AI
system or organization more efficiently, given the view of complexity implied by the
Turing machine. At the same time, this section has also illustrated how the complexity of
problems that search is meant to address goes beyond what is implied by the Turing
machine or our earlier example of the pin factory. How we conceive of search depends on
what we assume when we talk about the states in a search tree and what we assume about
how agents can evaluate them as a basis for making and selecting plans.
In the next two sections, we will see that such assumptions can build on either paradigm
that we have looked at so far — reinforcement learning and Shannon information, or
learning in a society and Simon information. What we will call von Neumann search
builds on the former, conceiving of search as akin to playing a well-defined game. What
we will call Simon search builds on the latter, conceiving of search as understanding and
structuring an ill-defined problem.

text_units.section: 4. Von Neumann search: search as game-playing
text_units.text:
4. Von Neumann search: search as game-playing
A first approach to search derives from, among others, the seminal work of the
mathematician John von Neumann in the 1930s and 1940s on game theory. You can
think of a game as simply a problem where there are two or more agents whose actions
are interdependent, yet who have conflicting goals. Put another way, the problem-solving
environment for an agent is not just external to it, but can be outright hostile. Hence,
agents’ search for a sequence of actions must consider the strategies of “opponent”
agents. This approach to search has focused on strategies for playing various well-defined
games, from tic-tac-toe to chess, Go, backgammon and many others.
4.1 Why games?
Why games? Unlike a simple division of labor problem, such as how to plan the
sequences of three or so tasks in a pin factory, the adversarial nature of even seemingly
simple games results in a combinatorially-explosive set of states and, hence, problems
that cannot be solved by brute force alone. On the other hand, games, at least of the sort
studied in von Neumann search, have well-defined rules, which enables precisely
studying search processes using mathematical approaches that appealed to von Neumann
and many other mathematically-oriented researchers.
In the AI field specifically, the assumption is that AI systems that learn how to play
relatively complex games such as chess or Go can serve as stepping stones for AI
systems that learn any problem, such as protein folding or science in general. In
management research, a further appeal of games has been for economists, who view the
adversarial nature of a game as akin to how a manager has to make decisions under
uncertainty and complexity in a competitive environment.
A disadvantage, as we shall see, is that this game-based approach to search mostly
abstracts away from the intuitions about the division of labor and programs that we
discussed in Section 2 above. Indeed, AI textbooks do not typically connect the idea of
search to examples such as the pin factory; discussions mostly focus on algorithms, rather
than their instantiation in programs; and typically this game-based approach makes what
is called a unitary actor assumption, in that it does not matter much whether one
assumes that nodes are assigned to different agents — the entire search process is
controlled by a single centralized agent.
4.2 Heuristics defined in terms of economic utility functions
In games such as chess or backgammon where all the rules and, hence, goals are defined,
there is no inherent need for physical symbols. All the information about the game can, in

text_units.section: 4. Von Neumann search: search as game-playing
text_units.text:
principle at least, be defined in terms of meaningless bits, consistent with Shannon
information. Likewise, all goals and intermediate feedback can be described without any
physical symbols, such that all states can be evaluated with respect to some numerical
reward value. In economics, and in game theoretic versions of search in the AI field, this
reward is called the utility for an agent. Hence, the search tree is really a purely syntactic
game tree, in which nodes are mapped to numerical values of the expected rewards for
pursuing a path through what is called a utility function.
To see this utility function in action, let us consider the figure of a search tree again, but
now instead of mice and T-mazes, the nodes will be moves in the game of checkers, as in
Arthur Samuel’s famous checkers program from 1959, mentioned in our session on credit
assignment, depicted below. Each path or “branch” of the tree refers to a particular
sequence of states of the checkers game from the perspective of one player. We will call
one player “Max”, since she or he will try to maximize the utility values shown in the
figure, while the opponent “Min” wants to minimize these utility values.
Max “explores” the game tree by starting from the top and considering the expected value
(utility) of the first move. Since 20 is higher than 7, Max selects that direction and, if
using a depth-first heuristic, then explores that path. Since it is combinatorially explosive,
Max cannot explore the whole game tree, it uses its utility function to calculate the rest
of the nodes for the branches that Max considers, then sends this information back up to
decide on a path, a process called backward propagation, or just backprop. Max then
selects the move with the highest value (“utility”).

text_units.section: 4. Von Neumann search: search as game-playing
text_units.text:
In the above game tree, how are the scores for the nodes assigned? In von Neumann
search, this is estimated based on what is called an evaluation function, which you can
think of as some collection of various amounts of intermediate feedback, such as
counting up the pieces remaining, the kings remaining, or any other information that is
found to be statistically correlated with the probability of winning. Such a function is
heuristic, in that it is calculated not by evaluating all the states of the game tree (which
would be combinatorially explosive), but by giving an estimate of the value of each state
based on various heuristic measures of intermediate feedback. By collapsing these

text_units.section: 4. Von Neumann search: search as game-playing
text_units.text:
heuristic measures into a single numerical value for the “utility” of each state, alternative
actions can be ranked to guide the search process (i.e., path selection).
4.3 Satisficing by extending the reinforcement paradigm of maximizing rewards
In von Neumann search, since the state of a game can be estimated using the evaluation
function as a single “reward”. Hence, under von Neumann search, where all the rules of a
game are well-defined such that it is consistent with Shannon information, the learning
mechanism is naturally from the reinforcement paradigm (and which may extend to other
machine learning techniques that we will cover later in the course). Samuel’s checkers
program, for example, famously used reinforcement learning to improve the evaluation
function itself. Hence, as the checkers program played many games, it learned heuristics
about which positions on the board are good.
The AI researcher Demis Hassibis, head of Google’s DeepMind, and creator of its
famous AlphaGo program for playing the game of Go, and AlphaFold for predicting
protein structures, has adopted a lot of this basic set-up, combining reinforcement
learning with a type of von Neumann search. Based on seeing such progress, Hassibis’s
point of view is that combining various search and reinforcement or related learning
strategies will be sufficient for intelligence. Hence, what becomes important are many
interacting heuristic functions, tied together through the ideas of search and
reinforcement or similar learning strategies, all broadly within the von Neumann
approach to search. You may contrast this with Richard Sutton’s preference to focus on
his reward hypothesis, which focuses on collapsing all such search and other functions to
a single scalar for reward.

text_units.section: 5. Simon search: search as means-ends analysis
text_units.text:
5. Simon search: search as means-ends analysis
A second approach pioneered by Simon, along with his colleague at Carnegie-Mellon
Allen Newell, developed by way of contrast with von Neumann-style search and its
emphasis on well-defined game trees. Simon’s focus was instead to start with realistic
models of how managers make decisions under uncertainty. The distinction that Simon
made was that managers have an open-ended world in front of them, rather than a
complete environment determined by well-defined game rules. For Simon, this
open-endedness meant search was not just about coming up with a utility function, and
corresponding evaluation function, but rather of the ability to manipulate physical
symbols to transform some simplified model into a model of some meaningful goal state.
5.1 Heuristics as general methods for manipulating physical symbols
In Simon search, heuristics are used to inform actions for manipulating physical symbols
in programs. Specifically a program would have: (i) A set of meaningful physical symbols

text_units.section: 5. Simon search: search as means-ends analysis
text_units.text:
organized based on lists, and which can be transformed into descriptions of intermediate
states; (ii) A set of operators, which refers to the actions for transforming symbols that an
agent can take; (iii) A set of rules regarding how operators transform symbols, which
determines how actions transition the agent to another state. When an operator is applied,
then the corresponding rule is invoked, and the symbols are transformed.
When an agent takes an action (invokes an operator) that does not immediately lead to
the goal state, how does the agent figure out what to do next? Newell and Simon’s
solution was that, if two states are not equal (i.e., current state and goal state), then this
difference can be thought of as a measure of intermediate feedback. The agent can then
quantify the feedback about the difference between the current state and the goal state.
The particular difference is then linked to a heuristic, and the heuristic invokes an action
likely to get the agent closer to the goal (to a new and better intermediate state).
Newell & Simon called their system the “General Problem Solver”, or GPS, as a model
of intelligent search (e.g., search with learning). In GPS, information is generated in the
form of differences between the current state and the goal state or any identified
subgoal states. To illustrate the idea, Simon gave the example of solving algebraic
expressions. For example, consider how to solve for X in the algebraic expression:
5X+3=2X+7
One could do naïve “generate and test” (pure search) by simply generating different
possible values for X and seeing if both sides of the equation are equal. Yet, assuming we
do not make a lucky guess, a generate and test strategy would not provide much
information (feedback), other than that the previous guess was incorrect. Instead,
intelligent problem-solvers would first rearrange the expression to read:
5X+3-2X-7=0
In this case, one can use a generate and test strategy more effectively as a source of
information or feedback. That is, since the X variables are all on one side, we can see
how close each guess gets to 0 and gradually improve our guesses, reducing the amount
of possible values to search. Still more effective, however, is to see that the above
algebraic expression is a general example of X = Y, and thus to rearrange with X all in
one coefficient:
3X=4
and then to:
X = 4/3

text_units.section: 5. Simon search: search as means-ends analysis
text_units.text:
Once the problem is described in this state, one can find the solution of X = 4/3 with no
search at all. The key idea is that the goal state is already represented in the initial
state. The operations for solving the algebraic expression were essentially symbol
manipulation by reasoning using the rules of algebra — that is transforming the initial set
of symbols into the goal state. In information processing terms, all the information is
given by the initial state and the rules about the domain that we assume.
As illustrated by the simple but powerful transformations in this algebra example, Newell
& Simon’s idea in GPS was to boil down the vast universe of possible heuristics to their
essentials — to heuristics for generating heuristics. They proposed, for example, that
there were fundamental heuristics at play, which they referred to as fundamental
“methods”, or “schemes” for setting up subgoals, and which describe the essence of
heuristic search, and include: (i) “Pattern-matching”: First, given a goal of transforming
object A into B, then the objects are matched and “compared element by element”. If
there is a difference among one or more elements, then a subgoal is generated of reducing
this difference; (ii) “Generate-and-test”: Second, select an operator, and try it out based
on the given rules, then apply the same pattern matching process and see if A is now
closer to B. Hence, in search, learning works by developing fundamental heuristics that,
given any goal state and initial state, could generally construct and “discover” new
heuristics through the search process itself.
5.3 Learning as the use of search operations to acquire new heuristics like an expert
Simon realized that a central challenge was how an AI system could have enough diverse
experiences to learn heuristics for solving any problem. This challenge of learning to
acquire heuristics became regarded among scholars of search as the central “bottleneck”
to intelligence. One solution is simply to hand-code the heuristics by interviewing human
experts and having them articulate them, a line of research called expert systems.
Simon’s idea, however, was not to accumulate many heuristics, but rather to closely study
how experts across many fields solved problems (e.g., chess grandmasters, scientists,
athletes) and generalize these findings into a model of search by experts — essentially, to
identify a small number of highly general heuristics such that an agent could learn to
acquire heuristics on its own. Subsequent research by his students found, for example,
that experts in various fields used heuristics related to “deliberate practice” to learn other
heuristics, or that entrepreneurs used heuristics to construct business ideas in a piecemeal
fashion (a process called “effectuation”) rather than plan things out ahead of time.

Course Notes — SESSION 4
EVOLUTIONARY STRATEGIES

1. Introduction
In the previous session, we introduced the idea that credit may be assigned efficiently by
viewing problem-solving as a search for merely satisfactory solutions. Yet recall our
examples from the first session: the shipbuilder learning to build ships, the app developer
learning to develop features, or the budget committee learning to invest. The real-world
complexity of their problems suggested a vast search tree. Using heuristics to “prune”
branches of this tree may still enable searching only a small part of it, implying that
satisfactory solutions are not guaranteed. We may need additional ways to learn where in
the tree to search effectively, not just how to search efficiently.

We will call processes of learning to search effectively for solutions to problems as ones
of adaptation, and AI ideas for how to adapt as evolutionary strategies, in that they
derive from Darwinism (more on this connection later). The overall strategy will be,
rather than just assign credit to sequentially-interdependent actions (the focus of
reinforcement learning), to assign credit across spatially-interdependent actions. Such an
overall strategy, we will see, essentially fleshes out the logic of Simon’s watchmaker
parable. In the parable, the challenge is not really the sequence of the watch assembly
tasks, but in the need for effective decomposition based on understanding how a large
number of parts are spatially-configured to function together. Likewise, in this session,
we will take the fundamental challenge of intelligence as essentially one of decomposing
the parts of a problem according to their functions.

This focus on spatial interdependence will call for us to shift to a new way of thinking
about what a program or plan is. From now on, we will treat programs as less like a
sequential, step-by-step procedure, and instead more like diagrammatic blueprints or
schematics that describe how the building blocks of a problem fit together. We will call
such programs as schemas or, alternatively, representations of problems.

Our goal in this session will be to relate these schemas or problem representations to
much vaster state spaces than our previous session, and thus to consider how to learn to
search effectively in these spaces (or whether even the idea of “search” still makes sense).
To do so, we will visualize problem-solving as an adaptive process of navigating the
surface of something called a performance landscape, in which solutions map to
different “elevations” that correspond to higher or lower performance.

Here too, we will see two paradigmatically-different approaches. In a first approach
closer to the reinforcement paradigm — which we will call the genetic approach for its
inspiration from how genes and chromosomes evolve — adaptation is viewed as simply

1
 another type of search process. In a second approach closer to the learning-in-a-society
paradigm — which we will call the biological systems approach for its inspiration in
how evolution happens at the level of more complex units such as cells or organisms —
adaptation is viewed as requiring distinct ways of manipulating symbols beyond search.

text_units.section: 2. Adaptation: linking evolution to problem-solving in AI systems and organizations
text_units.text:
2. Adaptation: linking evolution to problem-solving in AI systems and organizations
Evolutionary strategies in AI systems and organizations can be traced to the work of
Charles Darwin in the 19th century. Though Darwinism is familiarly thought of in terms
of animals and plants, it is a general approach to thinking about adaptation in artificial
systems as well. Darwinism implies that a fundamental way of thinking about the
intelligence of any complex system is its “fitness”, meaning its ability to survive and
reproduce relative to other systems. Fitness depends on the ability to adapt to changes
in the environment. In the parlance of our course, adaptation is essentially a
generate-and-test strategy for assigning credit at the population-level (e.g., among a
population of pin factories or organisms in a species).

2.1. The magic of adaptation
In AI, the magic of evolution is that some simple rules such as the market mechanism —
and more generally called evolutionary operators — can be astonishingly powerful for
adapting solutions to problems of vast complexity. These operators are commonly
summarized as VSR, standing for variation (generating different solutions), selection
(assigning credit to high-fitness (i.e., high-performing) solutions), and retention (using
high-performing solutions in the next “generation” of trials).

Consider that what Babbage would have observed in early 19th century England was a
vast number of competing factories. Whether by design or not, each of these factories
would divide labor a bit differently (variation). Their differences would, in turn, lead to
differences in the quality and cost of their pins. Credit would be assigned by market
forces (selection). Factories that made higher quality or cheaper pins would thrive
(retention). Factories that made lower quality or more expensive pins would go bankrupt.
Over time, the market would “learn” to assign credit (i.e., select) high-performing pin
factories.

In evolutionary terms, we would say that the firms that thrive have higher “fitness”. In
the AI field today, performance is often evaluated using benchmarks claimed to
correspond to some absolute measure of intelligence. Yet consider our mouse and the
maze. Its “intelligence” in learning to find the cheese was relative to how its actions “fit”
the mazes that were given to it. Even if its learning were to generalize to all mazes, the
mouse would still be specialized for maze problems rather than all problems in the

2
 universe. For this course, we will likewise think of performance in AI and organizations
similarly in terms of “fitness” of solutions to problems relative to the specific type of
problem. The intuition is similar to how, in evolution, “survival of the fittest” applies to
organisms that perform well (i.e., survive and reproduce) in specific niches (e.g., hippos
in the tropics; penguins in Antarctica) rather than the whole world.

text_units.section: 2.2 Visualizing adaptive processes with performance landscapes
text_units.text:
2.2 Visualizing adaptive processes with performance landscapes
The process of adaptively search for higher fitness in a problem-solving environment can
be usefully visualized through the metaphor of a performance landscape. A performance
landscape is a picture of the relationship between an agent’s actions (e.g., choices or
observations) and its performance with respect to a goal. The Y-axis (the “elevation” of
the landscape) is the measure of performance. Higher “elevation” corresponds to higher
performance. Though there may be multiple goals, we will assume that they are
aggregated into a single performance measure captured by the Y-axis. The X-axis (the
bottom of the landscape) is a set of actions, each of which has one or more states (i.e.,
possible values). As an example, imagine a laptop design problem that involves four
components, the screen, the CPU, the memory, and the keyboard, each of which have 10
possible types. The actions would be choices or observations of the four components, and
the states would be whichever of the 10 types are chosen or observed.

text_units.section: 2.2 Visualizing adaptive processes with performance landscapes
text_units.text:
If there is only one action on the X-axis, the “landscape” is a 2D depiction of its
relationship to performance. If there are two dimensions on the X-axis, then the
landscape becomes 3D, and so forth. More typically, solving real-world problems
involves taking vastly more than two actions. Since humans cannot easily visualize high
dimensionality, however, a landscape is essentially a highly simplified visualization of
the dimensions of the X-axis to 2D or 3D.

text_units.section: 2.2 Visualizing adaptive processes with performance landscapes
text_units.text:
Hence, performance landscapes are used in research on AI and organizations as visually
intuitive ways of depicting the feedback-driven processes (e.g., trial-and-error) by which
an agent learns to take actions to achieve goals — not as precise depictions. They allow
visualizing the learning process metaphorically as a “journey” across the surface of a
landscape. The “journey” begins when the agent takes some initial actions. The particular
actions that the agent takes lead to lower or higher performance, corresponding to points
at various elevations on the landscape. The agent modifies its actions based on feedback
about its performance (i.e., about its current position on the landscape), “journeying” to
different points on the landscape.

text_units.section: 2.2 Visualizing adaptive processes with performance landscapes
text_units.text:
To construct a landscape, we first need to define a performance landscape with respect to
a goal related to some problem to be solved. The problem may be specific (e.g., how to
get from A to B) or general (e.g., how to navigate in general). The “real” landscape is

text_units.section: 2.2 Visualizing adaptive processes with performance landscapes
text_units.text:
3
 called an agent’s task environment. For any real-world problem, there will be a vast
number of possible actions and performance criteria that belong to the agent’s task
environment. Given limited processing capacity, the agent considers only a small number
of actions and performance criteria at any one time. The agent hence works with only
simplified, imperfect symbolic representations of its task environment. We will refer to
these simplified representations of symbols as the agent’s schemas, though they are
sometimes referred to as models, candidate solutions, programs, plans, schematics,
frameworks or other terms.

text_units.section: 2.2 Visualizing adaptive processes with performance landscapes
text_units.text:
To interpret a landscape, we need to describe (1) a performance goal; (2) the set of
actions and states in the schema; (3) procedures for selecting actions in response to
feedback; (4) procedures for learning to modify the procedures (e.g., setting a learning
rate). Different AI ideas correspond to different procedures. In reinforcement learning,
the action process is based on a policy, such as the mouse’s policy of when to turn left or
right in the T-maze. In search, the basic process is the use of heuristics. We will see other
ideas throughout the course. Most generally, action processes are based on encoding and
decoding bit strings in Shannon information, and interpreting lists in Simon information.

3. Landscape topologies
The topology of a landscape depicts differences in the quality of solutions in a population
that we may expect to see. The “landscape” can be composed of “hills”, “valleys”, or
“mesas” or any other features one can imagine. We can depict this as a “single peaked”
landscape, with gentle slopes, a landscape with multiple fitness peaks, called a “rugged”
landscape, or one with no peaks and just thresholds (a “mesa” landscape).

3.1 Single-peaked landscapes: hill-climbing (a.k.a., gradient descent)
Perhaps the simplest “journey” in a performance landscape is a simple trial-and-error
learning strategy. The trial-and-error feedback can be depicted by “hills” or “gradients”
in the landscape that depict a basis for trial-and-error learning. The intuition is that hills
or gradients refer to points in the landscape that are close together, yet where there is a
noticeable performance difference. An agent whose current actions map to a position on a
“hill” in the landscape can “learn” to reach a nearby point just by moderately modifying
actions. If the performance measure is some value to maximize, then this process is called
“hill-climbing”. If the performance measure is something to minimize, then the
landscape is simply viewed upside-down, and the learning process is called “gradient
descent”.

4
     A 3D view of hill-climbing           ​    A 2D view of gradient descent

In this simplest landscape, there is just one “global peak” of performance, also called the
global optimum (or, alternatively, a single gradient to descend — the global minimum).
In a single-peaked landscape, the agent smoothly “hill-climbs” to the peak of the
landscape — trial-and-error will always lead to the global optimum.

Though simple to depict, it does not mean that learning in such a landscape is necessarily
easy. Remember that a 2D or 3D depiction of the landscape is just a visual aid, whereas
actual landscapes are hyperdimensional. If the number of interdependent actions is large,
then hill-climbing to the peak or gradient descent to the minimum may involve a steady
yet incredibly long journey. For example, in organizations, the single peak may refer to
the design of some complex product or system of activities that only becomes
competitive in the market if some single optimal configuration is achieved.

3.2 Rugged landscapes: hill-climbing and long-jumps
Let us go back to the earlier example of designing four components of a laptop — the
screen, CPU, memory, and keyboard. Let us call each component’s effect on performance
as its contribution to the “fitness” of the laptop (e.g., how valuable the laptop would be
for potential customers). For each laptop component, however, what we really need to do
is specify a more complex contribution function to account for how the contributions
are interdependent with other components. For example, the contribution of the CPU
component to the value of the laptop depends in part on whether it is fast enough to
support the memory component. Similar to how the multiple moves made by the mouse
in the labyrinth were interdependent, the possible configurations increase
combinatorially. It will be difficult to evaluate (i.e., assign credit to) all of them.

Due to interdependence and combinatorial complexity, even small changes to just a
single component can have large effects on the performance (i.e., fitness) of the laptop.
Simulations show that performance differences — gradients or hills — arise in similar
types of configurations, even if none of them are optimal. These clusters of performance
are called “local peaks” in the landscape, or simply “local maxima”, and make the
landscape look “rugged”. Given that the laptop designer initially starts somewhere

5
 randomly on the landscape, if there is a local peak nearby, it will be tempting to just
“hill-climb” to it. Once at the local peak, there is no more gradient, and the learning
stops. For example, a laptop designer might choose a screen size that is not ideal for
customers, but then simply modify the other components (CPU, memory, keyboard) to
“fit” the screen size. Such a laptop would be optimal given the choice of screen size, but
not “globally” optimal. This is called being “stuck” or “frozen” on a local peak.

Such learning is called “myopic”, in that the agent is only seeing things locally, rather
than the entire landscape, and hence missing the global optimum. Let us further assume
that actions are modified in the “neighborhood” of previous actions (e.g., as assumed in
hill-climbing), then agents just climb to the nearest peak. Hence, the costs of myopia
depend on the luck of wherever our initial actions map to in the performance landscape.
This is called path dependence, meaning that early actions have a large effect on the
overall learning process. Finally, you should see that a rugged landscape also helps
visualize the phenomenon of superstitious learning. When we go up the “wrong” local
peak, it is because we are getting feedback that our performance is improving, yet this
feedback may be just superstition or at best partially true.
​      A rugged landscape showing the possibility of getting “stuck” on a local peak.

Clearly, to avoid myopia and path dependence, we need to be able to move off of local
peaks to other peaks until, hopefully, we discover the global maximum. As distinct from
incremental hill-climbing within a peak, we will call such movement in the landscape as
“long-jumping”. To do so requires making bigger modifications to actions than in
hill-climbing — modifications that are not just informed by immediate feedback, but are
more risky (hence, the “jumping” metaphor). We will call such actions as “exploration”,
in that we are venturing into a part of the landscape about which we do not have good
feedback. Conversely, we will call smaller modifications — hill-climbing actions — as
“exploitation”, in the sense that such actions exploit the feedback immediately available
to us. Though exploitation clearly puts us at risk for myopia and path dependence,
exploration carries its own risks of venturing into the relative unknown. For example, the

6
 laptop designer could make a bold new change to the screen component, but may not
have any reliable feedback on whether that change will increase or decrease fitness.
The presence of multiple “local peaks” of performance in a “rugged” landscape thus
raises a fundamental tradeoff for learning in AI and organizations.

Given that both “exploring” and “exploiting” have risks, the idea in learning programs in
AI and in organizations is often to balance the two strategically. The ideal balance
depends on many factors, such as the rate or degree of change in the environment, the
skills of the agent to “explore” intelligently, or the importance of finding an optimal
“combination”. We classically see this tradeoff in organizations, for example, in the areas
of product innovation and strategy, where managers continually have to decide whether
to invest their budgets in doing what they do a bit better, or risk doing something
different.

text_units.section: 3.3 Satisficing and the landscape: lowering expectations vs. taking giant strides
text_units.text:
3.3 Satisficing and the landscape: lowering expectations vs. taking giant strides
We can depict satisficing in a performance landscape simply as a threshold for
performance, reflecting Simon’s term of an aspiration level. Any point higher than the
threshold is satisfactory (and, hence, stops the adaptive “journey” through the landscape),
and any point below the threshold is not satisfactory (such that the “journey” continues).
Let us think of satisficing, however, in two different ways.

text_units.section: 3.3 Satisficing and the landscape: lowering expectations vs. taking giant strides
text_units.text:
In one way, we can think of satisficing as simply lowering our expectations for desired
fitness for a given problem. Here, the adaptive actions can be exploratory or exploitative,
just as in rugged landscapes. You can think of this aspiration level as being higher than
some local peaks, but lower than the global peak. Hence, the benefit of satisficing is that,
even while economizing on information processing, the agent is able to avoid the worst
peaks, which may be “good enough”.

text_units.section: 3.3 Satisficing and the landscape: lowering expectations vs. taking giant strides
text_units.text: Satisficing in rugged (left) and mesa (right) landscapes.

text_units.section: 3.3 Satisficing and the landscape: lowering expectations vs. taking giant strides
text_units.text:
In a more fundamental way, however, we can think of a satisfactory solution with respect
to solving a problem that may be so complex that we may not even know quite how to
start. For example, in the laptop design problem, the product development team may be

text_units.section: 3.3 Satisficing and the landscape: lowering expectations vs. taking giant strides
text_units.text:
7
 asked to build an entirely new kind of laptop for which it does not have closely related
prior experience. Marvin Minsky referred to problem-solving environments of such
complexity as having “mesa”-like landscapes. In a mesa landscape, the agent starts by
taking actions that put it at some point on the bottom of the mesa (or so it seems to the
agent — it cannot be sure if it is closer to the goal). The top of the landscape is basically
flat, so the agent is not really concerned with the global optimum, or the risk of ending up
on a local peak (the peak is, at most, a trivial journey once the flat top is reached, as
depicted below). The agent somehow must get to some point at the flat top of the mesa —
the satisfactory threshold.

text_units.section: 3.3 Satisficing and the landscape: lowering expectations vs. taking giant strides
text_units.text:
Minsky referred to this threshold not so much as a personal aspiration level, but as some
threshold satisfactory understanding of a problem required to even think about engaging
in a search process. The key challenge here is different. Unlike a hilly or peaked
landscape, there are no obvious slopes for hill-climbing or long-jumping to a satisfactory
solution — exploration-exploitation strategies will not work. Minsky described the
process required instead as one of taking “giant strides” in the landscape, in that one has
to “climb the mesa” but generating and testing coherent pieces of evidence about what
the problem is (“strides” signifying that actions are always grounded in some sort of
coherent logical claim about the observations (i.e., data) for what to do next).
