3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
A set of constraints relevant to a complex problem in AI and organizations can be thought of as
structured into a network. A network (also called a graph structure) refers to any mathematical
structure that can be described in terms of some set of “nodes” and “links” (also called
“connections” or “relations”). You can think of a search tree as a very particular type of highly
restricted network, in which the nodes are states and the only links allowed between states are
sequential (i.e., the “paths” or “branches” of the search tree that each represent a possible
sequence of states or actions). The idea of a constraint network is far more general, and follows
from the definition of the elements in the table above. The nodes of a constraint network are any
set of variables. The links are any set of constraints that define relations among these variables.

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
7
 Recall the principle of locality, meaning that most of the time, we should only have to process
information about binary constraints (among two variables), such as Exterior color and Interior
color of the car, rather than the full combinatorial complexity of a problem. Now, we will look
into why this is the case, and where the power of representations really comes from with respect
to the fundamental intelligence problem of credit assignment. The credit assignment mechanism
can be explained in information processing terms through the concept of propagation.
Propagation refers to the sending of information across the links of a network.

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
To understand this idea, let’s again illustrate by way of comparison to search. In search, we could
kind of refer to a search tree as a network of states, yet the links between the states were not very
informative — they really just told us which part of the sequence we were in. In a constraint
network, in contrast, the links between variables are all defined clearly in terms of constraints.
Hence, any information about one constraint can potentially be a gold mine of intermediate
feedback for neighboring constraints to address the credit assignment problem. In fact, we can
say that (1) the more information about a constraint, the more potentially useful information can
be propagated to neighboring constraints; and (2) more connections among variables (i.e., the
more constraints that are defined) makes more propagation possible.

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
Consider a canonical example of constraints used in AI research of the game of Sudoku.
Sudoku is a puzzle game in which the problem to solve is to fill in each of 81 squares (the
variables) of a 9x9 grid with a number from 1-9 (the domain for each of the variables). The
rules of Sudoku stipulate that rows, columns and 3x3 grids of squares are all different in their
values. We can call these three rules the “all different” constraints of Sudoku. Now consider
how to solve the puzzle using a basic search strategy, similar to the example we saw earlier of
trying the combinations of a safe.

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
We saw for the safe that it would take an average of 15 days of trying a new combination every
10 seconds to open the safe, with just six numbers. In Sudoku, one would need to “guess” 81
numbers correctly out of 81! possible combinations, which would take vastly more time (or, in
reality, somewhat less, since some squares of the Sudoku board will typically come pre-filled,
but the results are qualitatively the same). The reason that we are able to solve Sudoku puzzles in
a reasonable time is that we use the constraints as a basis for propagating information across the
board. For example, in the figures below, consider how, given a Sudoku puzzle (left), one might

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
8
 make a move by guessing that there is a “2” in the top square of the middle 3x3 grid, and a “3” to
the right of it. Once you guess these values, however, you can “propagate” them across the three
constraints (the row, column, and 3x3 grid constraints, as highlighted in light blue), which shows
that the “2” guess violated the column and 3x3 grid constraint, and the “3” guess violated one of
the row constraints. This example illustrates the power of propagation as a mechanism for
processing information across a network, versus just processing information up and down the
paths of a search tree.

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
To visualize the power of propagation in Sudoku, the figure below on the left highlights how
each of the three basic constraints in Sudoku enables propagating information to distant areas
of a problem, using the “4” in the upper left corner as an example. The full set of possibilities
for propagation is depicted in the figure on the right, which shows how richly one can use
constraints to “put together the pieces of the puzzle” in Sudoku and, hence, the difference from
“searching” for combinations of a safe.

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
To further see the advantages of propagation across a constraint network (versus searching a
tree), consider a similar example of a crossword puzzle, as depicted in the figures below. In
search, we would ideally like to reduce the interdependencies among actions, since they lead to a
combinatorial explosion in possible solutions. Yet we had assumed only limited sources of
intermediate feedback. In crossword puzzles, solving each clue provides rich intermediate
feedback to help with neighboring clues, so the effect is the reverse. Hence, given that the clues
are the same difficulty, solving the crossword puzzle on the right will be easier than the one on
the left since there is more overlap among the unary constraints (the clues), and hence more
higher order constraints that can be used to propagate information. That is, the puzzle on the
right offers richer propagation, whereas the one on the left has less opportunities to propagate
information across the constraints.

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
9
 3.3 Satisfying constraints
Another major difference in AI ideas about representation versus search concerns the nature of
the goals. In search, the goal is to find a specific, ideally optimal, “path” through the tree. Agents
“satisfice” simply due to the fact that combinatorial complexity makes it impossible to process
enough information to search all of the paths. In representation strategy, in contrast, the idea is to
satisfy a set of constraints, where each constraint may have many possible satisfactory values
that can be said to each correspond to a particular goal. “Optimizing” any single constraint does
not necessarily allow you to optimize other constraints — it may be that the best that you can do
is pretty much to satisfice, even if you had unlimited information processing capacity. Depending
on the nature of our goal, we may assume either optimization or simply that all the constraints
are satisfied. You will see that this ability to just satisfy a set of constraints is fundamental to
addressing challenges of sparse learning, where understanding the representation of a problem
may be more important than finding an optimal solution (Minsky 1961).

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
We will think of goals in AI ideas about representation as relating to one of three ways of
satisfying a set of constraints: (1) “Find any solution”, where the goal is to identify any
combination within the full set of “possible worlds”, such as any car with different exterior and
interior colors; (2) “Find all solutions”: where the goal is to identify the full set of “possible
worlds”. In the car example, you may wish to know if a dealer has any cars that satisfy your
constraints.; and (3) “Find the best solution”: where the goal is optimization, given that the
constraints are defined in such a way as to make the “best” solution possible to find, such as
ordering which car colors you prefer the most.

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
In deciding how to frame the goals for solving a problem using representations, a key
consideration in AI and organizations is whether you assume the underlying constraints are
“hard” or “soft”. Hard constraints mean that a constraint is either satisfied by a value or it is
violated and, if it is violated, then the value cannot be part of a solution to the problem. For
example, if you care deeply about the car color constraint, then you will rule out any car whether
the exterior or interior colors are the same, regardless of any of the other features. Soft
constraints instead define constraints in terms of preferences or subjective beliefs, such as “I
prefer red over green for the car exterior”. Whereas hard constraints are defined in terms of an
if/then logic where violating a constraint ends the possibility of a solution, soft constraints are

text_units.section: 3.2 Propagating information across a constraint network
text_units.text:
10
 defined in terms of probabilities that impose a “cost” on violating the constraint such that it may
still be part of a solution.

text_units.section: 4. Four types of constraint networks used in AI
text_units.text:
4. Four types of constraint networks used in AI
The ideas of constraint propagation and constraint satisfaction characterize the overall idea of
using representations as a strategy for intelligence in AI systems and organizations. The precise
types of constraints and their structure (i.e., the shape of the constraint network) — and, hence,
the precise nature of propagation and, ultimately, learning — depends on underlying assumptions
about, for instance, the nature of information processing (e.g., Shannon versus Simon
information) and goals (e.g., optimizing versus satisficing). Next, we will go over three examples
of the AI ideas of constraints and propagation — (1) constraint satisfaction problems; (2) causal
nets; (3) Boltzmann machines — that will give you a broad basis for linking our discussion of
representations to their effects on intelligence in AI systems and organizations.

4.1 Constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs)
For given problems where the goal is to find a single solution (e.g. Sudoku), you can think of
constraint satisfaction as almost like a new type of search that interleaves representations. The
variables and domains can be of any type, but the goal should be given and usually is unique
(there is some optimal set of values for the constraints). We will refer to such representation-
informed search as constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs). In a CSP, the search part refers to
how finding a solution to a problem involves not just propagation, but some heuristic for
deciding which actions to take next (i.e., which particular constraints to focus on) to start a
propagation process. For example, in Sudoku, you have to start the game by guessing the value
of one of many possible squares, which then allows you to think about whether the guessed value
is consistent with the row, column, and 3x3 grid constraints (i.e., guessing the value allows you
to propagate information across these constraints to evaluate your guess and learn other
information).

After you propagate as much as you can, then you have to search by again guessing different
moves. In Sudoku, there are numerous heuristics for choosing which square to search, depending
on the current state of the game. Perhaps the most basic is called backtracking, which is a
depth-first search strategy that involves guessing the values of squares in a sequence then, when
a violation of a constraint happens, going back one move and guessing another value for it. This
is a type of brute force search, in that it is premised on being able to search for all possible
values for all squares of the board. Interleaving propagation with search is called
forward-checking — that is, a search action is taken (e.g., guessing the value of a Sudoku
square), and then this value is “checked” by propagating information across all the constraints
related to the square (e.g., by evaluating the neighboring rows, columns, and 3x3 grids).

11
 Example: scheduling production in the pin factory. One key challenge that CSPs are often used
for in organizations is scheduling tasks, such as the tightly linked sequences of tasks in factory
production. Recall that any constraint problem can be formulated in terms of sets of variables,
their domains, and the constraints on these. In factory production scheduling, the variables are
simply tasks, the domain of each variable is the number of minutes, and the constraints would be
any restrictions on the temporal order (e.g., a component should be produced before it is
assembled with other components) and the target range for the minutes that a task should take.
Let’s simplify things and say that pin production consists of just three tasks (variables): “Task 1:
Make pin base”, “Task 2: Make pinhead”, and “Task 3: Assemble pin”. Let’s assume that each
task takes 1 minute. Let’s also assume that Tasks 1 and 2 can be done in parallel, but they both
need to be done for Task 3 to be performed. Then we can write out the constraint as follows:
        Task 1 (pin base) + 1 < Task 3 (pin assembly)
        Task 2 (pinhead) + 1 < Task 3 (pin assembly)

We can conclude that, if there is only one worker, and only one task can be performed at a time,
then the task will take 3 minutes; if there are two workers who can do each task, then the overall
time will reduce to 2 minutes (by performing Task 1 and Task 2 in parallel). Depending on
factors such as our target production amount, the available workers, the possibility of defects and
so forth, we can calculate the optimal schedule for maximizing production efficiency. Though
this is an extremely simple example, the remarkable thing is that quite simple conclusions can
still usually be reached in the same way even if we had a vastly more complex scheduling
problem (e.g., if we had a product with 1,000 parts, which involved many specialists, complex
materials and shipments, etc.).

4.2 Causal nets
In CSPs, there are no challenges of superstitious or sparse learning. In scheduling tasks for the
pin factory, for example, we assumed that we knew the goal and the actions (i.e., tasks) to
perform — it was purely a question of whether we could efficiently find the best solution (i.e.,
the sequence of actions that would minimize the time for making a pin). How can we represent
the world when such learning challenges are present, and agents have to learn to take actions that
they are uncertain about? One approach, developed by the AI scholar Judea Pearl, called causal
nets (or also Bayesian networks), involves viewing a constraint network as a strategy for
representing and testing for cause-effect relations among variables. In a causal net, the
variables are called “events” or “random variables”. This is meant to refer to how variables in
a causal net can be tested for cause-effect relations as if in a scientific experiment. The domains
are any possible values a variable can take, which may be discrete (e.g., sunny or rainy weather)
or continuous (e.g., the temperature in degrees).

Let us go over the technical details of the constraints in a causal net, then we will look at a
concrete example. The constraints in a causal net refer to conditional probabilities between

12
 variables, meaning the probability of a variable taking on a certain value, given the presence of
another variable at some value. For example, if there is x chance of Event A, then there is y
chance of Event B occurring (this idea of conditional probabilities was famously formalized by
the 18th century statistician Bayes, hence the other name for causal nets of Bayesian networks).
You can think of these conditional probabilities as an agent’s beliefs about the cause-effect
relations among variables in a problem, given current information. The idea in a causal net is
to gather information about the variables to become surer about one’s beliefs.

To unpack how these constraints can be “informed”, it is useful to first know that causal nets
assume a specific structure for the constraint network called a directed acyclic graph. This
refers to how some variables in the network are caused by (i.e., are “directed” by) other
variables, and that these causal interdependencies only flow in one direction (they lack “cycles”,
and hence are acyclic). A variable that another variable depends on is called its parent, and the
dependent variable is its child. The constraints in a causal net refer to the structure of conditional
probabilities between parents and children that define a problem, meaning how the probabilities
of each variable occurring are related to each other. Constraint propagation refers to sending
updated information about the probability of one variable through the network (i.e., to its
“children”).

Consider a case of diagnosing a patient who has a toothache, and a dentist who believes with
80% certainty that the cause is a cavity (cf. Russell & Norvig). Of course, there is a 100% sure
answer to the question — is there a cavity or not — but knowing this answer requires more
information, which will allow the dentist to update the belief (e.g., to closer to 100% sureness).
Thanks to the magic of constraint propagation, the dentist can add even possibly a very large set
of variables (e.g., prior dental history of the patient, patient’s tooth-brushing habits) to the
representation of the problem to add more information that can be propagated to better
understand the likely cause of the toothache (if we know the parent-child relations). Hence,
unlike the fixed constraints in Sudoku (the three “all different” constraints that always hold), the
constraints in a causal net can be updated with more information. This is like scientists who
update their beliefs about hypotheses from doing more experiments. Here, the power of
representations is in being able to describe hypotheses and experiments formally as a constraint
network (which science did not know how to do prior to the development of causal nets in only
recent decades), and propagate information to improve its testing of the hypotheses.

What does all of this have to do with organizations? An influential recent body of research in the
business school views managers and in particular entrepreneurs as essentially like scientists, who
come up with theories (e.g., for new products, business models, or firm strategies) and seek to
test them (e.g., through prototyping, collecting data, or simply reasoning). Causal nets hence
offer an alternative view of problem-solving in organizations (as well as AI systems) as driven

13
 by cause-effect reasoning, rather than just the trial-and-error, heuristics, or statistical prediction
mechanisms that we have focused on so far.

4.3 Expert systems
Representations that are acquired and stored as heuristics for solving problems — that is, based
on search — is done in what is called an expert system. In an expert system, domain experts’
experience is assumed to be stored primarily as if-then heuristic rules — procedures for solving
problems by navigating a search tree. The if-then heuristic rules, called “productions”, are
acquired from “experts”, meaning agents who have experience in a specific domain.

The procedures can be “acquired” in a knowledge base by codifying them as if-then rules.
Rather than “learn” representations from large volumes of data, the strategy in designing an
expert system is to observe or talk to experts in a domain and do the codification of rules.
Codification could be automated by using some initial set of codified heuristic rules as a basis for
searching for and “discovering” other heuristic rules in the domain (XXXX). The acquired
knowledge is stored as a set of if-then rules, which may operate on minimal data. For example, a
canonical early expert system for diagnosing bacterial infections, called Mycin, contained around
200 such rules. It could diagnose and recommend treatments based on asking a patient just a few
simple questions. That is, in contrast to representation learning, there is little need for either large
volumes of data or to think carefully about structuring data in databases.

Knowledge acquisition bottleneck. Perhaps the most immediate limitation on expert systems is
what is referred to as the knowledge acquisition bottleneck (Feigenbaum 1964). The bottleneck
concerns the difficulty in getting experts to articulate all the heuristic rules that they know. Rules
that can be articulated, and thus codified, are called explicit knowledge; rules that are too hard to
extract are called tacit knowledge. A more serious version of this bottleneck was highlighted by
Prietula and Simon (1989), who noted that much of expertise is not just in storing the rules
themselves, but in knowing when to apply rules in complex situations — that is, expert
knowledge largely concerns what to pay attention to.

Brittleness. Similar to the credit assignment issue in representation learning, rules in expert
systems are ultimately correlations developed from specific problem-solving environments, and
often do not generalize well. This is called the brittleness issue, in that the usefulness of a rule is
brittle to even small changes in situations, even within the same narrow domain. Rather than the
issue of tacit knowledge within a specific domain, brittleness is thought to be the result of expert
systems needing commonsense knowledge, conceived of as a vast set of heuristic rules of
humans’ basic domain-independent understanding of the world.

Infinite regress. A final limitation is that it is unclear how many rules need to be codified for an
expert system to be adequate as a knowledge base in a domain. Drawing on the philosopher

14
 Wittgenstein, the famous AI critic Hubert Dreyfus (1965) called this the issue of infinite
regress, meaning that one would theoretically need an infinite number of rules to capture all the
contingencies that could happen, even in a narrow problem-solving domain.

4.4 Boltzmann machines and deep learning
Another idea about constraint networks called Boltzmann machines — invented by the recent
Nobel Prize in physics and deep learning leader Geoff Hinton — is perhaps the foundational
conceptual building block of deep learning models, currently the most popular idea in the AI
field. In Boltzmann machines, the variables are meant to resemble neurons that are either “on”
or “off”, hence their domains are binary (1, 0) as in Shannon information. A Boltzmann
machine largely “learns” constraints by processing information (as in causal nets), rather than
constraints being defined in advance (as in the Sudoku example).

Unlike in causal nets, the key idea is just to learn correlations among only two basic types of the
binary variables — input variables and output variables. These correlations are probabilities
called “weights”, rather than actual cause-effect relationships, which are the constraints in the
network. The key idea is to use soft constraints, meaning that unlike in Sudoku, when a
constraint is violated, it does not mean that a solution is not valid, but simply that a “cost” is
imposed on its quality. Hence, solutions are not initially “satisfactory or not”, but rather exist on
a continuum. Propagation refers to sending information across the network to modify the
weights until the overall “cost” is minimized (also called minimizing the entropy in the network).
The overall constraint network that is learned is essentially a probability distribution for the
entire set of variables. This probability distribution can be used to make specific predictions
(e.g., classifications of an image) or to generate new data that is consistent with the distribution
(similar to how LLMs use embeddings to generate new text).

The motivation behind the Boltzmann machine approach is generalization. That is, to build such
a machine, one does not even need to define a specific problem, much less the parent and child
variables and their causal relations. The constraint network is “directionless” and densely
interdependent, rather than “directed” and “acyclic”. All one needs is some input data and
output data, and one can learn how they are correlated. The outcome of learning in a Boltzmann
machine can be specific predictions, or also simply “learning” the constraint network, also called
“representation learning” (you should be aware of this term, since it is often used in the
machine learning community, but keep in mind that this refers only to learning the representation
of a very specific kind of correlation-based constraint network). You can understand the
“learning” here as a type of compression (i.e., “encoding”) of Shannon information, and some
alternative versions of the Boltzmann machine in deep learning that perform similar functions
are called “autoencoders” (meaning they are models for automatically encoding (compressing)
correlations among sets of input and output variables).

15
 What does all of this have to do with organizations? Many business school researchers and
managers of companies now view AI as practically synonymous with deep learning, and the
essential ideas behind deep learning are captured by Hinton’s Boltzmann machines. In this view,
organizations will increasingly be input-output mechanisms that are driven by simple data for
learning complex correlations (i.e., the weights in a Boltzmann machine). These correlations will
then be the basis for “learning” representations of problems, making predictions and, ultimately,
decisions. As we will discuss next, this deep learning-driven vision of how organizations will be
intelligent is, however, contested, in a debate that can be traced back to the early days of AI.

text_units.section: 5.1 The satisficing perspective in causal nets and other “mental models”
text_units.text:
5.1 The satisficing perspective in causal nets and other “mental models”
Pearl intended causal nets to define the essence of reasoning about a given problem where the
causes are uncertain. By “given problem”, I mean that we know what the problem is and are
provided with a typically small set of variables that are assumed to be relevant to the problem.
This is an example of what is referred to in AI, research on organizations, and research in the
social sciences as “mental models”, or also “decision models” — or in some cases, simply
“models”, “cognitive representations” or simply “representations”. We already have seen some
examples of mental models in the course in the form of heuristic search models and the policies
in reinforcement learning. What these and many other types of models have in common with
causal nets is that they assume that intelligence arises from having highly simplified
representations of the world that enable rational behavior under limited information — or what
Simon called satisficing.

5.4.2 Deep learning’s physics perspective
Hinton intended the Boltzmann machine to relate to a general purpose way of representing,
making predictions about, and generating new data about, any problem in the universe. It reduces
intelligence down to extremely simple mechanisms (1,0 variables, and simple correlations
between them). Hinton named the model after the 19th century physicist and founder of
statistical mechanics Ludwig von Boltzmann, who developed the modern definition of entropy
central to Shannon’s definition of information. Statistical mechanics refers to a way of
understanding the behavior of the universe in terms of a small number of statistical “laws”,
similar to Newton’s deterministic classical mechanics but accounting for the uncertain dynamics
of how particles moved. Hence, in this view, intelligence in AI or organizations can, like physics,
be reduced to a few laws and homogenous parts (e.g., “neurons”, or units of Shannon
information). The examples of representations given earlier in this session would, in this view,
simply be generated from such basic building blocks, and not the essence of intelligence itself.

text_units.section: 5.4.3 The knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) perspective implied by CSPs
text_units.text:
5.4.3 The knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) perspective implied by CSPs
In the examples that we looked at earlier, the constraints were given, rather than learned — just
as in the first AI idea that we covered of constraint satisfaction and CSPs. Unlike mental
models or deep learning models, one might claim, this idea of constraint satisfaction is a dead
end for intelligence since there is no learning involved (indeed, this is precisely the claim that
Hinton made when he developed his idea of the Boltzmann machine).
        Yet consider, firstly, how the constraints in our earlier examples were all far more general
than in the example of CSPs that we gave of Sudoku. The constraints concerned the rules of

text_units.section: 5.4.3 The knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) perspective implied by CSPs
text_units.text:
17
 algebra or geometry (or other principles of how physical objects relate that are built into CAD
programs), of double-entry bookkeeping for accounting, or of manipulating columns and rows of
data in spreadsheets or databases. Let’s think of these constraints as more like fundamental
principles or laws for reasoning about various basic representations of knowledge (e.g.,
algebra equations, accounting statements, engineering objects). Perhaps it is possible that a
Boltzmann machine — or, to be more current, a deep learning model or LLM — could “learn”
all of these constraints (e.g., by being given many examples of algebra equations, CAD
programs, datasets etc.). Yet even if this were done, it would be difficult for us to think of the
process of learning to be an intelligent mathematician, accountant, database user, or engineer, as
something other than the repeated experience of using these constraints (e.g., of manipulating
algebra equations, balancing the books, querying a database, or playing around with a CAD
simulation).
         This is what is called the knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) perspective in
AI and organizations, in which learning involves satisfying some given and fundamental sets of
constraints to construct new constraints. From this perspective, both causal nets and Boltzmann
machines would simply be two types of highly specialized constraints (i.e., for causal reasoning
and statistical pattern identification), among a diversity of knowledge representations needed for
general intelligence.

Course Notes — SESSION 7
INTERACTION

1. Introduction
Let us summarize our story so far: AI systems and organizations are intelligent if they can learn
to assign credit to actions when solving complex problems. They assign credit by manipulating
symbols. Symbols are units such as bit strings and lists, or composites of these such as search
trees, schemas, or constraint networks. Manipulations correspond to processing information
about a problem-solving environment, or to computing the steps of a program. Different AI ideas
or paradigms (e.g., reinforcement learning versus learning-in-a-society; search versus constraint
propagation) are essentially differences in strategies for manipulating symbols.

Diverse researchers in the AI field find this story wrong or misleading. The story suggests
intelligent problem-solving is all about internal cognition, or thinking about problems in the
world separate from the external world itself. Such a view of intelligence goes back at least to
the 17th century and the French philosopher René Descartes. His phrase, "I think, therefore I
am" implies that the very existence of intelligence is constituted by internal symbol
manipulations. In the view of these diverse researchers, all symbol manipulation approaches to
studying AI systems and organizations are repeating the same mistakes as narrow Cartesianism
(also called cognitivism) approaches of not dealing adequately with the external world:
Most AI ideas are stuck in the same narrow Cartesian approaches as 400 years ago.

These diverse researchers propose that AI systems and organizations be designed based on
identifying agents' interactions with the external physical and cultural world. The term
interaction is used to emphasize roles beyond internal cognition in intelligence of sensorimotor
action (perceptual senses and physical movements) and experiencing phenomena in the world.
Building a "model" of the world symbolically in programs or databases neglects the power of
these forces of intelligence, and needlessly complicates and bureaucratizes things. Instead, AI
systems and organizations can learn to assign credit more efficiently and effectively by just
directly interacting with it. This interactionist point of view is nicely summed up by a famous
phrase of roboticist and interactionist AI researcher Rodney Brooks:
"The world is its own best model".

Consider our previous session's example of Sudoku. Google's Peter Norvig claims to have
designed a Python program that solves any Sudoku puzzle. Is this claim plausible? From an
interactionist approach to AI, it is misleading. Norvig's Python program depends on the
computer being turned on, on whoever runs the program to be aware of what Sudoku is, and so
forth — an entire system able to interact with the physical and cultural world. In this session, we
will explore how we might understand and design AI systems and organizations based on
foregrounding such interactions, and not just symbol manipulations.

text_units.section: 2. Defamiliarizing our language for talking about AI
text_units.text:
2. Defamiliarizing our language for talking about AI
The basic AI idea described above seems straightforward enough: focusing on interaction with
the external world, not just internal symbol manipulation. Yet researchers of interactionism have
found that understanding this approach demands of us a major change in perspective. Symbols
are easily noticed, such as the text in these course notes. Paradoxically, our interactions with the
world are so ubiquitous that they easily go unnoticed. Cartesianism has dominated scientific
thought for centuries. Most of our language for talking about intelligence reflects its focus on
internal cognition — Cartesianism has become the water that we are swimming in.

text_units.section: 2. Defamiliarizing our language for talking about AI
text_units.text:
Consider how easily we thought of Sudoku playing as based on constraint propagation, while
putting aside our physical actions or experience of the game. Likewise, in organizations, going
back to at least Babbage, the dominant view has been industrial, in which economic activities
can be divided into symbolic tasks and managed through the symbol manipulation processes of a
bureaucratic administration. The interactionist argument is that, to see how all this may not, in
fact, be so intelligent, what is needed is to defamiliarize our Cartesian language that we have
inadvertently been using to talk about intelligence. We explore how to do such defamiliarization
in terms of our Cartesian metaphors of action, our stories about learning, and concepts of
complexity in organizations and other systems.

text_units.section: 2.1 Agre's critical technical practice: defamiliarizing Cartesian metaphors in AI
text_units.text:
2.1 Agre's critical technical practice: defamiliarizing Cartesian metaphors in AI
In pioneering work in the 1980s at MIT, the AI scholar Phil Agre introduced a method for
surfacing what he saw as the narrow yet vague language of AI ideas based on symbol
manipulation that he called "critical technical practice" (CTP). The CTP method involves (1)
surfacing assumptions in the language of AI ideas, (2) evaluating assumptions with respect to
observations and experience of concrete phenomena in the world, and (3) using the evaluations
to guide the construction of alternative AI ideas and systems. We will focus in this section on the
first aspect of CTP of surfacing assumptions.

text_units.section: 2.1 Agre's critical technical practice: defamiliarizing Cartesian metaphors in AI
text_units.text:
Linguists have pointed out that much of our everyday language relies on metaphors with the
physical world. For example, we say that we "grasp" ideas, "wrestle" with problems, or "move
forward" with plans". Agre proposed that how such metaphors are used in the AI field is often
harmful in that it casually conflates internalist (Cartesian) symbol manipulation with actual
real-world concrete phenomena. Consider the terms that we have freely used so far in this course
to describe what happens in AI systems, such as learning, planning, searching, reasoning, or
having goals or knowledge. Is how we described these terms really like how they actually happen
in real-world activity? "Searching" for your keys might involve looking around your house or
feeling through your pockets, which is not really like searching through a "tree" of
symbolically-represented states. Planning in organizations does not really resemble storing
sequences of actions in such a tree.

text_units.section: 2.1 Agre's critical technical practice: defamiliarizing Cartesian metaphors in AI
text_units.text:
Instead, Agre suggests, such activities are better thought of as improvised through our
moment-to-moment interactions for "coping" with the world rather than representing it. For
example, an organization's "plans" for launching a new product are continually negotiated based
on interacting with the physical product itself, the physical production environment, and with
customers to see how they experience and use it. Ignoring such improvisations is tempting, since
it enables us to understand search, planning or other terms solely in terms of well-defined symbol
manipulations. They serve as what have been called "wishful mnemonics" — memorable
(mnemonic) terms for symbol manipulation processes that allow us to "wish" that such processes
actually capture real-world phenomena. The danger is that such metaphors become a
self-fulfilling prophecy: we may start thinking about search, planning (or learning or knowledge)
as what happens symbolically inside of a computer. According to Agre, this will unnecessarily
constrain our design of both AI systems and organizations.

text_units.section: 2.2 Brooks' "creature hypothesis": defamiliarizing Cartesian stories about learning
text_units.text:
2.2 Brooks' "creature hypothesis": defamiliarizing Cartesian stories about learning
The AI field has often set the benchmarks for intelligent learning in terms of individual
Cartesian-style tasks for manipulating symbols. An early benchmark for AI was to learn to play
chess like a grandmaster; more recent benchmarks include learning the game of Go or passing
multiple choice tests. Whereas progress on such "complex" benchmark tasks has in some cases
been impressive, seemingly simpler tasks that involve interaction with the physical and cultural
world (e.g., getting a mouse to navigate a real-world environment, and not just a symbolic
representation of a maze) have proven much harder than had been expected. This is called
Moravec's paradox, after Carnegie-Mellon roboticist Hans Moravec:

text_units.section: 2.2 Brooks' "creature hypothesis": defamiliarizing Cartesian stories about learning
text_units.text:
Moravec's paradox: seemingly complex problems in AI are often simpler than expected;
    seemingly simple problems in AI are often (much more) complex than expected!

text_units.section: 2.2 Brooks' "creature hypothesis": defamiliarizing Cartesian stories about learning
text_units.text:
Roboticist Rodney Brooks proposed a "creature hypothesis" of intelligent learning that explains
the paradox from an interactionist point of view. The creature hypothesis is based on the
observation that humans developed language for symbolically representing the world only
recently in evolutionary time (thousands of years ago) — and only after millions of years of
adaptation directly with the physical world that originated in unicellular organisms and evolved
many organisms ("creatures") prior to humans. This observation suggests that it takes a lot of
evolutionary time to develop the ability to do seemingly simple sensorimotor actions (e.g., to go
from a unicellular organism to even a primitive animal). In contrast, once primitive humans
developed certain sensorimotor and experiential abilities (e.g., standing on two feet, using
thumbs), then language developed rapidly. Hence, counterintuitively, the simple sensorimotor
interactions with the physical and cultural worlds are the "hard" part of intelligence, while
language and representation are the easier part.

text_units.section: 2.2 Brooks' "creature hypothesis": defamiliarizing Cartesian stories about learning
text_units.text:
For Brooks, one consequence of a Cartesian view of learning is a recurring theme in the AI field
of extrapolation — of believing that a large gain in performance on one type of task (e.g.,
playing Go) means that the field is close to solving most other types of task and, hence, that
artificial general intelligence (AGI) is imminent. The danger is that such extrapolation leads to
large shifts in attention and resources to whatever the current paradigm is (e.g., LLMs today),
while all the actually complex parts of intelligence (as laid out in the creature hypothesis) run
the risk of never getting addressed.

text_units.section: 2.3 Wiener's "variety": defamiliarizing Cartesian concepts of complexity
text_units.text:
2.3 Wiener's "variety": defamiliarizing Cartesian concepts of complexity
Cartesianism implies a concept of complexity in terms of the amount of internal symbol
manipulations. We saw measures of such complexity as, for example, Shannon entropy or the
number of steps to run a program in a Turing machine. Consider how these concepts derive from,
or relate to, the idea of an industrial division of labor, as characterized by our pin factory
example, into isolated tasks that can be described symbolically.

text_units.section: 2.3 Wiener's "variety": defamiliarizing Cartesian concepts of complexity
text_units.text:
From an interactionist point of view, such derivations reflect a view of economic activity, and
systems in general, that is far too internalist and industrial — e.g., the pin factory is fully
characterized by the description of symbols about it. Such internalism reflects Cartesianism's
close affinity with Newtonian mechanics — a way of describing the world in terms of gear-like
metaphors (e.g., as individual tasks that map neatly to physical components). In this sense,
Simon's watchmaker parable neatly fits the picture: it continues to draw on mechanical clocks as
a canonical example of a complex system that has been around since Descartes' time. AI
researchers from an interactionist point of view argue instead that concrete, real-world
phenomena are far too complex to capture complexity in terms of such internal symbol
manipulations. Even in an industrial factory, the amount of complexity is vastly higher than one
would be led to believe by Babbage's concept of a division of labor or the Turing machine.

text_units.section: 2.3 Wiener's "variety": defamiliarizing Cartesian concepts of complexity
text_units.text:
Going back even before the formal emergence of the AI field, the MIT mathematician and
polymath Norbert Wiener proposed a concept of complexity in terms of variety, where variety
referred to a level of complexity more reflective of natural systems (biological organisms or
human societies and organizations) than internal symbol manipulations. Wiener's view has
influenced many interactionist researchers in AI to argue that what intelligence requires is a
"non-modern" (e.g., non-Cartesian, non-Newtonian, or non-industrial) concept of complexity
that foregrounds novel ways of organizing direct interactions with the physical and cultural
world rather than of structuring symbol manipulations.

3. Criteria for intelligent interaction
3.1 Goals: homeostasis or "comportment"
The earliest ideas about interaction in AI originated in the field's immediate predecessor called
cybernetics, which arose in the 1940s led by Wiener. "Cyber" means "to govern", and
cybernetics means "science of control". In cybernetics, control comes from feedback (i.e.,
information) from interacting with the environment. Perhaps the most canonical example of
interaction in cybernetics is an analog thermostat in a room. The thermostat is set to maintain
the temperature of the room within a certain range; if it gets too cold, the thermostat is triggered
and the heater starts. This canonical example illustrates the first major concept in AI ideas of
interactionism, which is an emphasis on goals of maintaining a state, rather than of optimizing
or satisfying a specific goal within a state. This idea of maintaining a goal was termed by the
cybernetician W. Ross Ashby as homeostasis ("same state").

In the early 1950s, another cybernetician W. Grey Walter designed a "tortoise" robot that used
a small set of simple analog circuits to navigate around a room. Consider the difference from
Shannon's Theseus labyrinth — rather than learn a specific path through a labyrinth, Walter's
tortoise was homeostatic in that it learned how to wander around the far less structured
environment of a house and find its way back from anywhere in the house.

[Figure: W. Grey Walter's tortoise robot (1951). Figure: Brooks' Roomba vacuum cleaner that
navigates any real-world home environment.]

In the 1980s, the MIT roboticist Rodney Brooks built a series of robots inspired by Walter's
ideas, which led to developing a commercial robot vacuum cleaner called the Roomba. It
remains easily the best-selling robot of all time, with more than 40 million sold. Brooks'
approach differed from the prior paradigm in robotics that was based on search and
representation (and from today's dominant paradigm, which is based on deep learning and
reinforcement learning using vast volumes of data). Brooks' approach with the Roomba
succeeded based on its simplicity — the Roomba had no CPU, no complex algorithms, and no
vast stores of data. Rather, it used only a small set of simple circuits to learn to react to any type
of room by wandering around. In addition to the ability to learn to navigate a new physical
environment, the other advantage of Brooks' approach was that "simple" meant far less costly.
Making super cheap robots enabled new strategies for using robots. For example, Brooks and his
colleagues used similar ideas of simplicity to design large numbers of cheap robots for exploring
Mars, different from the prior strategy of designing one complex and expensive robot. Whereas
if a single expensive robot broke down or got stuck, the mission could be a failure, Brooks'
"army" of robots tolerated the failure of potentially many such robots.

Overall, in Cartesian approaches to AI, the goals were to optimize or satisfice solutions, or
satisfy a set of constraints with respect to a problem with a well-defined goal state. In the AI idea
of interaction, the goal is instead about maintaining some sort of alignment with the physical
situations in the world as they unfold. Another term for this homeostasis is "comportment",
which means maintaining an authentic alignment between our goals and the physical world
based on our moment-to-moment coping. When an organization is skillfully "comported" to the
physical world, its members have become so familiar with it that most of the environment
becomes just background. Skillful could mean a specialized skill, such as a soccer team that
seems to play together effortlessly, or our everyday common sense, such as how a team of
medical professionals are able to navigate their way through cases mostly without consciously
thinking about it.

text_units.section: 3.2 Action as situated, embodied, and embedded
text_units.text:
3.2 Action as situated, embodied, and embedded
The above examples suggest important aspects of intelligently solving problems are learned
using sensorimotor actions to interact with and experience the physical world, and where goals
are homeostatic — about maintaining states, rather than finding a single optimal or satisfactory
solution to an isolated problem. Before we go into specific AI ideas about such interactions, let
us try to make sense of what types of actions are required for homeostasis and comportment.
What is it about interactions that enable intelligent credit assignment? Interactionist scholars of
AI and organizations understand intelligent action and problem-solving as situated, embodied,
and embedded. Understanding these characteristics will help frame for you why such scholars
consider representations to be less fundamental to intelligence.

text_units.section: 3.2 Action as situated, embodied, and embedded
text_units.text:
- Situatedness. Intelligent action is situated in that it depends on sensing and responding
  to ongoing changes in particular situations in the world. Solving complex problems
  requires not just being able to solve, for example, every kind of maze or possible chess
  puzzle. True generalization requires the ability to select the relevant characteristics of
  real-world physical environments in which actions are performed. In medical diagnosis,
  for example, beyond just adapting treatments for particular patients, situatedness also
  refers to the need to deal with all aspects of physical environments in which diagnosis
  actions are performed (e.g., medical facilities, rooms, equipment, etc.).

text_units.section: 3.2 Action as situated, embodied, and embedded
text_units.text:
- Embodiment. Intelligent action is embodied, meaning that it depends on the ability of a
  body to learn physical actions, not just the mind's ability to learn symbols. For example,
  "thinking" about and planning a route from KAIST to the airport in a Cartesian manner
  presumes our physical ability to move our bodies and sense where we are. Embodiment is
  important in that it emphasizes limits to intelligence that are not like, e.g., Shannon limits
  on information, but rooted in limits in the physical motions that our bodies can perform.
  For example, even if we expand our "channel capacity" infinitely for processing
  symbolic information, our ability to go from KAIST to the airport is still limited by how
  we can only take one step at a time with our feet.

text_units.section: 3.2 Action as situated, embodied, and embedded
text_units.text:
- Embeddedness. Finally, intelligent action is culturally embedded, meaning that it
  depends on the local culture in which it takes place, which changes the goals of
  intelligent action. For example, taking the train to the airport in Korea depends on
  obeying laws and norms that may vary from other countries, such as no eating and very
  little talking. As another example, a crosswalk in Korea is still something that must be
  crossed by a pedestrian with caution (since cars will tend to go through the crosswalk,
  even given a waiting pedestrian); in contrast, in Vietnam, even if there is no crosswalk
  (and a lot of traffic), it is often acceptable just to walk across the street without waiting.

text_units.section: 3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
text_units.text:
3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
Brooks' phrase "the world is its own best model" (where by "model", he was referring to the
use of Cartesian-style symbolic representations) implies that an AI system or organization can be
designed based on relatively simple analog mechanisms, such as the simple circuitry of the
Roomba that enable homeostasis. Hence, an intelligent AI system or organization could be
designed without any digital computers or even any other typical mechanism for symbol
manipulation.

text_units.section: 3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
text_units.text:
Nonetheless, there is nothing in interactionist views of AI that is against representations of
symbols per se. Interactionist researchers in AI do not deny that representations can be important
for intelligence. The claim is that symbolic representations are always secondary to more
fundamental mechanisms of moment-to-moment improvisation. Representations become
significant in particular moments when our homeostatic comportment fails, referred to as
"breakdowns". For example, you might walk through a building without giving it much thought,
but then, when encountering a door that you are not familiar with, you stop and think about how
to open it. Opening the door is clearly important for navigating the building; yet it is secondary
to the moment-to-moment navigation actions. In this sense, representations are thought of as
potentially valuable resources for action:

text_units.section: 3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
text_units.text:
Symbolic representations are not necessary for interacting with the world; they are
    resources for action.

text_units.section: 3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
text_units.text:
To consider the implications, first consider how this "resources for action" view compares to
our earlier notion of Simon information and its emphasis on designation — that intelligence
requires symbols that "designate" objects in the actual world by giving them names. For AI
scholars of interaction, designation is not enough — it only accounts for the real-world
meaning of symbols (i.e. lists) for a given problem, and not to the holistic experience of a
specific situation as it unfolds. We next consider two interactionist alternatives to designation
— called "indexing" and "registration" — that seek to reframe symbols and symbol
manipulation as grounded in our experience of real-world situations.

text_units.section: 3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
text_units.text:
Indexing. In this view, developed also by Phil Agre at MIT, objects in the real-world are
"indexed" in an agent's memory, which means that they are stored with respect to a specific
situation. This is like a word in an index of a book: it does not just have a name; the word also
has a page number that "points" you to the specific "situation" in the specific book to which its
meaning relates. To make our comparison of designation to indexing still sharper, consider how
the name "apple" can be designated, for example, also by "pointing" to another related symbol
such as "food". Yet, this is just a list structure (as Newell & Simon had in mind in their physical
symbol system hypothesis) — one name points to another name. Indexing, in contrast, refers to
using "apple" to refer to a particular physical object (a particular apple) in the world, just as
"banana" could be used to point to a particular banana.

text_units.section: 3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
text_units.text:
[Figure: indexical relationships (apple ↔ a particular apple image; banana ↔ a particular banana
image) versus symbolic relationships (apple ↔ food; banana ↔ food; ...).]

text_units.section: 3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
text_units.text:
As a broader example, think of the chair of the room at which you commonly study. You not
only know this object by its name ("that is a chair"), but by how it is related to your overall
study room. Hence, it is more accurate to think of it when you see it in the room as
"that-chair-right-there". In terms of AI and organizations, the key idea is that indexing the
objects in the physical world allows them to become familiar to us, such that our sensorimotor
actions can be far more efficient and real-time than if we had to "plan" all of them (e.g., by
processing information in lists). Consider, for example, how when you study in your study room
(or walk down the street, take the bus, brush your teeth etc.), the vast majority of objects in the
physical world are so familiar to you that you do not have to think much. In this way, our
embodied and embedded interactions with situations in the world can be thought of as ongoing
improvisations made possible by having indexed the objects in the world around us according to
how we experience them.

text_units.section: 3.3 Assigning credit efficiently: the world as its own best model
text_units.text:
Registration. In a complementary theory proposed also at MIT by AI researcher Brian
Cantwell-Smith, AI systems need to engage in the "registration" of symbols, where registration
refers to a process of understanding or making sense of coherent physical and cultural worlds in
which we are involved. In registration, representations are various schemes — collections of
symbols that cohere and make sense to us. Examples of schemes could be anything from
blueprints, to a database table, to a story. "Registration" refers to accounting for (i.e.,
"registering") (1) whether these schemes accurately reflect our experience of the world; (2)
whether our experience of the world is in fact accurate to the "reality" of the world. For
example, to design a building, an architect may have some vision for its form and function.
During the design process, the architect works with various schemes (blueprints, building
codes, images of similar buildings, etc.), and visits the actual building site. During this process,
the architect may realize that either that one or more of the schemes are wrong, or that the
actual site is wrong for the initial vision for the form and function of the building. It is this
ongoing interplay between representations (schemes), reality (the physical world) and our
experience of these — what Cantwell-Smith calls the interplay between "reckoning and
judgment" — that refers to processes of registration.

text_units.section: 4. Strategies for interaction in AI and organizations
text_units.text:
4. Strategies for interaction in AI and organizations
The previous subsection explained basic building blocks that can be used to understand any ideas
of interaction in AI and organizations. Intelligence arises from learning to homeostatically
"comport" one's body and experience with situations as they unfold on a moment-to-moment
basis. Actions for achieving such comportment are necessarily situated, embodied, and
embedded. Symbol manipulation can be useful, but only secondarily as "resources for action"
that help us "index" and "register" the external world as we experience it. What does all of this
mean for actually designing an alternative sort of AI system or organization? Next, we will
consider two main technical proposals: Brooks' subsumption architecture (which does not
require any symbol manipulation), and the notion of direct manipulation of symbols as
resources for action.

text_units.section: 4.1 Learning based on goals for interacting with the world: the subsumption architecture
text_units.text:
4.1 Learning based on goals for interacting with the world: the subsumption architecture
Brooks proposed that the sensorimotor actions fundamental to the evolution of intelligence could
be understood as corresponding to multiple goals (also called behaviors) that need to be
maintained by an agent. In this view, the challenge of intelligence is not so much to search a tree
of actions or propagate information across a constraint network. Rather, the fundamental
challenge of intelligence is to control (i.e., prioritize) goals (i.e., interactions) as situations
change in the physical world. In organizations, a canonical recent example of this view of
intelligence is the idea of a digital ecosystem, which has replaced the previous notion of a
well-defined industry as the basic units in which strategic innovations take place. A digital
ecosystem can be thought of as consisting of the various lower- and higher-level goals of a
"software stack". Lower-level goals are concern, for example, getting high-performing
semiconductor chips; higher-level goals could be, for instance, engaging user interfaces.
Intelligence is achieved by "orchestrating" all of the goals of the stack so that they work
together.

text_units.section: 4.1 Learning based on goals for interacting with the world: the subsumption architecture
text_units.text:
Subsumption architecture. Brooks proposed that an AI system or organization could be
formally designed as a set of multiple goals that correspond to fundamental behaviors to
maintain in the physical world and informed by sense perception (using very simple sensor
networks) rather than representations. The multiple goals in his proposal are learned and
implemented in order (i.e., simulating "creature" evolution) from the most general ones to the
more specific ones. The goals would then be given a prioritization, or what he labeled the
ability to "subsume" other goals to control intelligent action on a moment-to-moment basis. For
example, a robot would have the goal "do not run into walls" subsume other goals such as
"explore the room" since the former goal has higher priority than the latter.

text_units.section: 4.1 Learning based on goals for interacting with the world: the subsumption architecture
text_units.text:
In contrast to constraint networks, the goals or behaviors of the subsumption architecture are
structured as layers. Hence, the goals need not have explicit constraints that define how they
are related. The key idea behind this AI system design, or what Brooks called the "subsumption
architecture", was that (1) having multiple layers of goals that are fundamental to action, (2) a
strategy to learn them goal-by-goal, starting with the most fundamental, and (3) a way to control
their priority for real-world action, makes an AI system or organization highly robust to changes
in situations since the goals are so general that they will be relevant across these situations. Note
there is no representation in Brooks' idea in the sense that there is no real model of the world —
what is represented is only the behavior that is desired from the agent's interaction with the
world. Further, these goals or behaviors in his proposal are only implemented through highly
simple circuits, called finite state machines (FSMs), with no communication channels (i.e., this
is not like Shannon information).
