text_units.text:
[Figure: Basic elements of the subsumption architecture (Perception → Behavior 1 / Behavior 2 /
Behavior 3 → Response with highest priority). Figure: Example architecture for a simple robot
(Light Sensors, Audio Sensors, Obstacle Sensors → Explore / Follow Light / Avoid Loud Noise /
Avoid Obstacles → To Motor Drives).]

4.2 Direct manipulation of symbols
Another main area of research on interaction in AI and organizations concerns directly
interacting with physical media, and specifically digital representations in personal computers
and other personal or collaborative digital devices. The key insight in this area of research is that,
even when we explicitly use symbolic representations, we interact with them through
sensorimotor actions and on physical devices in particular situations. For example, we take
physical actions (e.g., swiping, clicking, viewing) to manipulate screens on our laptops, tablets or
phones. Businesses today frequently depend on designing these physical interactions with digital
representations — what we will call direct manipulation of information — to be intuitive and
"seamless". Apple's famous graphical user interfaces, for example, were fundamental to its value
proposition of enabling consumers to interact flexibly both within and across many software
applications. Ridesharing services such as Uber or Kakao Taxi depend on interactively providing
relevant information about location and prices in real-time on a smartphone screen. In short, we
access digital representations through interactive media.

The background for this perspective comes in large part from work by engineers, and
specifically electrical engineers from MIT and a few other institutions. In the 1950s and 1960s
at MIT, much pioneering work in electrical engineering was being done, such as designing and
building digital circuits and other hardware for digital computers and networks. Most of this
work did not have any obvious division of labor for specializing tasks, as in the earlier pin
factory example that we considered. A team of engineers must reason about an entire circuit, or
at least a large section of it. As in any engineering, this reasoning is largely based on "tinkering",
or physically manipulating the components of whatever is being built, to "debug" flaws in the
design that could not be discovered without physical testing.

The electrical engineers at MIT also had access, however, to some of the earliest digital
computers, and some of these engineers became pioneers in the AI field. Their focus was on how
symbols, though abstract in one sense, in fact need to be interacted with in the physical world to
solve complex problems. Just like an engineer (or architect) likes to tinker through constructing
and directly manipulating an actual physical system (e.g., by changing the physical components,
or by drafting the design of a machine with pen and paper), the idea was that an engineer could
directly manipulate the components as graphical objects on a physical screen — they could
tinker in the physical space of a computer screen.

The electrical engineering work involved solving complex problems by constructing and
reasoning about schematic circuit diagrams to capture the physical properties of the circuits (or
other devices). The budding AI scholars, epitomized by Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad system
(the forerunner to CAD software and the GUI (graphical user interface) of personal computers),
envisioned software that would enable drafting a diagram of a circuit or other complex machine
in digital form, and then "tinkering" with this by interacting with the diagram on a physical
screen. Here, the problems could be understanding the "flow of current" through a circuit, and
the performance goals could be based on physical laws of electrical engineering such as the
maximum current for a given circuit. The idea was that direct manipulation of graphical objects
on a digital computer would be more flexible than tinkering with the actual physical circuit, but
also much simpler and more flexible than writing sequences of code to describe a circuit.
Analogous to McCarthy's ideas about programming as declarative, the engineer only needed to
directly manipulate a computer since the computer stored constraints about what the circuit
should do, rather than precisely how to do it.

Course Notes — SESSION 8
REASONING ABOUT THE PHYSICAL WORLD

1. Introduction
In our last session, we based intelligence on interacting with and experiencing the physical and
cultural world. Such interacting and experiencing arose from moment-to-moment improvising
with the body. Representations were useful only when occasional breakdowns arose that required
reflection. In this session, we will view breakdowns not as the exception but the rule. Intelligence
in AI systems and organizations will involve reflectively reasoning about the physical systems in
which AI systems and organizations are situated and embedded to identify and resolve
breakdowns. We will refer to such processes as reasoning about the physical world.

Foundational AI ideas for reasoning about the physical world emerged in the 1970s and 1980s
from students at the MIT AI lab who were proteges of Minsky and his learning in a society
paradigm, and were also influenced by McCarthy's ideas about knowledge representation and
reasoning. Most of these students were from engineering backgrounds. Engineers typically make
use of detailed representations of physical systems (i.e., engineering schematics). In their
experience as engineers, these students at MIT found that the complexities of the physical world
inevitably make such representations messy and requiring continual modification (or, in the
parlance of our previous session, continual "registration" of the physical and cultural world).

A canonical example of reasoning about the physical world in this tradition of AI research is the
problem of identifying faults in either the design or repair of an integrated circuit board (ICB).
ICBs are devices that control the flow of electrical current in digital or analog machines. There
are a vast number of types of ICB functions, and thousands of possible types for each part.
Hence, the problem of designing a new ICB, or repairing an existing one with faults, is
combinatorially explosive. It cannot be solved just by representing the problem as a search tree
or simple (which we have associated with search) or prediction (which we have associated with
machine learning) are recast in this tradition as ones of constructing and repairing causal
interpretations of physical systems that describe how they function.

Overall, the approach is to view such reasoning about the physical world as a type of constraint
propagation. Unlike our simple Sudoku models, however, the constraint propagation needed
here is based on fundamental constraints on the physical world, which we will call "physical
laws" or, more commonly, "first principles". Hence, such constraint propagation is sometimes
called first-principles reasoning. For example, to design or repair an ICB, engineers use
electrical engineering "laws", such as how much voltage can flow between the components, to
represent and reason about constraints on variables such as transistors, resistors, and capacitors.

2. Credit assignment as a "debugging" process
2.1 Bugs and debugging
Let us first develop some vocabulary for talking about breakdowns with more of an engineering
flavor. A breakdown can also be thought of as a symptom of a problem. A symptom can also be
called a "discrepancy", or a "constraint violation" (i.e., when values of variables in a constraint
network do not satisfy a constraint). For our purposes, we will follow the engineering tradition of
AI research in this area at MIT and call all such symptoms, discrepancies, or constraint
violations as "bugs". Here, bugs are not, as in software programs, merely errors in the syntax of
the software code, but rather errors of registration (i.e., of aligning representations with the
physical world). Hence, we will call intelligence in this session (i.e., learning to assign credit
when solving complex problems) as the ability to learn to "debug" representations of problems
in the physical world.

You can think of debugging as manifesting in two complementary strategies. First, we can
assume that our AI system or organization has the correct representation of a problem regarding
some physical system, but that there are bugs in the actual system. We will call such debugging
"troubleshooting". An example is reconciling a malfunctioning ICB board with a schematic of
the board that is known to be correct. Second, we can assume that the physical system is fine, but
that bugs may arise in the representation of the system. Examples would be (1) using the wrong
schematic to reason about an existing ICB board, or (2) constructing a new schematic to design a
new type of ICB board based on the function that we have in mind, where this new schematic
will initially go through many rough drafts. We will call these latter debugging processes as
"theory formation".

Whether troubleshooting or theory formation, debugging involves an AI system or organization
that reasons about the physical world to reconcile "reality" with its representation of it. You can
think of such reasoning processes as fundamentally about deriving function (what the system
does) from the structure of it (i.e., from observing the components or parts of the system). Just
as Simon's watch was a metaphor for the structuring of any system, this view of intelligence as
deriving function from the structure of a physical system is held to be generally applicable,
whether to a product, an organization, or a manufacturing process.

text_units.section: 2.2 Debugging as a distinct problem-solving process
text_units.text:
2.2 Debugging as a distinct problem-solving process
Recall from our initial sessions of the course that learning to assign credit to solve complex
problems can be thought of as a generate-and-test process: candidate solutions to problems are
generated, and tested for whether they work. A limit of this process, however, is that it assumes
that we know the basic shape of the underlying problem — that the candidate solutions are
generated within a mostly known search tree or constraint network (i.e., a given performance
landscape, with given peaks).

text_units.section: 2.2 Debugging as a distinct problem-solving process
text_units.text:
In contrast, the AI idea of debugging proposes that this process also requires reasoning about a
physical system to understand it: to understand how function emerges from structure. While
there may be some optimal solution to the underlying problem (i.e., some "peak" in a landscape),
debugging assumes that the AI system or organization does not know this — it has to construct a
representation of the landscape from the ground up. Minsky first pointed out that, rather than
reach some optimal peak in a landscape, what is needed is to reach some threshold of
understanding (what we called earlier in this course a "mesa" landscape).

text_units.section: 2.2 Debugging as a distinct problem-solving process
text_units.text:
We will call such a threshold understanding as a causal interpretation of the physical system —
considered as a representation of meaningful information about its functioning (i.e., not just
using Shannon information, and not just describing how the components and parts are assembled
but how they produce behavior). This representation is then reasoned about to identify and
resolve any "bugs" in it. Hence, the process is really generate-test-and-debug, where debugging
involves not just generating candidate solutions, but possibly modifying the representation of the
problem (and even the goals themselves). Such modifications may involve adding or removing
actions or components or re-ordering them based on interpreting how the components causally fit
together to produce the system's functioning.

text_units.section: 2.2 Debugging as a distinct problem-solving process
text_units.text:
To see how this interpretative nature of the debugging process is distinct, let us consider how it
compares to some of the other problem-solving processes and representational strategies that we
have studied.

text_units.section: 2.2 Debugging as a distinct problem-solving process
text_units.text:
- Versus heuristic search: recall that this idea involved using some set of operators and
  heuristics to transition from an initial state to a goal state. Yet this assumes that both the
  operators and heuristics are based on some prior understanding of the global functioning
  of the system. There is no representation of the physical structure of any system and,
  hence, no mechanism for reasoning about its functioning. The idea of debugging is that
  an AI system or organization needs to piece together a tentative representation of this
  structure and functioning.

text_units.section: 2.2 Debugging as a distinct problem-solving process
text_units.text:
- Versus CSPs: recall that, in a standard constraint satisfaction problem, the constraints
  were discrete and precise. For example, in Sudoku, the "all different" constraints had nine
  discrete values and we could calculate precisely at any state of the game exactly how
  many remaining possible values for each variable (square of the board) there were. In
  contrast, the variables in any complex physical system are often continuous and messy.
  Interpreting its function requires, likewise, a messy and qualitative description of the
  system.

text_units.section: 2.2 Debugging as a distinct problem-solving process
text_units.text:
- Versus causal nets: as noted above, debugging involves coming up with some sort of
  causal interpretation of the functioning of a physical system from its structure. Causal
  nets, however, assume that such structure can mostly be specified in advance — recall
  that what is learned in a causal net are the strengths of the probabilities between variables
  in some given causal structure, rather than the structure itself. Hence, whereas causal nets
  are more like a scientist doing a controlled experiment in a lab, debugging is more like an
  engineer who constructively pieces together an interpretation of how the system fits
  together from the ground up. Causal interpretations are tentative "theories" that can
  themselves be "debugged" in place of new theories.

2.3 First principles reasoning
Consider that, even for a physical system such as a mechanical watch with relatively
well-defined parts and components, the number of possible "bugs" is combinatorially explosive
in ways far beyond even a complex search tree (i.e., state space). Due to this combinatorial
explosion, it is not realistic to reason based on acquiring heuristics (one would need practically
an infinite number of heuristics) or by representing knowledge about the entire system. Further,
even if one somehow could represent all the heuristics or other knowledge of a physical system,
the messiness of reasoning about the physical world means that an AI system or organization
cannot be assumed to be able to select which knowledge is relevant to represent without an
extensive process of "debugging" its representations.

Instead, the strategy for assigning credit by debugging is to reason from first principles — that
is, to use a small number of stable, fundamental "laws" about the physical world that are simple
and known to be relevant to a problem. Certain first principles, such as Newton's laws of
physics, seem to hold across a wide (or even universal) set of physical systems. In debugging,
the focus is typically on "first principles" specific to some broad class of problems, such as
voltage laws from electrical engineering that apply to any ICB circuit. We will call such classes
of problems as domains and, hence, view debugging as reasoning about a domain, as distinct
from searching through a state space. Put another way, what remains stable is not a predefined
state space (i.e., performance landscape), but rather a much broader domain in the physical world
and the "first principles" associated with it.

It follows that, in this view, an AI system or organization should be based on some sort of
mechanisms for applying the first principles of a domain to reason about the physical systems
underlying the problems to be solved. In the MIT tradition of AI research, this mechanism is
commonly thought of as a domain-specific language, meaning a language that enables
representing the fundamental entities and relations of the domain such that reasoning can be
based on the principles of this domain. Such languages can be developed at various levels of
abstraction of the same domain. For example, computer-assisted design (CAD) software offers a
broad range of engineers a way of reasoning about physical systems based on geometric
principles. Nvidia's CUDA language offers a more specific programming language for designing
functions for graphical processing unit (GPU) chips.

3. Debugging strategies
The previous section proposed that, to intelligently solve problems based on reasoning about
systems in the physical world, an AI system or organization needs to be able to causally interpret
this system and "debug" these tentative causal interpretations. In this section, we will explore
some foundational ideas from the AI field for doing so.

text_units.section: 3.1 Qualitative reasoning: "envisioning" how a physical system functions
text_units.text:
3.1 Qualitative reasoning: "envisioning" how a physical system functions
In addition to first principles reasoning, a second — and perhaps counterintuitive — strategy for
debugging representations of the physical world is to do so based on what is called "qualitative
reasoning" with these principles. By qualitative reasoning, what is meant is that information
used for reasoning need not (at least initially) contain any reference to precise numbers. As a
canonical example from this MIT tradition of AI research, used by alums from Minsky's AI lab
Ken Forbus and Johan de Kleer in their book Building Problem Solvers, consider if you have
three containers placed at different heights, and connected by pipes. What happens when water is
poured into the highest container? It is easy for you to reason that it will flow through the pipes
into the second container at medium height, and then into the lowest container. Such reasoning
did not require any numbers — just your commonsense about the laws of the physical world
(i.e., about gravity and liquids).

text_units.section: 3.1 Qualitative reasoning: "envisioning" how a physical system functions
text_units.text:
This strategy of debugging representations of the physical world based on qualitative reasoning
may seem strange to you. In the prior strategy of reasoning based on first principles, what might
have come to mind is the possibility of reasoning using formal equations (e.g., Newton's F =
MA) for quantitatively analyzing a physical system. Surely, one might think, such formality
would be preferable. Yet recall that a central premise of the AI ideas that we have discussed here
is that solving problems based on reasoning about the physical world is based on messy
processes of debugging (troubleshooting or theory formation). If an AI system or organization is
in the middle of a debugging process, by definition it does not have a precise representation of
the physical world, such that quantitative reasoning may initially be of little use!

text_units.section: 3.1 Qualitative reasoning: "envisioning" how a physical system functions
text_units.text:
Let us go back to the container example. How did you know that water would flow from the top
one to the bottom one? Surely, this is our commonsense knowledge of how the physical world
works, such that all of us have the "first principles" somehow internalized already. Interestingly,
de Kleer observed that even sophisticated engineers (or other systems designers) initially engage
in the same such qualitative reasoning, even regarding sophisticated systems (e.g., designing or
repairing an ICB). His intuition was that: (1) quantitative analyses enable optimizing the
performance of a system with known functioning; whereas (2) the functioning of the system itself
does not permit a quantitative description, and is most fundamentally understood in terms of
qualitative language.

text_units.section: 3.1 Qualitative reasoning: "envisioning" how a physical system functions
text_units.text:
What does the process of debugging based on such qualitative reasoning look like? De Kleer
characterizes this process as one of "envisioning" how the components and parts of a physical
system function together, which he describes as "running a qualitative simulation in the
mind's eye". More precisely, envisioning means predicting and analyzing changes of the
qualitative state of a system (e.g., from water being in one container, to flowing into another).
The end states are not goal states, so much as the "logical limits" of the physical system
according to the first principles of the domain. You can think of envisioning an entire physical
system as akin to a simplified picture of how initial states may unfold into other states (i.e., how
various "scenarios" unfold). Causal interpretations arise while doing such envisioning, as
principled ways of explaining how a system transitions between states.

3.2 Propagating qualitative information
You can think of qualitative reasoning to envision a physical system as a type of constraint
propagation process. In our example, the variables would be qualitative variables such as
containers or water, and the values could be qualitatively described, such as "full" or "empty".
We will assume that an AI system or organization knows the "domain" of the physical system, in
the sense that it has some library of variables that serve as the "building blocks" of the domain.
For example, in ICB design or repair, an electrical engineer reasons based on some library of
building block schematics and parts (e.g., transistors, resistors, and capacitors).

The constraints on these variables, however, are represented not just as allowable values (as in
Sudoku), but as causal interpretations on how variables are linked. Note, again, that the causal
nets that we studied earlier in the course are only specific ways of talking about such causal
interpretations that are possible only when we can treat things as if they are a controlled
experimental setting. For a typically messy representation of a real-world physical system to be
"debugged", the constraints are considered as variables that mutually influence one another — or
what De Kleer calls "confluences" — that reflect the first principles of the domain. For example,
the height differences of the water containers influence how fast water flows from one container
to another, as does the width of the pipes connecting them.

What you should see here is that the "magic of propagation" that we talked of earlier becomes a
much more iterative and interpretative process than was implied by our Sudoku example —
"debugging" involves understanding and reasoning about how various influences on the behavior
of a physical system come together in complex ways. Here, it is more useful to think of the
constraints (i.e., confluences) as not just tests or target ranges, but rather as populated by agents,
i.e., "propagators" in an organization. The propagators in this "organization" qualitatively
represent and reason about the constraints as a basis for deciding which information to propagate
to other constraints and, hence, to other propagators, for constructing and informing one
another's causal interpretations of local behavior. Next, we will look at how reasoning in this
"organizational" context involves propagating information not just about the constraints and
variables themselves, but about tentative assumptions made about them in a complementary
representation to the constraint network called a dependency network.

3.3 "Truth maintenance" using dependency networks
In the previous section, we framed the debugging process as carried out by an organization of
"propagators". Each propagator processes information about constraints on some physical
system ("confluences"). They propagate information to one another to qualitatively reason about
and causally interpret (i.e., to "envision") the behavior of this physical system. Given the
messiness of debugging, however, this constraint propagation process is not as straightforward as
the Sudoku example that we looked at earlier in the course. In the Sudoku example, we could
just store information on the remaining possible values (1-9) for each of the squares of the board
(81). Hence, we just had to have a theoretical maximum "memory" of 729 possible values (81x9,
assuming no predefined squares), as in the figure below.
[Figure: a partially-filled Sudoku board with candidate-value annotations in each cell.]

In contrast, as described in the previous section, debugging representations in the physical world
depends on qualitative reasoning, such that the "memory" of an AI system or organization should
represent diverse qualitative information or knowledge about a physical system. As depicted in
the photos below, for example, repairing an ICB board might involve annotating the components
of the board with codes (left), comparing the board to various schematics (middle), and selecting
replacement parts using a database of 1000's of parts with rich descriptions of their functions and
specifications.

[Figure: three photos — (left) "Indexing: ICB expert takes a photo of a faulty ICB and annotates
each component with codes"; (middle) "Registering: ICB expert tests each component referring to
the schematic and the annotated photo"; (right) "ICB expert has parts database on his computer
and physical catalog of parts to select a replacement".]

This need for qualitative representation and reasoning brings in all the issues raised by McCarthy
in our earlier session on knowledge representation and reasoning — the frame problem, and the
need to solve this problem based on common sense; and the need for expressive languages that
enable elaboration tolerance in the representations. We will confine our focus here, however, to
the nature of the constraint propagation process — i.e., of how "debugging" requires a distinct
way of inducing the "magic of propagation".

The key idea, pioneered by Minsky's student Gerald Sussman and his colleagues in the 1970s,
is that the constraint network needs to be supplemented by what is called in this tradition of AI
research a dependency network — a locally-stored (i.e., propagator- or constraint-level)
memory of all the qualitative information and knowledge representations to make them available
to the propagators. Think of a dependency network as, for example, a sort of systematically
recorded and continually-updated memory of all the annotations relevant to each of the
components of the ICB in the images above. Informally, you can think of it as sort of a
"scratchpad" or "whiteboard" maintained by each propagator to keep track of information and
knowledge during the debugging process.

The key idea of a dependency network is to enable debugging as a process of making and
modifying (or retracting) tentative assumptions about the inevitably partial, messy and often
conflicting qualitative representations of a physical system — referred to as debugging based on
"truth maintenance". Hence, a dependency network is part of what is called a "TMS", or truth
maintenance system. The key idea of a TMS is that, in addition to constraint propagation,
information processing involves a parallel activity of tracking interdependencies among tentative
knowledge representations and their assumptions. In this network, the nodes are qualitative
representations of knowledge (assertions, assumptions, contradictions, rules, etc.). The links are
beliefs called justifications, which represent things like consequences, antecedents, or
explanations, and labels that indicate whether such justifications are "in" or "out" (i.e., whether
they are tentatively believed to be true or not).

The key idea is that this TMS and dependency network dramatically (1) enhances the "magic of
propagation" by enabling qualitative reasoning; and also (2) greatly enhances the efficiency of
any search processes used. The key idea is that reasoning about the physical world becomes
"dependency-directed" — informed by rich and diverse information and knowledge about
interdependencies (constraints) that enables explaining assumptions, tracking provenance (i.e.,
which propagator made the assumption), handle or resolve inconsistencies in assumptions, and
store all the results of such reasoning for further use. Put another way, when "bugs" arise, an AI
system or organization can trace the bugs to specific assumptions in the constraint network,
"debug" the local representation based on reasoning about these assumptions using rich
representations, and debug the constraint network itself by propagating the results of such rich
reasoning.

Overall, the intuition can be seen by contrast to the earlier idea in search of Simon's means-ends
analysis. In that idea, problem-solving was less dependency-directed than it was chronological
— we assumed that we could just use operators and heuristics to transition from an initial state to
states closer to a goal state. In contrast, the idea of debugging based on constraint propagation
using dependency networks is problem-solving as a messy, iterative process in which assumptions
(even about the nature of the goal state) may need to be continually revised and explained. Seen
this way, "bugs" are not so much something to avoid (akin to taking a wrong path in search that
ends up "stuck" on a local peak in a performance landscape), as an inevitable and helpful basis
for maintaining tentative beliefs ("truths") until one has some threshold understanding of a
physical system.

text_units.section: 4. Approaches to reasoning about the physical world
text_units.text:
4. Approaches to reasoning about the physical world
As in our previous sessions, we will understand AI ideas for reasoning about the physical world
in terms of two paradigmatically-different approaches. One approach, developed mostly outside
of the MIT tradition described above but which is currently popular, is based on deep learning
(i.e., Boltzmann machines) and is commonly referred to today as the "world models" approach
to AI. Another approach, which Gerald Sussman calls simply the "propagator model", derives
from this MIT tradition and can be thought of as a distillation of ideas described above.

4.1 Machine learning-based "world models"
"World models" refer to several recent deep learning-based approaches for representing and
making predictions about the physical world. These approaches typically extract patterns from
large volumes of data that are structured in ways consistent with Shannon information (i.e., as
meaningless bitstrings such as vector embeddings). The goal of world models is to use these
patterns to predict the next state of some physical world that results from an action taken in this
world. Hence, rather than reason based on first principles about the physical world, the strategy
is to indirectly "learn" such principles from Shannon-style data (e.g., sensor and image data
stored in bit string-like structures) about this world.

World models are commonly compared, and proposed as an alternative, to GenAI programs such
as LLMs. Whereas LLMs predict the next word in a sentence, or whereas image generators
predict the next pixel in an image, world models are designed to predict, e.g., broader scenes
within an image or broad outcomes of actions in the physical world. This broadness is needed
since actions in the physical world are considered vastly more complex (in a Shannon
information sense) than actions to manipulate words. Due to this complexity, information must
be processed at a higher level of abstraction (e.g., areas in an image, rather than individual
pixels) to avoid combinatorial explosion. Hence, the strategy is, for instance, to learn our earlier
container example — that pouring water in the high container will flow through the pipes to the
lower containers — by extracting patterns from vast amounts of visual data (images, as well as
videos or 3D environments) about objects such as containers and water, their positioning, and
their interdependencies, again stored as Shannon information. Hence, such world models
essentially learn representations of regularities in the physical world as mappings of actions to bit
string-like structures (embeddings) about this world. They "reason" about the world indirectly,
by taking in what is called in machine learning some "context" (e.g., a prompt from a user, or
sensor data from the physical world at the moment) to predict the consequences of various
actions and select among these actions.

World models have shown impressive performance in many contexts, including self-driving
vehicles. On the other hand, compared to our discussion in the first three sections of this session,
world models do not represent knowledge in ways that can be qualitatively reasoned about, nor
do they allow for using a dependency network to precisely trace and explain bugs, nor are they
elaboration tolerant in the way that McCarthy had in mind and that the MIT tradition of research
in this area would emphasize (i.e., there is no clear way to incrementally add and debug
information and knowledge to the dependency network itself). Further, world models require
vastly more processing capacity, making their scalability possibly infeasible, or at least
undesirable, in the type of real-world organizational settings emphasized in the MIT tradition of
research about reasoning about the physical world.

4.2 Sussman's propagator model
Another approach, pioneered by MIT AI researcher and Minsky's student Gerald Sussman, is
what he has called the propagator model. This model is based on the building blocks of: (1)
"propagators" in a constraint network, who work with (2) "cells", or stores of memory about
tentative beliefs, who (3) reason about this memory opportunistically, meaning based on
whatever information has been propagated at any particular time. You can think of this
propagator model as a distillation of the approach to reasoning about the physical world that we
have explored in the first three sections of this session's course notes.

Designing AI systems or organizations in terms of propagators does not require extracting
patterns from vast volumes of bit string-like data. Rather, the idea of propagators is that they can
serve as a general model to support debugging processes — of continually constructing beliefs
about tentative causal interpretations of physical systems and "maintaining" an accurate
representation of these beliefs as propagation unfolds. Hence, the goal is not just (or primarily) to
predict the next state of the world per se, so much as to support the process of piecing together
tentative representations of how a physical system functions.

To see how the propagator model differs from world models (or LLMs) more fundamentally,
however, it will first help to compare it to the very idea of programming itself, as captured by the
example of the Turing machine from earlier in the course. Recall that we viewed the Turing
machine as a general way of thinking about plans or programs for solving problems — as
generating sequences of actions for transitioning from some initial state to a goal state. This
Turing machine-style view of AI systems (and programming in general), however, assumed a
single computer with a consistent view of the world, and where actions are sequential in nature.
In contrast, the propagator model offers a view of planning or programming that is (1) potentially
far more expressive (i.e., can reason about rich qualitative information and knowledge and
dependency networks) and, hence, which can potentially be far more elaboration-tolerant; and
(2) which is organized around constraint networks that are spatial rather than sequential, such
that problem-solving actions can unfold in any direction, which Sussman emphasizes is far more
robust and, hence, suitable for the debugging processes central to effectively reasoning about the
physical world; and (3) where the "propagators" in this network could be anything that can store
and process information.

It is this final point that should highlight for you the paradigmatic difference with machine
learning-based world models. Sussman's argument here is that, while it may be tempting to think
that extracting bit string-like patterns is the most general and powerful basis for reasoning about
the physical world, this is a trap. In fact, in his view, doing so is quite narrow — one can only
really propagate information in ways similar to the propagation mechanisms of a Boltzmann
machine (i.e., where the propagators keep track of weights between the bit strings). In contrast,
his idea of the propagator model is that the basic building blocks for reasoning about the physical
world could be anything (CSPs, causal nets, search trees, or deep learning or LLMs or world
models), and organized to propagate information in any order. It is this deeper generality, in his
view, that is needed to support the most flexible debugging processes for interpreting and taking
action in complex physical worlds.

Course Notes — SESSION 9
AGGREGATION

1. Introduction
In our second to last session, let us return to the AI paradigm that we sketched at the beginning
of our course: Minsky's idea of "learning in a society". Recall that we introduced Minsky's idea
using the example of constructing, rather than merely navigating, a T-maze. The key insight was
that constructing even a simple T-maze required "managing" a complex society (organization) of
agents and their memories, beyond just reinforcement learning. A premise of this course is that
Minsky's insight basically holds. AI systems and organizations are the same. Currently-popular
techniques within the reinforcement paradigm (including deep learning and LLMs) are always
just a part of larger organizations of human and artificial agents.

Armed with the diverse foundational AI ideas of our previous sessions, our goal for this session
will be to consider Minsky's idea more concretely: how can an AI system be organized as a
society of agents? To do so, we will view the general problem of learning to assign credit across
an organized society of agents as one of aggregation. "Aggregation" in AI can be thought of as
strategies for "managing" how information is propagated (i.e., aggregated) across agents. It
implies low-bandwidth ways of organizing, meaning ways that enable a society of agents to act
intelligently even just by propagating just a small amount of information among one another.

To illustrate foundational AI ideas about aggregation, we will first look at three basic
aggregation strategies: pattern recognition, blackboard systems, and ensemble methods. These
strategies correspond to basic ways of enabling diverse agents to compete, cooperate, or reach
consensus. We will then go deeper to frame the fundamental problem of aggregation, and its
fundamental solution, guided by the seminal work of Minsky's student at MIT Carl Hewitt.
Finally, we will compare two paradigmatically different approaches to aggregation, one called
deep learning, and another based on Hewitt's Actor model.

text_units.section: 2. Basic aggregation strategies: competition, cooperation, consensus
text_units.text:
2. Basic aggregation strategies: competition, cooperation, consensus
2.1 Competition: the Pandemonium system
Pandemonium refers to a hypothetical AI system proposed around 1959 by AI co-founder Oliver
Selfridge at MIT for pattern recognition (identifying patterns in symbols that are similar, but
not necessarily exact "matches"). Pandemonium is organized around agents that specialize in
recognizing simple patterns in meaningless (bit string-like) data that Selfridge referred to as
"demons". The simple patterns are called features of the data. Pattern recognition is also called
feature detection. Hence, aggregation here is essentially the aggregation of predictions about
patterns in bit strings made by agents-as-"feature detectors".

text_units.section: 2. Basic aggregation strategies: competition, cooperation, consensus
text_units.text:
In Pandemonium, whenever demons receive information from the world, they all make
competing predictions about whether the information corresponds to the particular patterns
(features) in which they are specialized to recognize. In Selfridge's metaphor, the demons
"shout" at a certain volume proportional to the extent to which a pattern corresponds to that in
which it is specialized. Pattern recognition "decisions" are organized based on a hierarchy for
evaluating who shouts the loudest, controlled by a "decision demon" (akin to a CEO). Since the
evaluation of a large number of "shouts" may get complex and noisy, the "decision demon"
depends on evaluations by additional hierarchical layers, called "computational demons" and
"cognitive demons". Think of these layers of "demons" as roughly like middle managers, who
aggregate subsets of the lower-level demons' prediction "shouts".

text_units.section: 2. Basic aggregation strategies: competition, cooperation, consensus
text_units.text:
[Figure: Selfridge's Pandemonium — image demons → feature demons → cognitive demons →
decision demon, illustrated with the letter "A" being recognized.]

text_units.section: 2. Basic aggregation strategies: competition, cooperation, consensus
text_units.text:
To illustrate, Selfridge used the example of "letter perception", such as recognizing the letters
of the alphabet in handwritten text. Imagine, for example, designing a Pandemonium-style letter
perception system for recognizing handwriting in English. There could be 26 "demons", each
specializing in recognizing the patterns of one of the 26 letters of the English alphabet. When a
letter of handwriting is presented to the demons, they "shout" according to the degree of
similarity with the letter. For example, if the letter "A" is presented (as in the image above), an
"A" demon will shout the loudest; a "D" demon might shout a little bit, since there are at least
some similarities in the appearance of "A" and "D"; and an "L" demon might shout even less,
since it looks even more different. Each of the shouts would then be converted into weights
between 0 and 1, and the weights would be aggregated according to models used for evaluating
them at various layers of the hierarchy.

text_units.section: 2. Basic aggregation strategies: competition, cooperation, consensus
text_units.text:
A limitation of the Pandemonium approach (including deep learning) is that, whereas such
"competitions" can lead to learning predictions in a general way (for virtually any problem), the
relevance of the predictions to the underlying problem is hard or impossible to verify. As
Selfridge himself pointed out, Pandemonium assumes the "demons" were the correct ones, such
that the problem is already understood. To analogize to organizations, it assumes that the CEO
has the right goal in mind, and has hired all the right mid-level managers and low-level staff.

2.2 Cooperation: blackboard systems
Compare the competition-based way of aggregating predictions ("shouts") in Pandemonium to
our prior example in the course of Sudoku. To do so, imagine that we assigned each of the 27
explicit constraints in Sudoku (nine columns, nine rows, and nine 3x3's) to different "agents". In
Sudoku, these agents need not just "shout" predictions up some hierarchy: they can solve the
puzzle cooperatively by propagating information about their local constraints horizontally to any
agents with overlapping constraints. In the AI field, this idea of solving problems by aggregating
information across multiple experts horizontally is called a blackboard system, where the
shared information space is a blackboard (perhaps "whiteboard" would be more appropriate
today).

Unlike Selfridge's "demons" as simple feature detectors, we will call the agents in a blackboard
system as "knowledge sources", in that they are assumed to have some specialized knowledge
(knowledge of Sudoku constraints) and memory (representing results of prior moves). Decisions
in a blackboard system are inherently decentralized. Rather than a single "decision demon", as
in Pandemonium, the "central management's" role in blackboard systems is reduced to more of a
scheduler of the updates to the blackboard (roughly analogous to the role of an operating
system in your computer that controls when to execute applications). Likewise, in organizations,
groups of experts commonly solve problems cooperatively by processing information and
updating a shared space, such as engineering schematics or management dashboards.

A limitation of blackboard systems is that, whereas such "cooperation" can lead to rich
problem-solving, it assumes a single shared information space (i.e., a constraint network-like
structure such as a Sudoku puzzle). As we explored in the previous session's idea of a
dependency network, however, complex real-world problems often require essentially each
agent to maintain their own "blackboard". Hence, such cooperation may depend on richer
mechanisms (discussed in the next session) for managing a proliferation of such "blackboards".

2.3 Consensus: ensemble methods
A third strategy in AI, called ensemble methods, is based on aggregating predictions across
multiple agents, called "learners", to reach consensus on a decision. The collection of "learners"
is the ensemble. The fundamental difference from "demons" in Pandemonium or "knowledge
sources" in blackboard systems is that "learners" in an ensemble do not specialize in prediction
tasks. Rather, they are assumed to make predictions about tasks for which they may be close
to novices. That is, each learner is assumed to have limited data and processing capacity and a
relatively simple model for making predictions about novel and complex problems, and is
expected to make a poor prediction. The key insight of ensemble methods is that, by combining
these poor predictions in particular ways, the aggregate prediction can be remarkably good — in
fact, almost as good as would be achieved under a machine learning system that would require
vastly higher information processing capacity.

The intuition for this effect of ensembling comes from the idea of error cancellation from the
field of statistics. Error cancellation refers to how, given a bunch of poor predictions, it is likely
that the errors in these predictions will be both too high and too low. By using statistical
approaches to combining these errors (e.g., averaging them or using a majority "vote"), they will
"cancel out" one another and lead to an overall accurate prediction. In popular discourse, this
effect has come to be called the "wisdom of the crowd" effect (Surowiecki 2004). It was
famously described by the British polymath Francis Galton in 1907, who asked 788 villagers at a
rural market in England to guess the weight of an ox. He found that all the villagers guessed the
wrong weight yet when he averaged the 788 guesses, the collective guess was virtually the exact
weight of the ox — the "crowd" (ensemble) was intelligent even though no individual was.

Beyond guessing the weight of an ox, this "wisdom of the crowd" or error cancellation effect can
be seen in many real-world settings in AI and organizations. In organizations, a canonical
example are decision-making committees, such as for hiring applications or selecting projects
to invest in. Such committees are characterized by voting rules, such as "majority wins",
consensus, or hierarchy (most of the committee advises, but the committee head makes the final
call). Regardless, the rationale of using such committees is the same as the ox example — that by
combining the predictions of multiple members of the organization (e.g., about whether an
interviewee will make a good employee, or whether an investment will have a high enough
return), the organization is less likely to make bad decisions (either of not hiring or making
investments that it should have, or hiring or investing in projects that it may regret).

A limitation of ensemble methods is that they concern isolated, predefined decision-making tasks
(e.g., whether to hire a given candidate for a given job), rather than rich, open-ended
problem-solving. A further limitation is that, even given such a decision-making task, the
fundamental error cancellation effect only works given certain conditions. The learners' must be:
    (1) Independent: predictions are not influenced by other learners to avoid herding;
    (2) Diverse: "learners" have diverse backgrounds, hence predictions are not correlated;
    (3) better than random: while they need not be experts, the "learners" need to on
        average do at least a little better than random to induce error cancellation rather than just
        contributing noise.

text_units.section: 3. Beyond basic aggregation strategies: the fundamental aggregation problem and solution
text_units.text:
3. Beyond basic aggregation strategies: the fundamental aggregation problem and solution
The previous section illustrated some basic aggregation strategies. We saw how we can think of
aggregation based on competition, cooperation, or consensus, in which agents may specialize in
only simple tasks ("demons" in a pattern recognition system), have some deeper expertise
("knowledge sources" in a blackboard system), or be close to novices ("learners" in an
ensemble). Minsky's idea of learning in a society, however, implies that aggregation involves
more complex strategies. For example, as studied in our previous sessions, each agent may need
commonsense knowledge of the world (i.e., to address the frame problem), and must interact
with and reason about this world to "debug" their representations of problems. Hence, an AI
system or organization needs to account for agents who engage in such rich processes of
representation, reasoning, and interaction by aggregating inevitably messy and complex
information and knowledge. Minsky's student Carl Hewitt framed 2 principles of such deeper
aggregation strategies: the credit assignment problem as one of inconsistent information, and
the solution as organizing like a scientific community.

3.1 The aggregation problem: inconsistent information
For Hewitt, the "agents" involved in aggregation are better referred to as actors. By actors,
Hewitt sought to emphasize that intelligent aggregation requires autonomy at the
individual-level. Consider, as a canonical example in this AI research tradition, the autonomy of
biological cells in an organism. Cells are autonomous in the sense that each cell's membrane
encapsulates it from other cells to enable persisting as a self-sustaining living unit. Likewise, just
as the sustainability of the organism as a whole counterintuitively depends on the autonomy of
the cells, the intelligence of an AI system or organism depends on the autonomy of its "actors".
This assumption of autonomous actors leads, for Hewitt, to a general problem of credit
assignment. The problem is simply that autonomy, pretty much by definition, means that each
actor is able to process information in their own way and, thus, to assign credit in ways that
differ from other actors. Hence, it follows, information propagated through the network by actors
can be inconsistent.

By inconsistent, Hewitt meant three things. Firstly, actors may interpret their local situations
(i.e., constraints) in ways that differ qualitatively from others, such that they may have different
points of view even if they share goals. Hewitt emphasized, therefore, that aggregation strategies
should assume an open system, or one in which there may be diverse ontologies or other
representations that may contradict — be logically inconsistent with — one another. In contrast,
many AI ideas that we have studied in this course have at least implied what is called the
closed-world assumption, which is that an AI system or organization is fully characterized by a
consistent representation of the world (e.g., a single ontology or constraint network that everyone
agrees on). For example, the idea of the Turing machine is of a machine that supposedly can
execute any program, yet it is really a single agent — whatever program it executes has to
assume a logically-consistent representation of the world.

Second, actors may interpret the same information inconsistently due simply to having
contradictory goals. For example, in a business organization, there may be many departments,
each of which have their own information and goals. Imagine that quarterly sales data comes in
and shows a decrease in sales. The marketing department might interpret this data as a sign that
the organization should invest more in marketing to boost sales; the budgeting department might
instead see the decrease in sales as a sign that the business should cut costs. The CEO of the
business may hear the contradictory claims from both the marketing and budgeting departments
and realize that there is no decision that can make both departments happy. Consider, in contrast,
the Turing test, in which a human observer evaluates an AI system based on perceptions of
whether it can imitate a human's ability. In this test, the evaluation task is given — there is no
accounting for multiple goals and points of view. Hence, one colleague of Hewitt's at MIT, the
anthropologist Susan Leigh Star, proposed an alternative "Durkheim test" for AI systems,
named after the French founder of sociology Emile Durkheim, in which an AI system is instead
evaluated based on its "ability to meet… [the] goals" of a community of actors (artificial or
human), including its ability to reflect real-time modifications of these goals by the actors.
Intelligence, according to Star, is then a "direct measure of usefulness applied to the work of the
community; it's ability to change and adapt, and to encompass multiple points of view while
increasing communication across viewpoints or parts of an organization".

Third, for Hewitt, inconsistent information may arise in an AI system or organization simply
because the laws of physics mean that units of information (messages) are propagated from
different places and times such that no one actor can consider all the relevant information at
once. Actors can only interpret information about their local situations; even given vast channel
capacity in the Shannon information sense, physical distance means that there will always be a
lag in how messages propagate through the system. Hence, neither a hierarchy (as in Selfridge's
Pandemonium system) nor a single cooperative space (i.e., a blackboard system) will be
adequate — an AI system or organization must figure out how to coordinate how messages are
passed (i.e., how information is processed) based on an unpredictable order across space and
time.

text_units.section: 3.2 The aggregation solution: organize AI systems like scientific communities
text_units.text:
3.2 The aggregation solution: organize AI systems like scientific communities
Hewitt and his colleagues observed that, though inconsistent information is a fundamental
problem, we have an existence proof that it can be solved: human organizations. Human
organizations achieve things like making airplanes and coordinating complex office work based
on somehow enabling large numbers of human actors to process information that is often
inconsistent in all three ways highlighted in the previous subsection.

text_units.section: 3.2 The aggregation solution: organize AI systems like scientific communities
text_units.text:
Inspired by this existence proof, Hewitt framed the solution to aggregating information in AI
systems as fundamentally organizational. In particular, he proposed that a particular type of
organization — scientific communities — exemplified intelligent aggregation strategies.
Scientific communities process inconsistent information in the form of "conflicting theories"
made by scientists who bring diverse points of view. Remarkably, Hewitt noted, scientists are
often able to cooperate (e.g., advance the state-of-the-art of scientific knowledge in the
community) despite not fully knowing each other's work, using different variables and methods,
and having distinct goals and time horizons. How is such effective cooperation possible?

text_units.section: 3.2 The aggregation solution: organize AI systems like scientific communities
text_units.text:
Hewitt characterized information processing in scientific communities as based on the assertion
of viewpoints (theories, papers, arguments made in conferences) as the fundamental messages
that are passed. A scientist's goals are defined as a set of messages (viewpoints) that it is
interested in, which may be a combination of its own messages and those of others. For example,
a scientist reads papers that are found to be interesting, and vice versa. Sponsors are agents who
provide resources to scientists for sending messages. Resource control (e.g., professor
appointments, paper acceptances, grants) can be viewed as another type of communication.
Viewpoints are "relativized beliefs", which means that it is a way of classifying the same
message according to different assumptions, or authors, times and theories, hence allowing for
inconsistent information. Each message can be associated with one or more viewpoints. A
scientist can then watch for messages from certain viewpoints that it may find interesting. He
then identified several strategies in these communities for organizing the effective propagation of
information contained in these "viewpoints".

text_units.section: 3.2.1 Assigning credit based on due process
text_units.text:
3.2.1 Assigning credit based on due process
First, credit is assigned to a viewpoint (i.e., theory) based on following what is called in scientific
research "peer review", and which is a specific example of a general credit assignment strategy
called due process procedures. Peer review means that a theory (viewpoint) is evaluated by a
"jury" of scholars and "judged" by a journal editor. Both the authors and reviewers agree to
abide by the editor's decision on whether to accept the paper for publication. There is no
guarantee that the decision will be objectively correct (poor theories sometimes get published,
while good theories sometimes get rejected), but there is a guarantee that the paper will follow
this procedure — this procedural guarantee is what is called "due process". Hewitt has argued
that scientific communities are intelligent in that, over time, scientific communication based on
due process is self-correcting. He characterized this feature of scientific communities as
pluralism, or a "tolerance of this diversity", meaning that even wrong arguments that persist will
inevitably be corrected.

text_units.section: 3.2.1 Assigning credit based on due process
text_units.text:
Consider the more familiar use of the concept of due process in the legal system. In the legal
system, due process refers to standard procedures that ensure that "justice is served" when these
procedures are followed. For example, in a criminal case, due process might mean that the court
and legal system follow procedures such as having a jury decide on the verdict, and allowing the
defense and prosecution adequate time to communicate their evidence and points of view. The
key insight is that due process procedures enable a negotiation between the multiple agents of
the defense and prosecution. Negotiation means an information process where two sides have
fundamentally inconsistent goals and points of view, and will to some extent have to "agree to
disagree". In the legal system, the defense and prosecution do not agree on the facts of the case,
but both agree to accept the verdict of the jury.

text_units.section: 3.2.1 Assigning credit based on due process
text_units.text:
In the AI idea of aggregation, such negotiation refers generally to procedures for communication
among multiple actors. The key insight is that, given inconsistent goals, problems cannot be
solved by other credit assignment mechanisms (i.e., reinforcement or search) that imply
consistent information. Further, there can be no reasoning process shared by the multiple agents
that could fully, logically resolve disputes among their points of view. In AI, then, due process
concerns any procedures for communication to negotiate "differing viewpoints… in a fair and
flexible manner". The intuition is that, to pass the "Durkheim test" of robustly achieving
community goals, an AI system needs to be able to manage processes of negotiating goals and
problems among multiple actors.

text_units.section: 3.2.1 Assigning credit based on due process
text_units.text:
Due process activities are not about optimizing. One can think of a good solution to a problem
under due process as one in which the outcomes are satisfactory above some threshold to all
members involved. Further, when problem solving is distributed across multiple agents,
satisfactory solutions emerge when all members believe they have been given satisfactory
reasons for the decision, and that due process has been followed. The concern is with the
"reasonableness" of decisions. In due process, the key question in problem solving is "how can
the decision-making process be improved?" instead of the question, "what is the right
decision?".

3.2.2 Concurrency in propagating information
Another aspect of scientific communities highlighted by Hewitt is their concurrency, meaning
that messages (theories) can be sent and received simultaneously about many problems and
many agents from the environment. For example, if a scientist presents a theory at a conference,
the message is (potentially) disseminated to the attendees of the conference (who may or may not
attend the particular presentation). Alternatively, another scientist may receive the message by
reading about the theory in a journal at some later date — sometimes decades, or even centuries
later. This concurrency is fundamental to addressing the third aspect that was mentioned in the
previous subsection — that information processing in an open system is necessarily distributed
across space and time, such that coordination does not have a predefined order in the sense that
we saw in the earlier example from our course of a pin factory where all tasks are well-defined
and sequenced.

Concurrency implies that aggregation in the sense of propagating rich information across actors
needs to be opportunistic, rather than intricately planned. Hewitt's insight in this respect is that
the key aggregation mechanisms concern protocols — basic rules or procedures for what to do
when a new message is propagated — for when to send, receive, and process messages. Note
that such protocols arise whenever concurrency is an issue, even given vast channel capacity, it is
the order of message processing that is complex. He noted that scientific communities have
protocols that correspond to the following basic rules for concurrent information processing:

- (1) Monotonicity: In AI, monotonicity refers to systems in which information only
  increases (literally, mono means "one" and tone means "step", so every new step (e.g.
  message that is passed) adds one more unit of information, and does not decrease
  information. In a scientific community, monotonicity means that, once a message (e.g.,
  viewpoint) is disseminated, it cannot be erased. This is the essence of a scientific
  publication system. If a scientist wishes to revise some theory that is published, the
  scientist can publish a new theory, but not eliminate the old one. Even a retracted paper
  (e.g., where there is faulty data) is maintained in the publication register as "retracted",
  rather than simply deleted.

- (2) Commutativity: This refers to the property that messages can be sent or received in
  any order. A scientist simply receives messages (viewpoints) in its interest set, regardless
  of whether some other message was sent before or after. For example, a scientist can look
  up theories in old journals, and also look up new articles in the middle of one's work.
  Thus, unlike the pin factory, there is no predefined sequence for propagating information
  across actors to solve problems.

- (3) Parallelism: This refers to how concurrent sending and receiving of messages among
  multiple scientists is possible.

- (4) Pluralism: This refers to how competing hypotheses are okay: a scientific community
  tolerates diversity based on due process (i.e., peer review), in which scientists may agree
  to disagree, or consensus about a theory is delayed until further evidence appears.

4. Approaches to aggregating information
Compared to the basic strategies that we discussed in the prior subsection (pattern recognition,
blackboard systems, and ensemble methods), the previous section illustrated how aggregation
more fundamentally requires sophisticated procedures and protocols to propagate inconsistent
information across a network of diverse agents or "actors". The overall claims here are, in the
emerging AI discourse of today, fairly uncontroversial. In recent years, the AI field has become
increasingly about "managing" large, diverse systems of agents, as distinct from perfecting
specific algorithms. Nonetheless, as we have explored in our previous sessions, paradigmatic
differences persist in the approaches to aggregation in the AI field. Next, we compare
currently-popular machine learning approaches with Hewitt's formalization of his ideas that he
called the Actor model.

4.1 Machine learning approaches to aggregation
Beginning in the 1970s, Geoff Hinton and his colleagues developed deep learning as a strategy
for generalizing Selfridge's Pandemonium system for pattern recognition to any problem. The
strategy was to consider demons at a much more fine-grained level: rather than specialize in, for
example, recognizing a whole letter of the alphabet, they could be trained on the simplest
possible patterns of bitstrings, such as pixels in an image. The goal could simply be to recognize
any such patterns, without having to be "supervised" to learn to recognize some predefined
pattern (e.g., the letter "A").

Hinton's key insight was that, by learning to recognize basic patterns in bitstrings in such an
"unsupervised" fashion, a system could simply learn regularities in the world. He called this
approach "procrastination", in that the system could spend some time simply learning about the
general patterns in the world — what is now called "representation learning" — without
initially trying to recognize patterns about predefined problems. Rather than define a hierarchy
of operations, middle managers, and executives as in Selfridge's Pandemonium, general patterns
in the world could be used to aggregate information about any problem efficiently and effectively.

In Hinton's parlance, the "middle management" aspect of aggregation for a specific problem just
became "hidden units", meaning that they could just be inferred from learning of bit strings
patterns in general. For example, recognizing the letter "A" could be informed by a general
recognition of curves and lines in pixelated images of text. Further, aggregating patterns
recognized by large numbers of such simple demons could be done efficiently, it was
subsequently found, just by decomposing them into basic layers of abstraction (i.e., elementary
bit strings → more compound bit strings, and so forth) rather than a hierarchy designed for a
specific problem. (the "deep" in deep learning refers to the use of a large number of these layers
to simplify the aggregation of information).

In current AI systems, Hinton's core idea has been implemented using two complementary
aggregation strategies. First, deep learning systems have been developed into generative AI
models that enable learning general patterns from simple units in various types of data such as
text, software code, and images. You can think of this as a strategy for aggregating information
to generate a sort of commonsense knowledge (in a Shannon information sense). Second, on top
of these systems, have been developed into what are often called systems of AI agents. These
agents are in some sense closer to Selfridge's "demons" rather than a scientific community per
se, in that they are usually quite simple. Most commonly, they resemble simple software
functions, whose actions are controlled based on reinforcement learning or similar
mechanisms.

4.2 Hewitt's Actor model
Hewitt proposed that such machine learning approaches can be useful, but are ultimately
inadequate as solutions to the fundamental aggregation problem that we discussed in the
previous section of inconsistent information. In his view, intelligent aggregation depends on
assigning credit based on due process procedures (as noted in the previous section), where an
essential part of due process is that actors also have their own procedures to reason carefully
about and evaluate information. Consider: peer review in scientific communities really assumes
that the reviewers are other scientists who, while having different points of view, can all do basic
scientific reasoning. Due process in the court of law implies that a judge has the ability to reason
about the law. Likewise, Hewitt emphasized that in any AI system or organization, such due
process implies that the actors (whether human or artificial) are able not just to extract patterns in
bit strings, but have procedures for carefully reasoning about meaningful information.

One approach, of course, would be simply to design a deep learning system that learns such
reasoning procedures indirectly, based on extracting so many general and simple patterns about
the world that the system gains a sort of common sense. Recent techniques, such as the
chain-of-thought prompting of an LLM to coax it to "think" in step-by-step terms, might also
enable something resembling such reasoning. Yet recall from some of our previous sessions (e.g.,
on knowledge representation and reasoning (Session 6), and reasoning about the physical world
(Session 8)) that, to reason about complex problems, AI systems really need to engage in
complex processes such as addressing the frame problem and debugging representations of
problems based on interacting with the world. Such processes are further complicated by, as
pointed out earlier in this session, how information that is propagated across diverse actors is
inevitably inconsistent and may arrive in an unpredictable order.

Instead of machine learning approaches, Hewitt instead proposed a formalism that he called the
Actor model as a simple model of aggregating information in any AI system or organization.
You can think of the Actor model as a general model of computation, like our earlier example of
the Turing machine, but focused on aggregating (i.e., propagating) information across multiple
actors rather than a single agent. Let us focus on three aspects of the Actor model to understand
how it works, and distinguish it from machine learning approaches.

First, the Actor model assumes that each actor may make use of a variety of procedures for
reasoning about (i.e., inferring) information that is propagated. Such procedures could include
deep learning-style pattern recognition, but only as a specific case. Procedures refer to rules
about which knowledge to use to reason about information that matched certain patterns, or what
Hewitt called the "procedural embedding of knowledge". Put another way, knowledge is not just
facts or assertions stored in a knowledge base, but it is attached to procedures for when and how
to use it (i.e., for which patterns of information). Hence, the actors do not just have ordinary
software functions (as is typically in machine learning-style AI agents), but have programs that
operate on sophisticated procedures for representing and reasoning about knowledge. Hewitt
called this paradigm pattern-directed inference, and you can contrast this with the pattern
recognition-focused proposals from deep learning. This is based on pattern matching of
variables, not values, (the latter is handled by constraints). The reason is that we want the
procedures still to be spare and to be as declarative as possible: the constraints handle the value
satisfactions. What we want is to do basic unification (where a set of values could exist, such that
the constraints and assertions are probably at least relevant) to kickstart the propagation and
reasoning processes.

Second, each actor maintains its own state (akin to truth maintenance), but there is no global
state among all the actors due to the need for concurrency (since messages are passed in
unpredictable order). Instead of representing the state of a problem, aggregation in the Actor
model is based on representations of events: partial orderings of message passing instances.
Hence, rather than some transition from an initial state to a goal state, the Actor model is based
on the open-ended unfolding of events among the actors, much like the ongoing, never
fully-resolved process of developing scientific ideas. More generally, this event-based view is
akin to views of organizations as "going-concerns", meaning that they are in continual
problem-solving processes for interpreting the world, and not just for pin factory-like discrete
problem-solving sequences.

Here, the goal state is more homeostatic and infrastructural. What homeostasis concerns is
maintaining the ability of actors to freely send and receive messages — i.e., to maintain a
healthy peer review system in a scientific community. Hewitt proposed that the use of rich and
diverse procedural knowledge within actors could be maintained by imposing only a minimal,
yet fundamental, set of procedures for controlling the propagation of information across actors.
He reduced his definition of actors in this model to just three basic actions: (1) Processing
information (getting things done). (2) storing information (remembering things), and (3)
propagating information (sending and receiving information from other actors). He further
highlighted three fundamental propagation actions that actors can take: (1) sending messages to
anyone; (2) creating new actors; (3) deciding what to do with the next message that it receives.

He called this homeostatic goal as "pure messaging". In "pure messaging", once an actor sends
a message, that message is secure, and it means that each actor can do its own computing or
information processing, without being subject to any communication channels. The classic
example is email. Compare, for example, the aggregation structure for an organization's internal
email system versus its hierarchies or networks of roles or departments. In a strict hierarchy,
messages are passed primarily only up and down the chain of command. In an email system,
however, technically the only restriction is that an agent has an email address. Any agent can
email any other agent with an email address. This communication structure clearly scales much
more easily than a hierarchy: one can just design a system that allows people to create an email
address and send and receive messages, without worrying about the precise channels for
communicating.
